In Cartersville new manufacturing enterprises are exempted from city taxation for five years.

Tallapoosa has a well possessing to a very large extent the mineral properties of iron and sulphur.

Snow in North Georgia and sunshine and flowers in the Southern tier is what travelers found last week.

A new railroad and college makes Monticello feel as if she had been touched by the gold-lined hand of prosperity.

J. W. Mann and family have left Perry for Milledgeville, where he will become proprietor of the Oconce House.

A negro girl named Lucy, who has been nursing for G. A. Hall, of Greensboro, was severely burned Wednesday. She may recover.

William W. Fleming, Sr., proprietor of the Blakely News, died a day or two ago. His son succeeds him in conducting the paper.

The mining business around Cartersville is being carried on to a considerable extent. But it is nothing to what it will be when furnaces are built.

Haile's Pottery, located six miles west of Gainesville, bids fair to grow into a paying business at once, as soon as he gets his firing furnace completed.

It is Campbell county's time to select a State Senator for the Senatorial disrict in which it is located, and the name of Hon. Levi Ballard is prominently mentioned.

R. S. Cook, of New York city, for himself and associates, effected a lease last Monday of the Satterfield ore banks near Cartersville, and will at an early day begin operating them.

There will be about 150 acres devoted to the cultivation of watermelons near Perry this year. In 1883 there were 515 acres planted in watermelons within that immediate vicinity.

There was a difficulty in the coach on the Gainesville, Jefferson and Southern a few days ago, in which a jug, a stove-pipe and a few citizens took part. No damage is reported except to the jug.

J. F. Rushin, of Buenavista, has a silver sugar ladle which he says is 150 years old. He received it as an heirloom from his grandfather's estate, and says it has been in the family for several generations.

A special train passed through Atlanta Friday night on its way from Philadelphia to New Orleans, having on board the Volunteer Fire Association of that city. The association was accompanied by its apparatus.

The Athens Banner-Watchman staff has been increased by the addition of a canary bird which entertains the callers while the editor works. Editor Dana's cat would not be allowed in the office under any circumstances.

At Augusta Friday Spencer Jones, a negro employed in felling trees at the exposition grounds, was caught under a falling tree and dangerously injured. His skull was fractured, and he is in a precarious condition.

At Brunswick the license account for 1888 is looming up handsomely. The receipts for February are $9,052—just $3,550 more than the corresponding month of last year. The entire receipts from this source for 1887 were $11,090.

Capt. J. G. Davis, of Perry, has a claim case now pending before Congress for $12.150. The claim is for cotton seized by United States officers in 1865, on the Hog Crawl plantation in the southwestern portion of Houston county.

A horrible tale of debauchery and crime comes from Bluffton in which a white woman and a negro were concerned. The negro, Aaron Dickey, was terribly whipped by the indignant people of the community and afterward died from the effects of the whipping.

At Dawson an old negro, Jim Spence, while driving home a six-mule team on Saturday last, was thrown from his mule and had one of his legs run over by the wagon, which was loaded with guano. His leg was so badly crushed as to necessitate amputation.

A negro house on the plantation of M.W. Champion, near Smyrna, caught fire a day or two ago and, with its contents, was entirely destroyed. In the house at the time of the fire were two small children. They were also burned, all efforts to save them being futile.

Reid's plantation, near Madison, a few days ago. The boy knocking down stalks in the next row let the stick he was wielding slip out of his hand, and, striking his companion, killed him.

There is now standing on the place of Capt. J. D Wilson, at Pineville a one room log house around which cluster some historical reminiscences. It is the house that was occupied by Mr. Temple, the first representative of Marion county after its formation in 1827.

At Byron last Saturday evening S. C. Norris was thrown from his engine by receiving a severe blow on his head from a scaffold that was located near the railroad track. It was thought at first that the wound would prove fatal, but after a careful examination he was pronounced seriously but not fatally injured.

The Blue Ridge mountains, though thirty miles distant, are plainly visible at Gainesville, and now that they are covered with snow, present an appearance grand beyond description. Blood mountain, the highest peak of this range in Georgia, towers above all the others, and looks like an immense marble statue erected by the hand of nature.

Joseph Dicken, of Watkinsville, was in Athens on Saturday and drank some very sour cider, after which he took a small drink of the ardent, such as is made nowadays, and the mercury in the whisky coming in contact with the sour cider formed a corrosive in his stomach, which is a deadly poison. After several hours of hard work the doctor got him relieved, and at last accounts he was doing well.

On Tuesday evening Deputy Collector and Deputy Marshal B. P. Thompson captured a still in Butts county belonging to Bud Harris and Ben Gray. The latter was arrested and taken from Hampton Depot to Macon and tried before Judge Erwin, and in default of bond was committed to Bibb county jail. Harris made good his escape. Several shots were fired at him, none of which is known to have taken effect. The only thing Harris left was his hat and breakfast.

Vigilantes Mete Out Terrible Punishment to a Colored Man.
Vigilantes Mete Out Terrible Punishment to a Colored Man.

CUTPERT, GA., March 5.—A shocking story of debauchery and the execution of popular vengeance comes from Bluffton. It seems that a white woman, whose name is not given, had become intimate with Aaron Dickey, a colored man, well known as a desperado. It had for some time been suspected that their relations were of a criminal character. A party of young men decided to make watch, and, seeing the colored man enter the woman's house, waited until night, when they broke in and found the couple as suspected. Dickey stoutly resisted the effort to handle him, but the young men pressed close around him and soon bound him. They took him out to a tree, to which they tied him, after baring his back. With stout twigs the men welted Dickey's back until the blood came. From cursing the man turned to pleading for mercy, but all to no purpose, as the vigilantes freely told him he would not live to see daylight. When one detail would weary in the work of lashing it would be relieved by another. As day began to dawn the men disappeared, but Dickey died from the thrashing which he had received.

COPIES OF THE CORRESPONDENCE MADE PUBLIC.
Secretary Bayard's Proposals—His Praise for the Treaty—Progress of the Negotiations—Words of Commendation from Members of the Commission.

WASHINGTON, March 6.—The senate at 6 o'clock last evening released all the papers submitted yesterday by the president in relation to the fishery treaty between Canada and the United States. The letter of Secretary Bayard transmitting the documents to the president is dated yesterday, and states that the accompanying papers embrace all the correspondence that has taken place between the state department and the British government since November, 1886, to the present time; also, the protocols of the conferrees preceding the conclusion of the treaty.

It is highly important, the secretary says, that the entire history of the case should be brought to the knowledge of the people of the United States as soon as possible; that its inspection will serve to demonstrate the practical and important results accomplished by the treaty, by which the interpretation and administration of the treaty of 1818 is transferred and elevated from the obscurity into which it had been suffered to lapse since the date of that convention and its restoration from the practical control of minor and local officials of the Canadian maritime provinces.

After referring to the vexatious course pursued by Canada toward America fishermen throughout all the years, the secretary concludes: "It is believed that a remedy is practically and fully supplied by the treaty now pending, and that by its terms now, and for the first time since 1818, a just and joint agreement is agreed to by our governors.

which will secure just and hospitable treatment to the United States fishermen, and secure to them unmolested the full measure of their rights, and that under the proposed arrangement every American fisherman pursuing his vocation in the waters adjacent to British North America can acquire a clear understanding of his right and duties while within the jurisdictional waters of Canada and Newfoundland; and that he may resort to such ports or harbors as casualty, necessity or convenience may suggest without fear of encountering such harsh and unfriendly treatment as he was heretofore subjected to, under uncertain, unwarranted and variant interpretation of his treaty rights."

The first inclosure is a letter from Mr. Bayard to Sir Charles Tupper, marked "Personal and unofficial," dated May 31, 1887. He refers to the awkwardness of conducting negotiations with Canada through Great Britain, and says:

"The immediate difficulty to be settled is found in the treaty of 1818 between the United States and Great Britain, which has been questio vexata ever since it was concluded, and to-day is suffered to interfere with and seriously embarrass the good understanding of both countries in the important commercial relations and interests which have come into being since its ratification, and for the adjustment of which it is wholly inadequate, as has been unhappily proved by the events of the past two years."

He proposes negotiations and suggests that Newfoundland should be represented, concluding as follows:

"I am prepared, therefore, to meet the authorized agents of Great Britain at this capital at the earliest possible day, and enter upon negotiations for a settlement of all differences."

Sir Charles Tupper replies under date of June —, received June 10, that he is entirely favorable to Secretary Bayard's proposition.

The largest inclosure consists of about 125 printed pages from the forthcoming volume of "Foreign Relations" correspondence, bringing the formal correspondence between the two governments down to the beginning of the negotiations at Washington.

These negotiations go back to the year 1886. In one letter Mr. Bayard says that his representations, candidly and fully made, have not produced the result of checking the unwarranted interference (frequently accompanied by rudeness and an unnecessary demonstration of force) with the rights of our fishermen.

The protocols of the conferences of the negotiators are thirty in number. In the first protocol the full powers of the plenipotentiaries are exhibited and found to be in good and due form.

The remaining protocols up to the last are merely formal, being an approval of the previous protocol and a statement that "after discussion of questions before the conference it was adjourned."

The last protocol, dated Feb. 15, 1888, states that after the signing of the treaty Mr. Bayard said that he wished to express his gratification at what had been accomplished. He hoped and believed the conference had laid the basis upon which Canada and the United States could look forward to a period of enlarged intercourse and increasingly friendly relations.

Mr. Chamberlain said that in behalf of the British plenipotentiaries he desired at the conclusion of the lengthened deliberations of the conference to acknowledge the uniform courtesy of their American colleagues. The same spirit had animated all who had been engaged in this work, and he hoped and believed had contributed to a joint and honorable settlement of a long pending controversy which has more than once threatened the friendly relations of the United States and Great Britain.

Sir Charles Tupper hoped that the treaty would remove all causes of irritation between Great Britain and the United States and conduce to the continuance of those intimate commercial relations which had so long existed between Canada and the United States, with marked advantage to both countries. He sincerely hoped that the settlement at which the conference had arrived would be accepted by the people on both sides of the boundary line as an equitable and honorable arrangement.

The conference then finally adjourned.

The first day (12 hours) of the 72 hour walking match closed with the following score: Cartwright, 84 miles 2 haps; Guerrero, 82; Hegleman, 79; Connors, 77.6; Day, 71.7; Taylor, 66.6; Collins, 63; Foster, 60; Quinn, 57; Bennett, 55; Cunningham, 54.7; Sullivan, 53.3; Cotter, 53; Murray, 52.2; Edwards, 51.1. Coal Trade Demoralized.

PITTSBURG, March 6. The railroad coal trade is in a worse condition than for a year past. There are practically no shipments to Chicago, while to the east the trade is very light. Nearly all the mines on the Baltimore and Ohio road have been closed. Many of the miners are in destitute circumstances.

Troy, N. Y., March 6.—The jury in the case of James Brown, accused of killing Jatrick Kelly, brought in a verdict yesterday of manslaughter in the first degree. Sentence will be pronounced to-morrow morning.

THE MURDER OF A STOCKMAN FOLLOWED BY THE LYNCHING OF TWO QF HIS SUPPOSED ASSASSINS.
CHICAGO, Nov. 19.—A dispatch from Little Rock, Ark., says: A stockman named William Durant was brutally murdered at his home near Tushomma, I.T., Friday night last. He was called from the house by a party of men who shot him in the yard, riddling his body with bullets. Durant had been quarrelling with two neighbors, Davis and Jeffries. His assassination aroused his friends, who, arming themselves, hunted and killed Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis, who were suspected of having led the party that murdered Durant.

NEWS IN SHORT ORDER.
DOMESTIC HAPPENINGS TOLD
IN A FEW BRIEF WORDS.
Interesting Paragraphs Condensed from Many Redundant Columns.
John Keeland was run over by a Boston & Maine Railroad train, at Lawrence, Mass., and killed.

A stone was thrown through the window of Simon Lewis, a pawnbroker in Boston, and immediately a man from outside reached through the hole thus made and grasped a tray containing the diamond rings. In his flight the thief dropped all but two of the rings. Those which he dropped have been recovered.

The Interstate Oklahoma Convention, held in Wichita, Kans., was the largest demonstration ever known in the West for the purpose of securing the opening of the Territory, 3,000 delegates being present.

A wreck occurred on the Bloomsburg and Sullivan Railroad near Bloomsburg, Pa. A passenger car jumped the track and rolled over, going down an embaakment of several feet. No one was seriously injured.

The annual convention of the League of Base Ball Clubs is being held in New York. The championship was formally awarded to New York. Cleveland was admitted to the League to take the place of Detroit.

A costly wreck occurred on the Union Pacific at Rock Creek station, Wyo. A work train returning to Laramie collided with a freight train pulled by two engines. An engineer and a fireman were fatally injured, and ten or twelve laborers on the work train slightly hurt. The three engines were demolished. The wreck completely blocked travel.

The Harrison accommodation of the Cincinnati, Indianapolis, St. Louis, and Chicago road was turning a curve near Cincinnati when an outer rail broke, overturning five cars in the old canal bed. The rear car had a fire in it, and the wreck caught fire. The engine ran back and soon put out the flames. There were about forty passengers aboard, nearly all of whom were injured.

George H. Fobel, a forty-year-old Chicago broker, shot and killed himself at his residence. No reason is assigned for the act.

John Armstrong, an engineer in the Grape Creek mines, near Danville, Fla., and his wife had a quarrel. Joseph Glascow, a boarder at the house, undertook to interfere, when Armstrong drew a revolver and shot him through the heart. Armstrong took to
his wife had a quarrel. Joseph Glascow, a boarder at the house, undertook to interfere, when Armstrong drew a revolver and shot him through the heart. Armstrong took to the woods, and officers are now in pursuit.

William Hawk was arrested at Hutchinson, Kans., for moonshining within a stone's throw of the City Marshal's residence. Hawk had an old thrashing machine engine, which he kept fired up all the time, and he was supposed to be making a chop mixture for feeding hogs. This he had kept up for nearly a year until it was discovered that he was making a poor grade of whiskey. He was sent to jail.

Mrs. John Broadman, of Sundusky, O., left her two children alone in the house while she went out in the yard to milk the cow. While gone, the children, who were playing near the grate, were burned to death, their clothing catching fire.

While an experiment with a patent process for using oil as fuel was being made at the Beaver Falls (Pa.) Iron Works, the oil tank exploded, terribly burning six men. The inventor, Richard Vaughn, is reported fatally injured. The mill was ablaze immediately, and was damaged by fire and water about $20,000.

It is reported at Ottawa that a full measure of responsible government in the Northwest will be granted next year.

G.W. Leeser, of Pottsville, O., who has been at the Cincinnati Exposition received $3,000 in money. He carried it on his person, and during the night exhibited it at a drinking-place. Some time after midnight as he was going home he was sandbagged and robbed of $2,500.

Mrs. Anthony Newell, of Pittsburgh, Pa., committed suicide by shooting herself through the heart. Despondency over the death of her husband, and fear that the estate was heavily involved are the causes assigned for the need.

Judge Blodgett, in Cincago, denied the petition of the American Cushman Telephone Company for a re-hearing of its case against the American Bell Telephone Company. The case will now go to the United States Supreme Court on appeal.

The head of the match fell off and set fire to her clothing. She ran down stairs enveloped in flames. Her father and son tried to smother the flames, and both were badly burned. Another son threw water over them and quenched the flames. Mrs. Fitzpatrick and her father were fatally burned.

—Two inches of snow fell in Cumberland, Md.

—At Greene, N. Y., George F. Matthews, while temporarily insane, committed suicide by cutting his throat with a razor. He was a native of Savannah, Ga., and was 48 years old.

—The schooner Nautilus, of and from Rockland for New York, with 1,700 barrels of lime, took fire off Thatcher's Island and was beached. Her cargo will be a total loss, but it is probable that the vessel will be saved.

—S. R. W. Heath, of New York, for many years Chairman of the Finance Committee of the Trustees of Rutger's College, has resigned on account of ill health. He has given the college $10,000 toward the endowment fund.

—The public school building of Carrollton, Ill., was burned. Loss, $50,000.

—The first heavy snow in Indiana, Illinois, and Michigan of the season has fallen.

—Major Henry J. Farnsworth, Assistant Inspector General United States Army, died at Fortress Monroe, where he had gone for his health.

—Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis, of Little Rock, Ark., were murdered by friends of William Durant, who suspected them of having killed Durant.

—The last of the mackerel fleet arrived in Gloucester, Mass. The catch was 22,000 barrels, the smallest known for fifty years. The catch last year amounted to 44,000 barrels. The result of the light catch will be shown in the increased prices during the season.

—Pilot Evans and his boat's crew of four men were drowned off the bar at Nassau, N. P., by the capsizing of their boat during a squall. They were attempting to speak the steamer Clem fuegos, from New York.

—First Mate G. G. Tibbetts of the schooner W. Jewett, of Portland, Me., and a Swedish sailor, were drowned at Cambridge, Md., by the sinking of a small boat.

—Alabama is proving a profitable field for the Mormon missionary just now. Thirty converts in charge of a Mormon elder passed through Montgomery the other day, all coming from that neighborhood. Most of them were women, all ticketed for Utah. A carload went from North Alabama a few days before.

A San Francisco despatch says that fears are entertained that the whaling bark Ohio was lost on October 3, off Cape Lisburne, while preparing to start on her homeward voyage. She had thirty-two hands aboard. Steps are already being taken to have the government send out a relief ship.

Three Danes and an American went out rowing in a small boat on Jamaica Bay, Long Island. When but a short distance from the shore the boat sank, and as none of the men could swim they went down with it.

A special from Summerfield, Ala., says the family of William Morgan, a farmer, were poisoned, and all are very sick. Some of them may die. They ate food for dinner prepared by a negro servant, and immediately all fell ill. The food has not yet been analyzed. The negro was arrested and confessed.

A fire in Pocomoke City, Md., destroyed the entire business portion of the town, only two stores remaining. Loss estimated at $500,000.

Another Fight Between Whites and Negroes in Louisiana.
St. MARTINSVILLE, La., Aug. 24. An encounter between negroes and whites occurred on Thursday afternoon in Bayon Martin, nine miles from St. Martinsville. The whites had learned that the negroes were arming themselves with rifles, which had been secreted in the house of a negro named Albert Narcisse. About 250 whites surprised Narcisse and his brother walking in a field. The two negroes ran to the house and attempted to baricade it. They were fired upon and comptlled to surrender, after Narcisse and a 10-year-old boy had been shot. Thirty guns, all new and heavily loaded with buckshot, were found in the cabin. It is not known what was done with the two men captured. Trouble between the whites and blacks is also feared above Breaux Bridge, as the whites have called upon the negroes to surrender their arms. They probably will not comply with the demand.

A Wharf Falls with 300 Persons on It.

WILMINGTON, Del., Aug. 24.—As the steamer Wilmington, from this city, with an excursion party on board, was about making a landing at Newcastle at 8 o'clock tonight, the whole wharf went down with a crash, carrying three hundred people with it. The scene that followed was indescribable. The crowd shrieked and fought its way back. Just at the edge of the water the front of the wharf caught on a piece of piling, which kept the struggling mass from pitching into the water. No one was even wet, but many fainted, and several women were badly bruised in the mad rush for safety.

BROOKLYN.

The Rev. John Conway, the Rev. James H. Barden, the Rev. John H. Kenny, and the Rev. Francis McCarty were ordained priests yesterday in St. James's Cathedral. The services were conducted by Bishop Loughlin.

Joseph Capevitz, an Italian rapgieker of 66 Adams street, called at a saloon in Pearl and Water streets yesterday and tendered a counterfeit $5 bill in payment for a pint of beer. Mr. Nagel, the proprietor, refused the bill, and when the Italian started to run he drew a revolver and covered him with the weapon until the arrival of a policeman, who placed him under arrest. The prisoner is supposed to be connected with the gang of Italian counterfeiters arrested in this city on Wednesday night.

NEW JERSEY.

Caroline Beekman, tall and good looking, who lived with her parents on the Hackensack plank road, near Homestead Station, has been missing from her home since Tuesday last. She was employed in Givernaud's silk mill. She had no money when she left home. Her parents say she had no reason for going away, and think that she may perhaps have been abducted.

The Commissioners in Chancery who have been investigating the charge of habitual drunkenness made against Sebastian Ball, a wealthy resident of Union Hill, by his son-in-law, decided yesterday that Ball was unit to take care of his property and should be put in an inebriate asylum. Chancellor McGill will appoint a guardian for him. Ball is one of the best known men in Hudson county, and is something of a politician.

Edward Bogart, aged 23, of 154 Bloomfield street, Hoboken, a lamp trimmer in the employ of the Hudson Electric Light Company, forgot to turn off the current before he attempted to adjust a carbon light at Willow and First streets on Thursday night, and received a shock. In falling to the ground he was heard to exclaim: "My God, I'm killed." When picked up a moment afterward he was dead. It is said the fall did not kill him, and that he must have died of an after effect of the shook.

JACKSONVILLE, Aug. 25.—There were 14 new cases of yellow fever reported during the 24 hours ending at 6 o'clock last evening.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 25.—[Special.]—Dr. Hamilton has just returned from Florida and reports a satisfactory condition of affairs, all things being considered.

CINCINNATI, Aug. 23.—[Special.]—At the Republican Congressional convention held here today, Butterworth was renominated, but Brown was defeated by Judge Caldwell.

SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 23.—[Special.]—The latest estimate on the loss of life in the latest between the steamers Oceanic and Chester yesterday, places the number at thirteen.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 25.—[Special.]—A fire in the waste paper room of the post office department here did very little damage but caused a big scare, almost a panic, among the employes.

NEW YORK, August 23.—[Special.]—The report that Robert Garrett's case is hopeless by attending physicians, and that he has been taken to Bloomingdale asylum, has the air of truth, but is not officially confirmed.

LEETONIA, O., Aug. 23.—[Special.]—The report that Chas. N. Schmick, a leading Democrat of Columbia county had flopped to Harrison, is pronounced by that gentleman "a lie out of the whole cloth." He is enthusiastically for Cleveland and Thurman.

PORT HURON, Mich., Aug. 24.—[Special.]—The Chicago escort for Thurman arrived early this morning and took charge of the party. A very handsome procession escorted the Judge to the train. His two sons, Allen and Lee, and Dr. Swartz have joined the party.

NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 24.—[Special.]—A crowd of negroes at Martins Bayou, secretly armed themselves. The whites Tuesday learned of the fact, seized the guns in a struggle, in which Albert Narcisse and his son, in whose house the guns were concealed, were fatally shot.
CHICAGO, Aug. 23.—[Special.]—Last night Augusta Frederich's lover called on her. The family objected and a quarrel ensued. "I can't stand this, said she, and walked into an adjoining room, took a dose of poison, and died shortly thereafter. The family are in a terrible state of grief.

CHICAGO, Aug. 23.—[Special.]—E. A. Gardner, opium smuggler, under arrest here, proves to be the late Chief Inspector of customs at Seattle, W.T. He left there two months ago. It is claimed this is proof that the former assertions that the whole government force there is engaged in smuggling is true.

NEW YORK, August 23.—[Special.]—The news of the nomination of ex-Secretary of War Goff as Republican candidate for Governor of West Virginia is taken as an indication that the Republicans have finally determined to make a struggle for the state. Goff is their most popular man and has several times been elected to Congress from the Wheeling district.

BOSTON, Aug. 23.—[Special.]—There are symptoms that the State insurance board are working at several leads that promise great sensations of astounding magnitude. It has been quietly asserted for sometime that several of the largest companies were as crooked in their transactions as a "fabled ram's horn." Considerable uneasiness is manifested in those circles, which gives color to the revelations expected.

WASHINGTON, August 24.—[Special.]—The President's message was read in the Senate to-day. It was listened to with much interest. Senator Sherman moved its reference to the Committee on Foreign Relations. Senator Edmunds took the floor and said he honored the President for his pa riotic words, but could not understand why a President who has had full power for eighteen months past should delay so long doing what has just been done.

CHICAGO, Aug. 25.—[Special.]—Judge Chicago's right hand was so occupied this morning that it gave out and he was compelled to use the left. The route to Cheltenham Beach, twelve miles distant, where he speaks this afternoon, was lined almost the entire distance by a wildly enthusiastic throng. The air was full of cheers for the "Old Roman." Fully fifty thousand people are in attendance at the meeting, and the greatest enthusiasm prevails.

CHICAGO, Aug. 25.—[Special.]—Great crowds forced Judge Thurman to rise early this morning, he being unable to sleep from the hurrahing and enthusiasm that prevailed. The city is crowded with strangers and each incoming train ados to the number. The visiting clubs are marching and countermarching through the city waiving red bandanas and shouting for Cleveland and Thurman. The excitement is far greater than at the recent Republican convention. Business is almost entirely suspended.

NEW YORK, Aug. 23.—[Special.]—The quarrel in the Republican National Committee over Blaine, grows gradually more bitter, and an open rupture is expected. Quay and his friends are still determined that Blaine shall discuss only such questions as the committee select or leave the stump. The Plumed Knight's friends are equally determined that their man shall remain the star of the campaign, and Blaine himself shows a disposition to run things after his own ideas, regardless of the committee's wishes. There is fun on ahead. Considerable comment has been created by the disclosures made, and it begins to become more and more apparent that Harrison will be but a figure in the campaign.

AGENTS' NOTICE.

Those agents of THE GAZETTE indebted for copies of this paper, will not be mailed any more copies of this paper until they have paid for those already sent them. We are endeavoring to close all accounts and start this our sixth year square with all of our agents. Those who fail to make satisfactory settlements of their accounts by October 1, will have the satisfaction (?) of seeing them published in THE GAZETTE. A copy of this issue, with this notice marked, will be mailed each delinquent agent, and we hope every one will respond promptly, as honest and busines-like men and women should.

OUR ESTEEMED contemporary, the Grip, passed into its third year recently. Editor Doty has reason to feel proud of his newspaper, for it is one of Cleveland's best weeklies. The Grip has our best wishes for future success.

PERHAPS IT IS NOT generally known that the Representatives in the General Assembly of the State, in making an appropriation to establish a Normal and Industrial School at Wilberforce University, are each entitled to send one colored student to that school with free tuition. Young colored men who desire to enter this fall had better call on their Representatives and interview them as to the matter, or write to the authorities concerning it. They are making preparation now to begin active operations this fall, and our young men can't be too active in this line.

Again the Negroes are in trouble at the hands of the Democrats. A suspicion that the colored people were preparing to protect themselves against Democratic outrages was the cause of the rebel alarm. LAST WEEK THE Jury Commissioners of Dodge County received a petition from colored citizens asking that some of their names be placed in the jury-box, and in their revision the Commissioners put the names of ten Negroes in the grand jury box and forty-one in the petit jury box. This gave rise to much excitement, and last night, at eleven or twelve o'clock, forty or more armed men demanded of the Clerk of the Superior Court the jury boxes, the jury list and the jury book, and the boxes were broken open and the slips containing names with the list and books were burned five or six hundred yards from the court house, leaving the county without a jury-box.—Ex.

It will be a long time before the black man will get what belongs to him in this country. It will be by constant warfare if he succeeds at all. The opposition expressed to Negro jurors is simply disgraceful. We would like to see a little more manhood exhibited by our people in Georgia. We are too patient, too cowardly. Wake up, gentlemen, and stab this prejudice to the backbone if it cost's you your life. What have our Negro Democratic papers to say about it. It is done by members of their party, openly and defiantly. Will you, can you conscientiously ask your brothers to support a party that leaves no stone unturned to humiliate, to disgrace him, to outrage and take his life? Come, now, don't all speak at once; but what is your candid opinion—if you have one. It is a serious matter, and THE GAZETTE thinks you ought to look at it in that light. We hope that our readers who are inclined to vote the Democratic ticket will consider carefully these outrages upon their own fellows because of their color and condition. Spurn the party, spurn the ticket, avoid it and pass not by it. Vote for Harrison and Morton.

He was born in Ontario County, New York, May 10, 1841, and has resided since 1866 in this city. RALEIGH, N. C., May 26. — It is learned that there is great excitement in Jackson county growing out of the murder last Tuesday of the Bumgardners, father and son, by Dills. The pursuit of the murderer is active. Hundreds of people are engaged in the search. It is stated that Dills is in Transylvania county. The pursuit will now be made there, also.

It is reported that W. T. Walker, who is the nominee of the third party for Governor, will be asked to resign to make way for a more available candidate.

It has been decided to enlarge the Eastern North Carolina insane asylum at Goldsboro. This asylum is for colored patients. Statistics show that in North Carolina insanity is on the increase among the negroes.

Robert H. Penland, one of the leading citizens of Haywood county, fell dead yesterday while at the railway station at Pigeon River.

The State Engineer and Quartermaster General will spend Monday at Wrightsville, making preparations for the approaching encampment of the State Guard. The preparation of the ground, &c., has already begun. The people of Wilmington are certainly not surpassed by any in the South for hospitality, and will make the encampment a memorable affair. A great many comforts and conveniences for the troops will be prepared.

The Democrats are worked up to a state of high excitement just now over the State Convention so near at hand. Never was there more excitement of a quiet kind, and more uncertainty as to the nominees. There is no "slate." It is a fair and square race. For at least four offices there will be no contest. The interest is in the gubernatorial fight. Nobody dares to bet on any of the three leading candidates. That is the best proof of the uncertainty of the matter.

The Republicans have thrown a sop to the Knights of Labor. A member of that order was nominated for delegate at large very ostentatiously, but got beaten badly. Then he was put on the State Executive Committee with an equal flourish of trumpets. The Republicans are "codding" the Knights and are trying to treat the farmers the same way.

DISAPPOINTED.

There were two disappointed men in the State Convention of the "grand old party"—William Pitt Canaday and R. Z. Linney. The former was beaten all to pieces as a candidate for elector at large (thanks to Dr. Mott's treachery, people say). Linney wanted, though so young in the cause, to go to Chicago likewise. He was not even mentioned in that convention. It was really enjoyable to see how hacked Canaday was as he left here yesterday morning for Washington. He carried Sherman some bad tidings. Some of Sherman's good money has been turned loose in this portion of the vineyard. His henchmen now try to bolster themselves up by saying that the delegates to Chicago will "bolt" their Blaine instructions given by the convention. So there is no harmony after all the bluster and pretence and talk of a united party.

Yesterday evening, at Salem, the cotton-gin of Dr. J. H. Shaffner, with thirty bales of cotton, was burned, the loss being $5,000, with no insurance.

THE TEACHERS.

The session of the North Carolina Teachers' Assembly will be attended by visiting teachers from ten States. Virginia has quite a number of such representatives.

Some of the Republicans are doing considerable talking about John Nichols, the congressman from this district. He does not appear to have prospered greatly in the convention if what is said be true. It is stated that he has torn up his district by working for J. W. Hardin for delegate at large as a Knight of Labor candidate by combining for Harrison and Williamson in the district convention. A HORRIBLE CRIME.

News has been received here of an awful crime in Craven county. An estimable young lady, a teacher, was taken by a negro, carried into the woods, bound hand and foot, and assaulted. Then the brute tied her to a tree and told her he intended to kill her. With this threat he left her. Search was made for the young lady and she was found. Her friends cut the cords and then told her to stay where she was. She did so. They hid in the bushes to await the return of the negro. Presently he came. As he crept up a dozen guns were leveled at him.
He surrendered. His victim was then asked to name his fate, and said she wished him flaved alive. Death came a few minutes after the conclusion of this terrible punishment. Such is the story told by Mr. J. T. Winfield, of Craven county.

The friends of both Hons. D. G. Fowle and Charles M. Stedman claim that their favorite will on the first ballot receive the nomination for Governor.

A CYCLONE.

A cyclone passed over the old town of Bath a few days ago. It did much damage. A colored Methodist church was partially wrecked. A large tree was blown 300 yards, and striking the residence of William McNeill, damaged the latter considerably.

A petition is being circulated in Beaufort county praying Governor Seales to commute the death sentence of William A. Potts to life imprisonment.

A party of masked men went last Tuesday night to the residence of James Simons, at Rockahock, and took away a negro woman.

FLAYED ALIVE.
The Terrible Punishment Meted Out to a Negro Brute.
RALEIGH, N. C., May 26.—[Special.]—News was received here today of a terrible crime and its awful punishment in Craven county. A young lady teacher was taken by a negro, carried into the woods and bound hand and foot, the negro following up his vile deed by outraging her repeatedly. Boasting that he would return after a while and take her life, he left her. Friends missing her, searched the country in large numbers, and at length discovered her bound to a tree. She stated the facts as given above, and expressed the belief that the wretch would soon return. The friends cut the cords which bound her and relieved her otherwise, but requested her to remain in the same place while they secreted themselves to await the return of the negro. Ere long he steadily approached. A dozen rifle barrels were leveled at him and he surrendered. The lady being asked what she wished done with him, replied that she wished him skinned alive, whereupon he was flayed, living but a few minutes afterward. His friends were informed of the facts and got his body.

Col. John A. Fagg, one of the last surviving officers of the Mexican war from North Carolina died suddenly in Asheville on the 23d ult., aged 81 years.

Contrary to custom, at this season of the year, no complaint is heard of a poor stand of cotton. It is therefore to be hoped that the stand is good, and, if this were not the case, somebody would be heard from. — Wadesboro Intelligencer.

GETTING BETTER PRICES.—A very few years ago fine walnut logs sold in this country for from one to three dollars each, as they stood in the woods. Things have changed somewhat and very rapidly. Gen. Hampton informs us that three walnut logs sold at Sylva this week for nine hundred dollars cash. This is a big improvement. — Asheville Citizen.

We learn that at their recent meeting in Greensboro that excellent organization, the I. O. O. F., determined upon the establishment of an Orphanage in this State, and to this end a committee was appointed to take the matter into consideration and with full powers to act. — Goldsboro Argus.

The Supreme Court has decided a very curious case. A woman murdered her husband and was sent to the penitentiary—she sued for dower out of the estate—the Court granted her claim for dower.

The United States Fish Commission recently distributed 1,000,000 young shad in the Catawba River. Other streams are also being stocked.

The Supreme Court holds that an Administrator who at his own sale of land to make assets, collusively purchases the land himself, and sells it at an advance, is liable to the estate of his intestate for the full amount for which he sold the land, even if it be in excess of its value, for he shall not be allowed to make any profit by his collusion.

JUDGE RUSSELL.—The nomination of Judge D. L. Russell by the Republican Convention for the Judgeship, will leave a vacancy on the Republican State ticket. A gentleman who is in his confidence assures us that the Judge will hardly accept the nomination and for the same reasons that prompted the refusal of his name for the Gubernatorial nomination.

—Wilmington Messenger.

DEATH AT GOMBROON.—Mr Harvey Cooper of Louisville, Ky., and a nephew of Mrs Senator Vance, died at Gombroon, the seat of Senator Vance among the Black Mountains, on Sunday. We have no further particulars. The young gentleman had been in the habit for several summers past of spending his summers here, or in the vicinity.—Asheville Citizen.

A severe storm prevailed in the lower portion of Gaston county on the 28th ult. Fences were scattered and trees blown down, but so far as reported no great damage was done.

Private Joe Fifer, the Republican nominee for Governor of Illinois, is in trouble. Mr Fifer is a native of Virginia, and when he was nominated a number of papers of that State announced the news with the aged but ever fresh comment, "Old Virginia never tire." But even the credit of having been born in Old Dominion will not atone for everything—and Jos. Phifer is in trouble. The Democrats of Illinois have started the report that Joseph is a rank infidel and a disciple of Robt. G. Ingersoll. It is said that he will lose a large number of Republican votes unless he makes a satisfactory denial of the charge. He is just now being deluged with telegraphic inquiries.

A bill was introduced in the House last Monday by Mr Plumb of Illinois, providing a new security for national banks. It authorizes the issue of 21/2 per cent. interchangeable bonds to run fifty years, the principal and interest to be paid in coin. The bonds are to be given in exchange for the bonds held by national banks. The Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to issue Treasury notes, redeemable in coin or exchangeable only for these bonds in amounts of $100 or any multiple thereof. The bill further provides that the national debt shall not be reduced below one billion dollars, and shall be funded in these 21/2 per cent bonds.

Death of the last Pensioner of the War of 1812.—Mrs Willie Hancock, widow of the late Henry Hancock, who was a soldier in the war of 1812, died at her home in this county on the 18th inst., at the age of 82 years, 8 months and 8 days. Mrs Hancock has been drawing a pension for the past twenty years and would have suffered for the necessaries of life had it not been for the bounty of the government. She is the last pensioner of the war of 1812 in this county.—Lancaster Ledger.

Mrs Hattie Marshall, a fashionable dressmaker, died under very painful circumstances at Jacksonville, Florida, Wednesday. A few days ago a pimple appeared on her nose, and she pricked it with a pin. The pimple, after this treatment, began to swell, and she expired in great pain from blood poisoning.—Ex.

John Wanamaker used to make $1.50 a week in a clothing store. His dinner, when he had any, consisted of a piece of pie and a glass of milk, costing two cents. Each year his salary was increased, and at the time he was twenty he had saved $200. A lesson. Now he is one of the great merchants of America and very rich and benevolent. And yet we hear boys complain of not being able to get along.

Congressman L. C. Latham publishes a letter in the Greenville Reflector declining to be a candidate for re-election. This leaves in the field in the First district as candidates, Messrs Skinner, Brown, Moore and Warren.

The Washington Gazette says that Mr. J. T. Winfield tells a reporter of a most terrible tragedy, which rumor has it, took place in Craven county. The truth of the report is not vouched for, but from the version given us seems plausible. The affair, as reported to Mr. Winfield, is in substance as follows: A very estimable young lady teacher was taken by a villian of a negro, carried into the woods, and bound hand and foot, following up his vile deed with crime too shocking to mention. Poasting that he would return after a while and take her life, the fiened incarnate left her Friends, missing her, searched the country in large numbers, and at length discovered her bound to a tree. She stated the facts as given above and expressed the belief that the wretch would soon return. The friends cut the cords and relieved her otherwise, but requested that she
her otherw ise, but requested that she remain in the same place while they secreted themselves to wait the return of the negro. Ere long he stealthily approached, when seeing a dozen rifle barrels levelled at him he surrendered. The lady being asked what she wished done with him, replied that she wished him skinned alive, whereupon he was flayed, living but a few minutes afterward. His friends were informed of the facts. If this rumor be true, we have a veritable Rape of Lucrece, so vividly pictured by Shakespeare.

Skinned Alive.
The Raleigh correspondent of the Whig sends the following:
The Washington Gazette reports a horrible occurrence in Craven county this week. A very estimable young lady teacher was overtaken while walking, dragged to the woods, bound and gagged, and fearfully on traged. The fiend who perpetrated the crime left her bound to a tree telling her he would return soon. Some friends, uneasy at her protracted absence, instituted a search and found her. She was released, but was requested to remain at the spot till the negro returns. She did this, and several men placed themselves near by. The negro did return, and was captured. The lady was asked what punishment, she thought, should be meted out to her assailant. She replied, "Skin him alive;" and in a few minutes the punishment was inflicted just as she wished it.

ben-brand-1888-08.A1:
Lynch Law in Salem.
Lynch Law in Salem. We are informed that Ben Brand, a negro, was found dead, hanging to a limb of a tree, last week, near Douglass swamp in Salem. Brand went to a white man's house in that neighborhood, three weeks ago, and obtained permission to spend the night. During the night he attempted some undue liberties in the house, for which he was severely whipped, and ordered to leave the county, on penalty of death for failing to do so. He didn't leave, and the result is as above given.

LATER NEWS.
DR. H. R. MINER, a prominent physician of Chester, Penn., committed suicide by shooting himself through the head. He had been despondent since the death of his wife, which occurred a year ago.

JOSEPH BREED, the Assistant Cashier of the Hartford (Conn.) National Bank, committed suicide by cutting his throat with a razor in the bank hallway. He was an embezzler of trust funds to the amount of $20,000.

The Democracy of Iowa met in Convention at Des Moines and nominated a State ticket, with the exception of candidates for Governor and Lieutenant-Governor. The platform adopted indorses President Cleveland and the Mills bill, and condemns prohibition as injurious to business interests and the cause of temperance.

BEN BRAND, a desperado who had been detected in a burglary at Salem, S. C., was taken from his captors and hanged by a mob.

Over one hundred cases of typhoid fever have occurred recently at Caldwell, Ohio, with twenty-five deaths.

The Nebraska Democratic State Convention met at Lincoln and nominated John A. McShane for Governor and Frank Folda for Lieutenant-Governor.

The Senate has confirmed the following nominations: L. Austin Spalding, at Brunswick; J. Russell Parsons, Jr., Aix la Chapelle; Charles Deblanc, at Puerto Cabello; and Ernest W. Smith, at Mozambique.

PRESIDENT CLEVELAND has sent the following nominations to the Senate: William Gaston Allen, of South Carolina, to be United States Consul at Kingston, Jamaica; Vincente M. Baca, of New Mexico, to be Consul at Piedras Negras, and J. G. Cisco, of Tennessee, to be Consul at Nuevo Laredo, Mexico.

A HEAVY rain, accompanied by a gale, recently prevailed over England, doing additional damages to crops. As a result of the expected shortage in breadstuffs the bakers have raised the price of bread.

Five hundred dervishes attacked an Egyptian fort near Wady Halfa and captured a portion of it. The Egyptians received reinforcements from Wady Halfa and finally succeeded in driving out the dervishes, killing more than one hundred of them. The Egyptian loss was sixteen killed and twenty-seven wounded.
ben-brand-1888-08.A6:
Was not a Case of Lynching.
Our Bethlehem correspondent, writes us, under date of Sep. 5th: I have investigated the reported hanging by Klu Klux in Salem of one Ben Brand, alias Ben Evans, recently reported in the Times, and find there is no truth whatever in it. Brand or rather Evans was publicly whipped in the day time by a party of unmasked citizens, white and colored, and ordered to leave the county for grossly insulting a married white woman. He left, and I am reliably informed is picking cotton on the Fulwood place in Sumter county.

The New York Mayoralty Fight.

NEW YORK, Oct. 14.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—George H. Forster, Tammy's candidate for president of the board of aldermen, created a sensation among politicians last night by declaring that Mayor Hewitt had assured him that under no circumstances will he vote for Grover Cleveland. The speech was made when a committee waited upon him and notified him of his nomination. It tickled the sachems much, and they will use it for all it is worth to flay "Father Abram." Filled Him With Buckshot.

St. Louis, Oct. 14.—George Meyer, a cigar maker of Belleville, 19., was fatally shot by Joseph Schaandt, sr., aged 83 years, to-night. Schrandt has a half-witted daughter, twenty-five years old, and he found Meyer in her room. He seized a shot-gun and filled the intruder with buckshot. Schrandt is in custody to await investigation.

An Italian Stabbed.

NEW YORK, Oct. 14.—An Italian, Antonio Giaconio, was fatally stabbed to the heart in front of the Cooper Union to-night while a meeting was in full blast in the big hall and many people were walking along the crowded thoroughfare. The unknown murderer escaped. The victim had $147 in his pockets.

Smithland, Ky., shakes a big new gas gusher in the faces of its envious contemporaries.

A large crack has been discovered in the steel stern post of the new cruiser Baltimore.

At Bucyrus, O., Hoteling was found guilty of manslaughter for the killing of William Jones.

At Cochran, Ga., Bill Johnson, a negro, was hanged by a mob for brutally assaulting a white woman.

The annual session of the Northern Indiana Lutheran synod closed at North Manchester, Ind., Sunday.

J. W. Edloe, a prominent colored Republican, was killed by Texas Clewes, a politician, at Williamsburg, Va.

A German emigrant was found dead in the closet of a train on the Chesapeake & Ohio railroad, near Quinnimont, W. Va.

Gottlieb Hassman, a Wooster, O., hermit, was killed by the cars, and his hovel if found to contain $2,000 in money, and loads of fine clothing.

Hopkinsville, Ky., youths take a business way of getting to spark their girl alone. They shoot the old folks. Seymour Baggett and Jeff Boyd are in jail for just missing Miss Gibson's mamma when she entered the parlor uninvited.

J. U. Santee, of Akron, O., created a sensation in Elba, N. Y., by disappearing and leaving a note saying that he contemplated suicide. As a search resulted in finding no trace of his body, it is supposed that he concluded to stay with it.

Near Stilesville, Ind., Logan York and an unknown man attempted to murder and rob Jesse Mason, an aged farmer. While York was assaulting Mason's daughter, her brother Oran Mason, nearly blew York's head from his body with a shotgun.

Within a period of two weeks Miss Lena Chapin, of a prominent family residing near Ute, Iowa, has been three times seized by two men and tortured to make her tell where her uncle, Mr. Edwards, kept his money. Four hundred citizens are scouring the country for the scoundrels.

A special from Macon, Mo., says Thomas Wardell, wealthy coal a mine operator was killed at Bevier by striking miners during a riot. Nearly all of the mine owners have engaged new men and these have been coming in from abroad for several days past. This action of the operators greatly incensed the strikers, who have been bitter in their expression against their former employers, especially Wardell. Threats have been made by the strikers against the new men, but there was no violent demonstration until Thursday, when some of the new men were set upon by the strikers and a general battle followed. During the riot Wardell was shot and killed. There is intense excitement at Bevier, and fears are entertained of further bloodshed. The sheriff and a posse have gone to Bevier.

—Pauline McCoy, a negro girl aged 19, was hanged at Union Springs, Ala., for the murder of Annie Jordan, a 14-year-old white child, last February. The execution was private, only the necessary persons being admitted. The crime for which the woman was hanged was a peculiar one. The victim, Annie Jordan, strayed away from her home in Montgomery and nothing was heard of her until her dead body was found in a plum thicket at Three Notch. Circumstances pointed to Pauline, and she was arrested with the dead girl's clothing on her. She was found guilty last spring and sentenced to death. Efforts were made to get the governor to interfere, but to no avail.

Pursued by Bloodhounds and Hanged by a Mob.

[Detroit Free Press.]

There had been an accident up the road, and the passenger train ran upon a siding in the woods to wait for a couple of hours. The only habitation for two miles either way was the little cabin on the sidehill in which lived the switchman and his wife, and the forest was as dense as the day Columbus discoved America. A crowd of us were sitting on the rocks beside the train, smoking and talking and waiting, when a man suddenly rose up and exclaimed:

"Everybody listen! That's the bay of a bloodhound!"

All rose up and listened.

"Ow! ow!" We heard it afar off, but pretty soon the ominous sounds came plainer and nearer, and the man who had first spoken pulled his revolver and shouted:

"Spread out, all of you, and make the line as long as you can! The dogs are coming this way, and a convict or a nigger is in front of them!"

More men came out of the cars, the line was drawn out until it was a quarter of a mile long, and then we waited again. Not for long, however. Not more than three minutes had passed when a stalwart black man, his clothes torn and tattered, with blood on his face and hands, came running through the woods. He was right upon the line before he discovered us, and when two or three men covered him with revolvers he threw up his hands.

"Ow! ow!" bellowed the hounds, and next moment three great hounds rushed up, saw that the fugitive was captured, and lay down to pant and rest. Two minutes more brought a dozen horsemen. Not ten words were spoken. A rope was produced and flung over a limb, the noose dropped over the negro's head, and as seven or eight men ran him up until his toes were two feet above the earth a dozen bullets were fired into his body.

"Assaulted a white woman near Birmingham," explained the leader of the party as his crowd was ready to go.

That was all, but that was enough. Had there been 1,000 of us, and all officers of the law, no man would have stretched forth a hand. He would not have dared to.

GEORGIA AND FLORIDA.
NEWS OF THE TWO STATES TOLD

Augusta is ripe for the building of a big hotel.
Douglasville has the only canning factory in the state.

There was a negro woman in Hawkinsville last week who is the mother of twenty-two children.

The state Sunday school convention meets in Gainesville next Wednesday, and will continue in session two days.

The new National bank company of Dalton has purchased the Tibbs' building at the corner of King and Hamilton streets, and will proceed at once to convert it into a handsome and convenient banking establishment.

At Griffin a year and a half old child of Green Butler, a negro working at the ice factory and living near T. G. Maney's place, was poisoned by eating mushroom growth on Wednesday night and died shortly afterward.

At the meeting of the policy holders of the Southern Mutual insurance company, held in Athens on Tuesday, C. B. Willingham of Macon was elected a director to fill the place made vacant by the death of Col. William B. Johnston.

Rev. Dr. Callaway, president of Emory college, Gainesville, will preach the commencement sermon at the Gainesville college Sunday, June 17th, and Hon. P. H. Adams of Washington will deliver the address on commencement day.

Douglas county will have a county fair at Douglasville on the first Saturday in August. Full preparations have been made and a building and grounds secured. Nothing will be left undone to make it a complete success and the display a fine one.

At Dahlonega in the class about to graduate at the North Georgia agricultural college, John Charles Woodward of Locust Grove was awarded first honor. The second honor was shared by Mr. Henry M. Fletcher of Jackson and William A. Sheldon, of South Carolina.

In Pulaski superior court last week, a white man, who, it is said, was a gallant confederate soldier, was tried for the offense of stealing a cow from a negro. He was found guilty and sentenced to pay a fine of $75 and costs, or be confined six months in the county jail.

At Gainesville, Tuesday noon, a young lady employed in the match factory discovered a pistol (unloaded, of course) in the watchman's room, and at once decided to have a little fun by snapping it at some of her companions, when it weet, off, the ball striking one of her friends in the forebead, inflicting a slight wound.

At Macon Thursday morning, as W. G. Solomon was driving up Cotton avenue in the direction of his home, his pocketbook, containing $125 and some valuable papers, dropped from his pocket and has not been yet recovered. He was on his way home after his family, and was soon to leave for St. Simon's Island, where they will spend ten days or two weeks.

Bridges & Land, who are doing a butchering business at Cuthbert, took from the panch of a fat cow, one day last week, seven No. 8, two No. 6, and four No. 4 nails, and one staple such as is used for putting up wire fencing. The staple and some of the nails were very sharp-pointed, and no doubt all of them had been in the cow's stomach a long while, as they were worn quite smooth.

At Atlanta, Thursday, Thomas F. Ashworth entered a damage suit against the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia railroad for $15,000. The plaintiff, in his declaration, sets forth that while employed as a brakeman by the company in their yards he was knocked down by an engine, and one of his arms so badly crushed that amputation was necessary. He also claims that his skull was fractured.

Alex Blue had his foot so badly crushed at St. Simon's mill on Tuesday as to necessitate partial amputation by a doctor over on the island. Thursday it was found in Brunswick, where Blue had been taken for treatment, that another amputation was necessary. Dr. Tucker, assisted by Drs. Butts and Dunwody, performed the operation, cutting off the foot just below the ankle, leaving the heel still in the possession of the unfortunate negro.

Augusta is reaping some solid returns from the recent advertising given her by the western tour of the exposition directors. Real estate men are daily receiving letters of inquiry, and Thursday Col. E. C. Sheperd, of St. Paul, purchased the S. K. Johnson residence, on Greene street, for $12,000. He and his wife and daughter, Mrs. F. M. Sheperd, have been in Augusta for the past two days, and are charmed with the place. Col. Sheperd is now looking for a home for his son on Greene street, and is also commissioned to buy a residence for another St. Paul friend.

Charles Blackman, the murderer of Stonewall Tondee, who was confined in the county jail at Americus under sentence of death, effected his escape Wednesday night by means of a cell key given him by a confederate. Great excitement prevailed when it became known that the black flend was at liberty, and no little indignation was expressed at the action of the jail officials in allowing any and everybody to visit the prisoner, unaccompanied by a guard. The county commissioners have offered a reward of $250 for the apprehension and delivery of the murderer.

At Atlanta, Thursday, a strange and distressing case was brought to light. Dr. R. A. Holliday, a well-known dentist of that city, while at Davenport, Iowa, with his family, lost by death his little son. He shipped the remains to Atlanta, and on the same train he and his wife took passage. When they arrived at Atlanta they immediately applied at the express office for the remains, but none of the officials of the company had seen them. Telegrams were sent to almost every point along the road before the corpse was located at Chattanooga. Upon telegraphing it was immediately forwarded, and arrived for interment about ten hours behind time.

A letter received at Atlanta Thursday from W. J. Wilkinson, of Stone Mountain, says that Eddie Armistead, a painter by trade and a resident of Atlanta, was drowned Thursday on Yellow river while out fishing. The writer asserts that no one saw him drown, but he got lost from the party, and they suppose he is drowned, as letters which he received from a girl in Atlanta, and which he is known to have had in his pocket, have been washed ashore. The girl is said to have been very much in love with him. It is not known who she is, as the letters were simply signed Ella. Armistead is well known at Conyers and at other points along the line of the Georgia railroad.

A Desperate Murderer Escapes.

MACON, GA., June 10.—If the bloodhoods do their duty there will be a lynching in Schley county soon. Wednesday night Charles Blackman, a notorious colored desperado, effected his escape from the American jail by means of a false key furnished him by confederates. Three years ago, on Christmas eve, Blackman shot Stonewall Tondee, a merchant in Ellaville, to death. The assassination aroused the deepest indignation, but somehow Blackman had friends who saw to it that he was unhurt. He has been three times convicted of the murder and has been as often before the Supreme Court, where new trials were allowed. Day before yesterday the Supreme Court affirmed the third sentence, and thus he seemed to be at the end of his rope. It was at this stage he was assisted in his escape. The suspicion has now become open that the assassination of Tondee must have been prompted by some white man, who is taking care that his instrument does not meet the punishment he deserves. Blackman is believed to have returned to Schley county, where large bodies of men have organized to run him down.

BLACKMAN'S ESCAPE.
A Thrice-Convicted Murderer at Large.

Schley County Indignant.

ELLAVILLE, Ga., May 7.—[Special.]—Our sheriff has just received a telegram from Mr. Cobb, deputy sheriff of Sumter county, saying that Charles Blackman, the murderer of Stonewall Tondee, who has been confined in the jail at Americus for safe keeping, made his escape last night by means of false keys.

This negro has been convicted three times of murder, and twice granted a new trial by the supreme court. News was received yesterday of the judgment of the superior court being affirmed by the supreme court. Our people are loud in their denunciation of the jailer of Sumter in allowing him to escape, Some even go so far as to say that it is impossiblefor such a thing to happen without the assistance of the jailer.

Any way it seems as if we certainly selected the wrong jail and wrong jailer. A fear is upon our our people that he will return and kill others here. A lion loose in our midst would not begin to create as much alarm as the freedom of this fiend incarnate. We can do nothing except to curse those those who are responsible for his escape, and we we are not not slow in doing that.

Chas. Blackman, the murderer of Stonewall Tondee, and who escaped from Sumter county jail last week, was captured Friday morning at Banks's landing, on the Ckattahoochee river. by Deputy Sheriff Holder, of Stewart county. Holder arrived at Americus Thursday with the desperado bound. He was at once committed to the dungeon of the county jail, where heavy irons were afterward put upon him.

Blackman is a desperate criminal, and fought like a tiger when Holder and his assistant, a trusty negro named Kendrick, caught him. He was just in the act of crossing the river when his pursuers arrived on the spot and handcuffed him.

Blackman was trying to make his way to Mississippi where he hoped his identity would never be discovered. He had a small map of the southern states concealed about his person, upon which his route was carefully located with a pencil.

Mr. Frank Davis, residing near Fairburn, on last Wednesday, upon going to the house from the field, Wednesday, found his little three year old child sitting in the door crying and when asked what it was crying for, it replied that its mother was gone. Mr. Davis looked over the house and seeing nothing of his wife went out to the potato patch where her body was found, she having been dead for some little time. Mrs. Davis had been in bad health for some time and it is supposed that while in the potato patch she died suddenly of heart disease.

Tuesday, at Canton, Mrs. Gober was feeling badly and thought she would take paregoric to relieve her suffering. By mistake she took up a vial of medicine which Dr. Turk had left with her some months ago to be given the baby in small doses, and drank a large swallow out of it. She at once realized a burning, tingling sensation and went down stairs to see her mother about it. As she turned to go up the steps she found her limbs were becoming benumbed and it was with difficulty she ascended the stairs. She soon grew worse and becoming alarmed sent for Dr. Coleman, who came at once, and, after making a hurried examination, found that she had taken a large dose of a deadly poison and that it would be next to impossible to save her, as the poison had been taken upon an empty stomach and had become well digested. In about two hours after he was called in she died in great agony with convulsions. She and her three little children were living with her mother, Mrs. Sarah A. Johnson, at Canton. Mr. Gober is working in the mines of Colorado, and has not been home in several months. Mrs. Gober was not quite twenty-two years old.

Tuesday evening last Elisha Pruce, a white man, who three months ago quit his wife and left her and family, near Swainesboro, returned and asked her to live with him again, which she refused to do. He then wanted pay for some guano which he claimed to have furnished her to use on her farm. She refused to pay, and he left very angry. That night he procured a pistol, and going back the next morning, saw her, hoe in hand, hoeing some cotton. Without saying one word, he commenced shooting at her, missing the first time. He shot again, this time hitting her in the hand. She broke and ran, and he shot again, missing her.

He then ran and caught her, throwing her down and shooting two bullet holes through her head, and her brains run out all on the ground. The pistol he used was a 38-calibre Smith & Wesson. The news spread rapidly, and the coroner of Emanuel county, James M. Cowart, was sent for. When he arrived to hold the inquest over the remains of the woman, he was sent for about half a mile to hold an inquest over Elisha Pruce himself, he having taken strychnine and killed himself. The bottle with the poison was found by him, half of it gone, and the pistol with which he shot his wife was found in his hand. The post mortem, held by Dr. George L. Smith, developed the fact of the poisoning.

Americus Republican: Blackman, the doomed murderer, will not hang until late in the fall. This seems to be an accepted fact among all concerned. Judge Fort, when interviewed in regard to the appointment of a day for the execution, said that he would not call a special term of the court simply for the purpose of fixing a day, and that unless he were petitioned to do this by citizens of the county that Blackman would be resentenced at the regular term of Schley superior court in September. Blackman is securely confined now in the Americus jail, and will be on hand on the day fixed by the court for the expiation of his crime upon the gallows. He seems very despondent, and has little or no hope of escape from his doom. He has very little to say upon any subject, and is careful and guarded in his words. It is not thought that he will likely ever confess the crime for which he was thrice convicted, even when he stands upon the trap.

Pineville was treated to a regular cloudburst on Friday morning. As a small wagon, says the Marion County Patriot, with two mules, on its way to Americus, the driver of the wagon stopped his mules in the stream to let them drink. While they were drinking the rush of the water from the hills came upon them and washed mules, wagon and all under a water gate just below the road. There were three negroes in the wagon, but they got out safely after passing under the water gate, and followed the mules and wagon down the stream. One of the mules was drowned, and, strange to say, it was the one that got loose from the wagon. The other one remained hitched to the wagon, was washed across three lots of land and the wagon and mule knocked down the center pier of a new bridge which was built since the March flood. How the mule went through with all this without being killed is something remarkable, but he was gotten out alive, though badly crippled, and will never do much more service.

The Morning News published several days ago a short account about the Sycamore affair. The following fuller particulars are clipped from the Worth Local at Sumner: A week or two since Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Horkan left their home, and during their absence a negro man from an adjoining place came for water. Finding no one at the house but a little white girl about 13 years of age, who lives with the Horkans, he made insulting proposals to her. Upon the return of the Horkans she informed them. Mr. Horkan went after the negro and attacked him. He shot at him four times. The first shot was aimed directly at his forehead. The negro dodged and the ball cut his hat directly in two without striking his head. Three other shots were fired, two of them taking effect, one in the back, lodging in the region of the shoulder blade, and the other in the fleshy part of the hip. The neighbors threatened to lynch him and finish the work, but Mr. Horkan wouldn't let them touch him, but said he would give him a chance for life. He was permitted to go to Jehu Branch's place, in Irwin county (where a brother stayed and where he could receive attention), under promise if he recovered from his wounds he would leave the community and never return. It seems that this was not the first meanness he had been guilty of in the Sycamore neighborhood and over in the edge of Irwin county, and that he was generally disliked by the citizens, both white and black. Consequently, as soon as Mr. Branch learned he was on his place he sent him word that he must leave. This he did, going back to Sycamore. A day or two after his return to Sycamore he mysteriously disappeared, and it is generally supposed he was lynched, as his father says he does not know where he is, having failed to find him after diligent search. The father seems indifferent about the suspected fate of his son, and speaks of it as not at all unexpected.

An expert from the Industrial institute, Columbus, Miss., has been engaged, who will teach the S. T. Taylor scientific system of cutting, fitting, artistic draping, and the full details of dressmaking.

At Thomasville Tuesday, Dr. A. P. Taylor, surgeon of the S., F. & W. railroad, amputated a finger for a negro boy who had met with an accident on the road. It took four men to hold him while the doctor administered chloroform. After recovering from the drug, though suffering no pain from the operation, he howled for half an hour worse than a Comanche Indian.

Tommie Laney, a 13-year old lad living near Smithville, met with a horrible death a day or two ago. He was riding upon a wagon heavily loaded with lumber, when by some means he accidentally fell off, the wheels passing over his body and fatally crushing him. After the accident he attempted to raise himself from the ground, but the effort was too great and he fell over dead.

Politics are brightening up a bit in the Fourth district. In view of the attack in the rear made on Hon. Thomas W. Grimes, some of his friends have urged him to return to his district and canvass for reelection. His reply has been characteristic of the man: "My party needs the vote of every democrat, and my duty calls me here. I would not abandon my post for a seat in congress."

One night last week, while James A. Ray of Monroe was in Atlanta, Mrs. Ray saw a man at her window and fired two shots at him with a pistol. There was some misunderstanding about some one to stay at the house at night, and she was alone and sitting up late. The window was raised, the blinds closed. Mrs. Ray detected the would-be burglar by seeing him stealthily turn the blind.

Capt. Moller of the bark Charlotte A. Littlefield, who arrived at Brunswick from quarantine Wednesday, reports having seen, on June 26, a sinking steamer twenty-five miles northeast of Hatteras. The steamer was in the channel, obstructing navigation, and the topmast could only be seen about eight or ten feet above water, but Capt. Moller was able to make certain that it was a steamer.

her pet hems drooping and ailing, made an examination and found some irregularities in the region of the craw. Thereupon an incision was made near the clavicle, the craw was taken out, turned, cleaned, sewed up, placed in its natural position, and the incision closed by several stitches. The doctored hen may now be seen cutting high shines with a drove of chicks.

Holly Embanks, the negro who was committed to jail at Americus, two weeks ago, to await the October term of superior court to be tried upon the charge of having aided the murderer, Blackman, to escape some time since, succeeded Tuesday in making the requisite bond of $500 and was released from custody. Holly is also under a $300 bond for burglary in addition to the bond of $500. A Mr. Boyd of Albany acts as bondsman.

A son of Harrison Allen, of Monroe, plowed up an odd coin a day or two ago. The coin in circumference is between the sizes of a half dollar and dollar, as coined now out of silver. It is an eighth of an inch in thickness and heavy enough to be gold, though it looks to be copper or brass. On one side can be made out the words, "Joannes D. G. Port et al. G. P. Regens." These circumvent an image; below it the figures 1812. On the other side a crown engraved, "Utilitati Publicae," and 40 in figures at the bottom.

Henry Thomas, a white tenant of Sam Tolbert, was drowned, Sunday, while bathing in a pond on Maj. Bland's farm, two miles east of Cedartown. Henry Thomas, Ben Jordan and Sam Kettle went to the pond to bathe. Thomas jumped in first from a spring board, diving. Jordan saw him rise to go down, and said, "He's drowning." But knowing him to be a good swimmer, the others said, "He is fooling us." Jordan was right. He did drown. It is supposed in leaping in he hurt himself in some way. His remains were shipped to Gainesville, from which community he came. He leaves a widow.

This shows an increase for the fiscal year just ended of $43,967 16. When Collector Crenshaw first came into office the total collections from all sources footed up $304,384 29. At Macon, Wednesday, there was a case almost similar to the well-remembered Jim Moore case. A handsome married lady, aged 18 years, who said she lived four miles from Dalton, arrived in Macon on the East Tennessee train from Atlanta at 11:15 o'clock a.m. She was en route to Thomasville to visit her aunt. While she was at the East Tennessee depot, Ella Davis, a well-known prostitute, stepped up to her and offered to escort the Dalton lady to the Central depot, and have her trunk transferred. The lady, being a perfect stranger to the city, accepted the Davis woman's offer, not knowing her character. On reaching the Central depot, it was found that the Thomasville train would not leave until after 6 o'clock. Ella Davis suggested to the Dalton lady that, as she seemed very tired, she had better go with her to the hotel and get a milk punch or a little wine, which would strengthen her for the journey to Thomasville. She consented. Instead of taking the lady to a hotel, the procuress carried her to a Fourth street grocery store, led the lady to the bar and called for wine, which the lady, in her confusion, being unused to city ways, drank. Officer Joe Porter's attention was called to the matter by a gentleman who had seen the lady on the Atlanta train. The officer investigated the case, found that the Davis woman's motives were unholy and that she was trying to entrap the lady for evil designs. When the lady found out the truth she was greatly shocked. Officer Porter took charge of her until train time, and saw her safely aboard for Thomasville.
