Georgia.
"Athens Graphic: Mr. William Reynolds, who lives near Georgia factory, was in the city this morning, and tells us that his father-in-law, Mr. J. G. Connell, has been troubled for some time by a thief stealing eatables from his dining table every night. Various fruitless attempts had been made to capture the burglar, but on Tuesday morning last he was caught in his lair. Mr. Connell went to the kitchen quite early that morning, kindled the fire in the stove, and all at once noticed the table cloth to be somewhat out of order. He at once knew the thief had visited him, but little expected that he was concealed in the room with him. He began fixing the table in order, and as he lifted the table cloth discovered the thief—a large 'possum. The animal sat contentedly munching a piece of meat until Mr. Connell grabbed him. The thief was lynched without judge or jury, and furnished a 'square meal' for Mr. C. the following day."

A correspondent of the DeKalb Chronicle: We will say to the young men who wish to find them a brave, daring, courageous, and adventurous girl, come to Seuffle Town, We can boast of two. Will give a detailed account of an adventure that they had recently. One evening they were out horseback riding when, unexpectedly, they came in contact with an army of yellow jackets (now comes in the important point.) One of them jumped off the horse, and over the fence at one jump.
Wade Merritt, who lives in the Friendship district of Sumter county, had a lively encounter with a mad dog a day or two ago. The animal belonged on a plantation two miles distant from Mr. Merritt's, and the first knowledge that he had of the presence of the dog was a terrific battle being waged on the back veranda of his residence between the rabid cur and his own faithful watch dog. Mr. Merritt says that the bloody fight lasted nearly two hours, despite his efforts to separate the dogs, and it finally became necessary to call up a force of negroes to exterminate the rabid animal. Mr. Merritt's dog was badly torn up in the fight, and has been chained up to await the result of his injuries.

Athens has a prophet in Mr. Wm. Barber, the Chronicle says. His father before him was a prophet of the weather. He says that in exactly three months from the time the first katydid is heard there will be a frost, and that the first one this year was heard on the 7th of July, and, as a matter of course, on the 7th of October there will be a killing frost which will reach Jacksonville. It is to be hoped that the little insect was heard about a month earlier.
A favorite temperance drink in the county of Pike is sorghum poured upon peaches and allowed to ferment. It is said to make drunk come and cause as big a head the next morning as genuine redeye.

The editor cares not for tariff reform
When the bait for the day is dug.
He hears not the din of political storm.
But he lures the perch with the wriggling worm

'Tis joy when equipped with a rod and line.
From the care of the paper away;

—Griffin News.

DUBLIN, Ga., September 27.—[Special.]—The returns of the prohibition election in Laurens county gives the antis 41 majority. Notice of a contest has been filed.

AMERICUS, Ga., September 27.—[Special.]—Charles Blackman, the murderer of Stonewall Tondee, has been sentenced to be hanged on the 19th of October. Blackman was self-possessed and did not seem to appreciate the solemnity of the situation.

BOWMAN, Ga., September 26.—[Special.]—At about 2:30 o'clock p. m. today little Emerson David, seven years old, son of W. A. David, our depot agent here, was playing with some other little boys at the gin of W. M. Deney & Co. It being in motion, he was caught by some of the shafting and was horribly mangled before the machinery could be stopped. He was a very bright child. It is thought that it will be impossible for him to recover.

About two hours later Mr. D. W. Gloer, son of Mr. J. D. Gloer, went down to the gin to see how little Emerson was caught, and he got caught by the same shafting and at the same place, his hand and arm being torn up, his arm broken in three places. He is resting pretty well. Being so fleshy, it is feared his arm may have to be amputated. Mr. Gloer is about twenty years old and weighs 225 pounds.

ATHKNS, Ga., September 26.—[Special.]—A special dispatch has been received from Mr. J. L. Bartow, from San Antonio, announcing the killing of Mrs. C. W. Long and the fatal injuring of Mr. Ed Long in a railroad accident last Saturday night. Mrs. Long was the widow of Dr. Crawford W. Long, discoverer of ether as an anesthesia.

ALBANY, Ga., September 26.—[Special.]—A gentleman who trades extensively in the market, while in town the other day indulged too freely in the ardent and became as full as a tick. We started to drive to his home some miles away and started off with a bag of crackers, two boxes of axle grease and two boxes of deviled ham. Before going a great distance he became terribly hungry, as it is said that persons in that condition often do, and accordingly he got out his box of crackers and other articles and made a square meal. The next morning he went out to grease his buggy, when to his amazement he found nothing left in the buggy but the two cans of deviled ham which he thought he had devoured. To his horror he found that he had eaten up the axle grease with the crackers.

Chas. Blackman, as the evidence goes, walked deliberately up to the back door of the store in which Mr. Tondee was clerking, and there, in the darkness of night, with malice aforethought, deliberately murdered the said Tondee. The deed was committed in September, 1885, since which time every effort has been made to save Blackman's neck without avail. Now, for the last time, he is sentenced to be hanged. He has cost Schley county thousands of dollars, and when he is disposed of the county will breathe a breath of relief. After the sentence was pronounced the sheriff and guards returned to the train, which immediately left for Americus.

Tennessee.

Oliver Scalf was married to his own sister near of Chattanoooglast spring by Squire Ford. Immediately after the wedding both parties were arrested on a charge of incest. Oliver was convicted of the charge and sentenced to the penitentiary for five years while his wife was acquitted.

Virginia.

The following note was picked up by J. J. J. Ellitt, on Main street, Libety, Saturday morning, supposed to have been dropped by a balloonist. There were two keys attached to it. It created great excitement;

If this should chance to fall into the hands of any one, tell my wife, Mary Brooks, 204 Green street, Cleveland, Ohio, that I am high in the skies with my balloon, and it is unmanageable, dashing along at a fearful rate. I think I am moving eastward The sun has not been in view for for for more than an hour. (Signed) CHARLES BROOKS.

South Carolina.

SOUTHERN GLEANINGS,
Meinert. This property now belongs to John R. Winters. The old barn had been torn away and some wooden tenement houses erected on the site. The men are very sanguine, but at last accounts had unearthed nothing.

Levi Brown, who murdered Mrs. Davis, proprietress of a boarding-house in Chattanooga, Tenn., last May, was convicted of murder in the second degree, and sentenced to the penitentiary for twenty years. The murder was entirely unprovoked, and was a cold-blooded one.

As a north-bound cattle train was pulling into the yards at Muskogee, L. T., a few days ago, a young man attempted to jump from a cattle car into the caboose after the caboose had been cut off from the rest of the train. He fell between the cars and the caboose ran over him, mashing his head into a jelly, and otherwise man-ging his body. Upon investigation it was found that his name was Reuben B. Legate, from Abilene, Tex. He was in charge of two cars of cattle consigned to a St. Louis commission house.

At the Baptist Church in Cisco, Tex., a few nights ago, while Rev. Kelly was admonishing and advising his flock, a young gentleman who was sitting by the side of his best girl suddenly jumped up with a yell that caused all the eyes in the house to be turned on him. He knocked at the wall like a madman, and for the time being the preaching was stopped, while the man continued to jump and stamp and knock until he finally, almost out of breath, held up a large tarantula that was crawling on the wall close to his head, after which the preaching continued.

By a boiler explosion at Horton station, Kry., a few days ago, Thos. Bryant, Berry Kuykendall and his son were killed.

Light frosts are reported from various localities in Alabama and Tennessee, and the apprehensions of the further spread of yellow-fever are dying out.

A sea-serpent was seen recently in Winyah Bay, near Gorgetown, S. C., by Captain Springs of the tug Henry Buck, while towing a schooner down the harbor.
Hiram S. Bond has sued Wm. E. Forrest for $30,000 damages for libel, the suit growing out of libel published in the latter's paper, Truth, at Decatur, Ala., last May.

Senator Beck, of Kentucky, has been considered improved by his sojourn at Old Point Comfort. He will probably return to Washington in a short time, but will not take part for the present in the proceedings of the Senate.

The last rail on the Thomasville and Monticello railroad, in Georgia, has been laid and traffic be un.

Advices from San Antonio, Tex., announce the killing of Mrs. Crawford A. Long in a railroad accident. Mrs. Long was the widow of the late Dr. Crawford A. Long, of Atlanta, Ga., who discovered the use of ether as an anesthetic.

The detectives at Mobile, Ala., believe that in arresting W. Aug. Fonde, at Biloxi, Miss., recently, they have captured the leader of a gang of counterfeiters numbering at least fifteen men, most of whom were recently driven out of Illinois.

Miss Amelia Jackson, of Washington, D. C., daughter of W. H. Jackson, who shot and killed Colonel Ellsworth in Alexandria, Va., at the outbreak of the war, has been promoted from a $720 clerkship in the Patent Office to a $901 position.

Peter Clder was shot by Wm. Stephens at Petersville, Ky., a few nights ago. The killing grew out of a controversy about a woman. After slaving his victim Stephens robbed him of $219 and a pistol and fled.

Mr. James M. Gibson, Sr., died at his residence, fourteen miles from Vicksburg, Miss., a few days ago, from blood poison, caused by a malignant carbuncle. Mr. Gibson was past his sixtieth year, and was born and reared in the vicinity where he died.

Charles Blackman was sentenced at Americus, Ga., to be hanged October 19. This is the fourth time sentence has been passed upon him, but he has now reached his last chance. He crept up behind Stonewall Tandee in the dark and shot him to death.

The sun began drawing water from the paper-mill dam in Cobb County, Ga. There were six feet of water in the dam and in about five minutes the water was so low that the mill had to stop. The singular phenomenon created great consternation among the neighbors.

Judge Thomas W. Hayes, formerly probate judge, died recently at his residence at Hayes Landing, Issaquena County, Miss., very suddenly. He was the oldest Mason in the county, one of its best men, and stood high in the estimation of his people. At the time of his death Judge Hayes was a levee commissioner, and was seventy years of age.

The monument to the Confederate dead at Staunton, Va., was unveiled a few days since in the presence of about five thousand persons. A granddaughter of Albert Sidney Johnston, assisted by young ladies from every State represented in the cemetery, unveiled the monument, and addresses were made by Governor Lee, General Early, General Rosser and Mr. McCulloch, of Annapolis, Md.

A untiting affray took place upon the street in Dixon, Ky., a few nights ago. Rich Wall was returning home about midnight, alone, when he chanced to run against Ambrose Spillman, who stabbed him in the chest with a knife he carried, inflicting a deadly wound. Spillman has been arrested, and says Wall frightened him, which the dying man denied. Spillman is in jail.

Rhembold Eberhard, aged forty-five, was found by the roadside near Louisville, Ky., a few mornings since, dying of morphine poisoning. He was taken to his home, a few blocks away, where he died without recovering consciousness. Some letters he left showed that he was about $200 short in his accounts with J. F. Stone & Co., whisky dealers, whose looks he kept, and that he had committed suicide for that reason.

Oh for a nipping frost.

Jeff Baker, a young farmer from Russellville, Ky., while attempting to board a moving freight train near the depot, at Hopkinsville, that State, for the purpose of stealing a ride, a few nights ago, lost his hold and fell upon the track, the wheels of a car passing over his right leg between the ankle and knee, crushing it to a jelly. His sufferings were terrible to witness, and his leg had to be amputated as the only hope of saving his life.

The champion rattlesake of ten years has just been killed near Everett, N. C. It weighed twenty-seven pounds and measured seventeen inches about the body.

The entire South is becoming alarmed by the advance of yellow fever.

James McGinnis was instantly killed at Memphis, Tenn., a few days since, by a shock from a dead telegraph wire that was crossed by an electric-light wire. The manager of the electric-light company has been arrested for criminal carelessness.

The first train of the Mexican National railroad passed over the company's new iron bridge across the Rio Grande river at Laredo, Tex., a few days ago, and regular trains are now crossing.

Investigation Among Exiles.

There are thirty colored ex
There are some thirty colored exiles from Crittenden in this city. A majority of those negroes permitted to remain at home are warm sympathizers with the banished parties, and manage to keep them moderately well posted as to the status of affairs. An APPEAL reporter went after these Crittenden relics last night, and found them still the center of attraction around Beale street, Hadden avenue and DeSoto street, and the Beale Street Baptist church. Most of them, in fact, attend every service at this house of worship.

Tue first exile encountered was Clerk Dave Ferguson. Dave's troubles seem to prey upon him, and he was endeavoring to drown them in the flowing bowl. Asked about the indictments, in his drawsy, drunken sort of way Dave replied:

"I seed several warts from over dar today. One of dem wuz a member ob de gran' jury, John Murray, I beliobe his name wuz, from de lower part of de county. He said dar wuz twelve or fifteen indictments foun' against white and culld men. He didn' know none of de names."

"Where is Murray now?"
"He's done gone home."
"What else did you hear?"
"John Oglesby to me dat one of de white men who wuz indicted fur carryin' a gun wuz tried and acquitted."
"Did you hear that the grand jury had traced the anonymous letters to your office and that they were in the writing of Ramsey?"
"No, sah. I didn't hear dat. Dat's all wrong, cause dey wuz not writ in dar."
Judge Dan Lewis, another of the deposed and exiled negroes, came in at this juncture, but left soon after putting a few questions to Ferguson and learning his muddled condition. The reporter accompanied Lewis, who repudiated the story of Oglesby as the merest bosh. He did not believe any white man had been tried.
"Mr. Nightingale, in his sermon at the Beale street church tonight, referred to the first act of violence growing out of the troubles," said Lewis to the reporter as they walked from Ferguson's boarding-house toward the church.
"What did he say?"
"He said, in speaking at length on the Crittenden county troubles, that a woman who came from there today told him the body of a colored man had been found swinging from a limb, with his throat cut."

"Who was the colored man?"
"I understood him to say that the first impression was that it was Sandy Odom, but investigation proved it otherwise."

"What had Odom done to be thus treated?"
"Nothing at all. He was a farmer, lived about six miles from Madison, and represented Crittenden county in the Legislature. He was in Memphis last week, and had been warned not to return. He did so, however, last Thursday or Friday."

"Who found the body?"
"I did not hear."

"Where was it found?"
"I heard it was near Odom's house."

"What were the particulars, as related by Mr. Nightingale?"
"He didn't know any further than the discovery reported by the woman."

"Was Odom in Marion frequently?"
"Yes, he came there whenever he had business to transact."

Associate Editor Harvey, of the Watchman, came up about this time, and had a version about the lynching. He was at the depot when the afternoon train on the Kansas City road came in. In conversation with A. Stevenson, a colored passenger agent for the road, he learned of the summary vengeance. His information was that Odom was the victim; that it occurred between Marion and Crawfordsville, and no contradiction had reached his ears.

"You heard about Dr. Stith, didn't you?" asked Lewis of Harvey.

Harvey had, but the reporter had not, and asked for the facts surrounding his case.

Lewis answered: "Dr. Stith was in Memphis at his own volition, and returned home Saturday in response to an urgent summons to the bedside of his sick wife. No sooner had he landed at Marion than he was arrested and put in jail."

"May be he was one of the parties indicted by the grand jury," suggested the reporter.

"May be so, but they couldn't indict him any more than they could you."
"How many indictments were returned?"
"I heard there were between thirty and forty."
"Are you involved in them?"
"I don't know; if so I have not been molested."
"What are you going to do about getting back?"
"They sent word over here that if you returned you would be hung," interrupted Harvey, addressing Lewis. "The others could return and be put in jail, but they would hang you."
"Then I won't go back," said Lewis, emphatically.

THE STITH CASE.

It is true that Dr. Stith is under indictment, charged with conspiracy. It is also true that he is in jail, vainly hoping that his bond of $1,000 will be duly signed at an early day and he released. Both these latter anticipations may never be realized, and Stith will remain a prisoner until the next term of court, in January next. Were he released the immediate requirement would be for him to forsake Arkansas soil, which militates heavily against him in the skirmish (by proxy) for sureties.

Is Stith guilty, as charged? But for one singular and marked weakness in his statement, his defense would be hard to combat. It is, in substance, this: He went to Marion some time ago, a graduate from the medical department of Fisk university. After standing a creditable examination by a regularly organized local medical board, he soon acquired a lucrative practice. It was among a class that the white physicians had no especial desire to attend, hence they received him with genuine cordiality, and really liked him. Stith soon fell into rapid company, such as Lewis, Ferguson, Fleming, et al., and became editorially connected with the Headlight. According to his story, he became aware that his associates were going too far, and withdrew. Since then he has had nothing whatever to do with them further than professional visits and friendly intercourse when meetings occurred. He left Arkansas Thursday, coming to Memphis. Sunday morning the wife of Dave Ferguson, who came over to see her husband, told him his wife was dangerously ill. Here comes in the inconsistency, said by those who know him to be the result of nervousness and excitement. The doctor's first statement was that he had received a letter from his nephew to the same effect, but when reminded of this could not produce the letter. Another discrepancy is the fact, according to his own story, that he was on his way to the train for Marion when Mrs. Ferguson's message was delivered. The white people of Marion are inclined to give him the benefit of a certain amount of doubt, but look upon his incarceration as a partially just punishment for his suspicious associations, and also as a barrier to further disturbance from the exiles. Mrs. Stilt has undoubtedly been sick.

ANOTHER WILL LEAVE.

The Hon. Sandy S. Odom, colored member of the Legislature from Crittenden, and who resides six miles from Marion, has not been lynched, as was reported from the Crittenden refugees in this city Sunday night. On the contrary, the sable hued legislator is meek as a lamb and anxiously inquiring the way of salvation from the wrath to come if he tarries. Inquiries were numerous in this direction yesterday morning, both verbal and by note. The one directed to Col. W. F. Smith was replied to in this language: "I think the best thing you can do is leave the county. If you remain there is sure to be dangerous risk, and from a direction which you do not expect it." During the day the expected information came from Odom "I will leave." The vacancy will be made in a few days, as soon as he can arrange his business affairs, which consist entirely of farming interests.

THE SITUATION AS IT IS.

Were the visitor to Marion at this day uninformed concerning the late affairs, he would probably leave no wiser on the subject than when he arrived. Aside from a small guard posted at night, there is not one remaining sign or visible relic. The feeling has not died out, however, and questions on the subject never fail to elicit long-winded discourse. But for the conservatism and caution of older heads, there would have been a tragic climax to Stith's arrest and imprisonment Sunday. A number of indiscreet young fellows collected soon after the catch, and earnestly advocated hanging him to the nearest tree. Penetrating minds in the older bodies brought this proposition to an abrupt and beautiful goose egg. It is not believed that the appearance of any banished negroes, other than Lewis, Ferguson and the few ringleaders, would excite anything like violence. It would not be healthy for the excepted ones, though, as a number of inviting limbs await their victims. The negroes are aware of it, too. It would require an inch hemp rope to pull them upon Crittenden county soil. Dan Lewis has already so expressed himself, and Mrs. Ferguson stated to the writer that her husband had left Memphis to find them a new home. "If he ever put his foot in dis county agin, I'd leave him." The woman was then asked for a sample of her husband's writing for comparison with the notes of warning. She cheerfully made a pretense of search, but found nothing, a fact which she explained with the statement that "Dave never wrote any at home, and never writes me a letter when away." If Dave Ferguson was as incendiary in his speech as the woman who rejoiced at being his wife, the wonder is how Crittenden county endured him so long. There are no witnesses to say he and his co-conspirators were not as bad and even worse. As for York Byers, he was a holy terror, and no one mourns his absence.

EVEN THE NEGROES REJOICE

Col. Smith was asked how many of the negroes were involved in the conspiracy. He replied, "The actual number engaged in the warring movement, and familiar with the consequences in case of apprehension, did not exceed twenty."

"Then the majority right here at home were either ignorant of or frowned upon it?"

"Why, of course. More than two-thirds of them are heartily glad the scoundrels have been expelled, and would resist their return as actively as we."

A canvass of the colored citizens established the accuracy of Col. Smith's statement; but whether the corroboration came from further than the lips cannot be said. Mrs. Ferguson and her sympathizing female friends say they are miserable cowards, and speak the sentiment from a motive of self-interest.

PEACE IN CRITTENDEN.
THE statement of Traveling Auditor Townsend, of the Gulf road, as it is telegraphed to THE APPEAL by the Associated Press, asserting that a negro official had been lynched at Marion, Crittenden county, is a falshood from beginning to end. Peace prevails in every part of the county, and except at night no armed guards are to be seen. Mr. Townsend has evidently taken counsel of his fears and has by the magic of his tongue turned a rumor into a realism of hair-raising power. All is quiet at Marion and at Crawfordsville, and the two races are a unit in maintaining the peace, with the concurrence of the Sheriff. The Circuit Court is in session, and the Grand Jury also; the course of justice is uninterrupted and free, and the people are attending to their crops.

How long, O Lord, how long will the wild-eyed, long-haired idiotic romancer about Crittenden county be allowed to roam over the face of the earth!

The following harrowing details of a lynching over there, that may be properly classed with "The Letter That Never Came," were telegraphed to THE APPEAL by the Associated Press last night:

IT WAS AWFUL!

St. Louis, Mo., July 24.—A dispatch from Springfield, Mo., says: Traveling Auditor Townsend, of the Gulf road, arrived in that city at noon from the south and verifies the report of one of the negro county officials having been lynched by a mob of white men. Mr. Townsend says that it is a difficult matter to get any details of proceedings at Marion, which is under a guard of armed men, and a great state of excitement prevailing. Neither couriers or messengers are allowed in or out, and the telegraph operator is confined to the sending of train orders. Mr. Townsend states that the victim was a county official and one of the banished eighteen. The mob seized him while he was endeavoring to effect an entrance into the court-house, dragged him to the woods at the edge of the town, and after a desperate struggle strung him up. It is claimed that Gov. Hughes, at Little Rock, has been called upon for protection, and if this be true the details must be forthcoming. It is also claimed that an armed force of white men have gone from Walnut Ridge to Marion to aid the whites who look for a serious uprising of the negroes.

THE WORST KIND OF BOSH.

The rumor of an affair similar to that described by Mr. Eli Perkins Townsend to a Springfield, Mo., reporter stalked through this city all day yesterday. It also made a gallant charge upon St. Louis, as evidenced by numerous inquiries for particulars. The APPEAL yesterday printed a faithful resume of the situation from the beginning up to the time the reporter left Marion Monday afternoon. There was no trouble over there then, or anticipation of any. All that the white and ninety-nine one-hundredths of the colored people there desire is for the banished negroes, who would kill any territory they infest, even were there no other inhabitants, to keep away. It may be a bold assertion, but THE APPEAL does not believe $5,000 would induce any one of them to return. They know what sort of treatment would be meted out to them.

Even Little Rock caught the excitement, as will be seen from the following special telegram to THE APPEAL:

IT IS AWFULLY UNKIND.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., July 24.—Considerable excitement was caused here today on the circulation of a rumor that the Crittenden county troubles have broken out afresh, and that the whites had last night lynched County Judge Lewis, a colored man. Judge J. W. Blackwood is said to have received a dispatch containing the intelligence this morning. Gov. Hughes has had nothing in confirmation of the news, and if it is true, Crittenden county officials feel able to cope with the existing state of affairs. The Governor says, however, he is ready to act instantly on being called on for assistance, as the laws of Arkansas are supreme and must be obeyed. There is no equivocation in this. Sheriff Werner, of Crittenden, arrived in the city today bringing a couple of prisoners to the penitentiary, but says he knows nothing of the reports. Everything was quiet on his leaving Marion yesterday morning. THE APPEAL correspondent mentioned the affair to Judge John McClure, of this city, who he found at the Capitol tonight.

"I only know what Blackwood's dispatch is said to contain," remarked this biggest of Arkansas Republicans. Everybody knows Judge McClure in this section, as well as a great many outside of this State have the honor of his acquaintance. Powell Clayton, McClure & Co. are the Republican party of this State. "Yes, that is all I know about the matter. They ought to have hung Lewis. He was a bad character. At the Republican State convention in this city, some time ago, Lewis objected to something that I said, and I told him then he would not last until the election, nor he hasn't. He evidently didn't know the whites of Crittenden county as well as I do. They treated Lewis very nicely. Bought him a ticket, took him to the train and put him aboard, told him to leave the country and not come back again. Lewis did not leave, but came here and stayed a few days, when he made fool of himself. He thought the whites down there didn't mean anything when they told him to leave the county. But they did, and he found out what they meant, too, and I don't blame them one bit. He deserved to be hung, and so does any other man who thinks he is bigger than the law."

DRIVEN FROM HOME. Colored Men Expelled by an Arkansas Mob. The Men Nearly Ali Well Educated and Prominent-Property Holders Ejected On Pain of Death - The Facts in the Case.
MARION, Ark.—The Democrats of Crittenden County have made the record. Their action in wiping out "Negro domination," as it is called down there, deserves the first place among the like acts which have taken place this side of Mason and Dixon's line since 1876. Crittenden County has a history full of bloody deeds.

"It would take a mighty big book to tell of all the killings we've had, sir," said one of the citizens to-day. But this wholesale banishment did not have the inspiration of any bloodshed, and stranger still, it was carried out without the taking of a single life, although there have been times during the last two weeks when every breeze was expected to bring the crack of the Winchester and when hundreds of colored men thought they had seen sunshine for the last time. But, perhaps, it is too early for congratulations. The Circuit Court is presided over by Judge Riddick, a white man and a Democrat. One afternoon Judge Riddick received a request for the use of the room immediately upon adjournment, and granted it, adjourning court. The colored clerk was asked to step down stairs and write up his docket away from the court-room, as the meeting was to be with closed doors. The white men met. There was some talking and considerably applause. The next morning there were 150 white men in the county seat. They came from all parts of the county, and every man carried his Winchester rifle or his revolver. Before twenty-four hours passed the county had been "reliaved" of the following, all colored:

LEWIS, DANIEL W., County Judge, educated at Oberlin, who has held office since 1870 as Deputy Clerk, and then as a member of the Legislature.

FERGUSON, DAVID, County Clerk and exofficio Clerk of the Probate Court and Recorder, a triple position worth $6,000 a year. He was serving his sixth year and was thought well enough off in the State to be sent to Chicago to help nominate the Republican National ticket.

ROOKS, J. W., County Assessor, who lived at Edmundson Station on the Memphis & Little Rock railroad.

HUNT, F., Deputy County Clerk. He is well-educated, better known in Tennessee than Arkansas. He was at one time Register of the City of Memphis.

BYERS, YORK, deputy sheriff. His home was at Crawfordsville, where he had a plantation and growing crops.

LAWRENCE, the Rev. J. F., pastor of the "Rising Sun" Baptist church.

BEAVER, W., formerly deputy sheriff.

FLEMING, J. L., Editor of the Marion Headlight. He was raised in the county, but was educated in Memphis.

SMITH, GEORGE, a laborer.

NEMIS, "Tice," a laborer.

RAMSEY, J. W., deputy in the County Clerk's office.

METCHUM, O. W., a one-armed man. He is a lawyer and was formerly deputy postmaster at Jericho, on the Gulf road in this county. Metchum is of considerable more than ordinary education. He was admitted six months ago to practice at the bar.

RAGSDALE, the Rev. J. R., a Methodist preacher.

ODOM, "Sandy," a member of the Legislature from Crittenden County.

MOORE, F. T., a magistrate at Marion. His family is still here. He was prominent in the "Rising Sun" church and is on the list of "conspirators."

BAYBEE, HENRY a laborer.

FLEMING, E., brother of the editor of the Headlight.

GREEN, MOCK, a blacksmith.

BROWN, LOUIS, a music teacher.

FLETCHER, C. A., a school teacher.

Ten other colored men were driven out whose names are not given. Ferguson had bought property in Marion, but it was in his wife's name. She is still here. It will seem to some a striking coincidence that the chosen leader of the white men who exiled Ferguson was the former owner of the property which the county clerk had bought. This white man had thought well enough of Ferguson at one time to let him have the property at one-half what he was offered for it by others. Ferguson has been a political leader in the county for many years. He came here from Ohio, having received his education in the Cincinnati high school. His account of his departure, as he told it after getting out of the county, is as follows:

"I was at work in the Court House on Thursday morning, when in stepped eighty white men armed with Winchester. They said: 'Ferguson, this county is too small for you and us. Which of us will remain? You'll have to leave. If you don't, we hope you'll go to Heaven.' I replied: 'Gentlemen, I am the clerk of this county. I'm under bond and must protect my bondsmen, who are all white men.' While the men were in the office my bondsmen, who are all white men, held a consultation. They said: 'Dave, what are you going to do? We are your friends, and will stand by you.' I replied: 'Gentlemen, I will leave. The court is in session. The grand and petit jurors are impanelled and every thing is in readiness to hold the July term of court. Who is going to be responsible? Who is my successor?"

"I returned to my office, and with seventy-five Winchester flashing in my face, I was ordered to copy and sign a resignation, which they had already written—a very unpleasant task, and not the safest place in the world to perform the duty. After I signed the resignation I was escorted to the train by I dont know how many white men, who told me to git, and I got."

SWIFT VENGEANCE TAKEN.
A South Carolina Desperado's Terrible Crime.
COLUMBIA, S. C., May 27.—[Special.]—Great excitement is reported to exist in the upper portion of Union county, this state, in consequence of the brutal murder of Gunnings Byers, a white youth of sixteen years, by a negro named Ben Cunningham. This negro had previously had a difficulty with Byers's father, on whose farm he was a tenant, swearing vengeance against the whole Byers family. Cunningham took it on the first member he met unprotected. Meeting young Byers alone in the woods he dealt him a mortal blow on the head with an ax and then fled. A party are already in pursuit, and it is not likely that Cunningham can escape. There is much talk of lynching him, and unless he falls into the hands of the authorities before the pursuers take him he will doubtless never come to trial.

The finest private collection of old almanacs in America is said to be owned by one of the justices of the supreme court of the United States. The rarest almanac in the country probably is one published by William Bradford in 1686. It is in the collection of the Historical society, of Pennsylvania and is valued at $350.

SOUTH CAROLINA NEWS.
Mrs. M. E. Keys, proprietress of the Keys Hotel, Anderson, S. C., has been accused of being an accomplice to the numerous fires that have occurred there, but has been declared innocent by a committee of inquiry. Mrs. Keys is a daughter of Mrs. Cochran, formerly a popular hotel proprietress in Anderson.

In the United States Court at Charleston, last Thursday, judgment for $10,000 was given by a jury against the bondsmen of Chas. E. Bartlett, cashier of the Sumter national bank, who absconded after stealing the entire capital of the bank. There is no knowledge of Bartlett's whereabouts. He has not been heard from since his departure. The bondsmen will accept the judgment without appeal.

On Tuesday of last week, while Theron Earle, son of the Rev. T. J. Earle, of Gowensville, in Spartanburg county, and his sister, Miss Juliet Earle, were attempting to cross North Tyger river at Turner's mills, the buggy and occupants were swept down the stream by the flood and drifted over the mill dam. Miss Earle fell on the rocks, and her skull being fractured, she sank and never reappeared until her dead body was found the next morning. Young Mr. Earle was separated from his sister and was saved in a half drowned condition by the miller, who had seen the accident and had gone to the rescue.

Calvin Williams and Allen Smith, both white farmers living near Greenville, were drowned last Saturday in Reedy river at Fork Shoals mill. A large fishing party had collected there, and Williams and Smith were drawing the seine. Williams was taken with cramps, when Smith tried to save him, and both were drowned. Among the fishing party were Mayor Townes and several lawyers from Greenville. Mr. J. A Mooney, a young lawyer, plunged into the river and tried to save the drowning men, but failed. Each of the drowned men leaves a family.

— About 11 o'clock on Monday morning of last week, says the Greenville News, a little eight-year-old son of Samuel Brown, the miller at Richardson's mills, two miles from Piedmont, was fishing in the stream near by the water wheel of the mill. There was an upright shaft near which was revolving rapidly. The little fellow jerked his fishing rod for a bite, when the line was caught around the revolving shaft and was twisted around the shaft and around the boy's arm at the same time. The tough cord refused to break, and the terrible result was the cutting off of the unfortunate little fellow's arm about three inches from the shoulder. The limb was cut off as smoothly and as sharply as if by a knife, and almost before the victim could realize his position.

— A few weeks ago, Joe James, a citizen of Darlington county, was assassinated and killed by being shot under circumstances of atrocity that startled the people in that community. Investigation leads to the belief that his son, Joe James, Jr., procured two negroes to commit the deed, agreeing to pay them $500 each to murder his father. He and two negro men are in jail charged with the crime, or being accessory thereto, but Bob Arthur, colored, who is thought to be the one who fired the shot, has evaded arrest up to the present time. Young James is chained down in the dungeon, and the trial justice who committed him refuses him a preliminary hearing, although his counsel has repeatedly demanded it. It is possible and indeed probable, that the sheriff is in possession of some very strong evidence which he does not care to have made public before the case goes to trial.

— A terrible tragedy occurred near Wilkinsville, in Union county, last Thursday evening. It appears that Mr. William Byers, one of the largest planters in that part of the county, had a difficulty a few days ago with one of his tenants, a negro man named Ben Cunningham, which so enraged the negro that he swore vengeance against the whole Byers family; and on Friday, meeting young Gunning Byers, son of Mr. William Byers, aged about 16 years, attacked him with an axe, striking him in the head, inflicting a wound which will prove fatal. The negro made his escape and had not been captured at last accounts. The foregoing is from the Greenville News of Sunday. The News and Courier of Monday has a dispatch from Spartanburg dated Sunday, which says: "Yesterday Mr. Byers was resting quietly and was rational. The negro was arrested at noon yesterday. He was hiding out several miles from home. The officers have started towards the Court House with him."

THE CROPS OF THE COUNTRY.—The South Carolina weather service furnishes the following concerning the effect of the weather on the various crops in the State for the week ending last Saturday:

The rainfall for the past week has been above the average, and for the same period the temperature has been below the average, with but little sunshine.

In the northern counties, the weather for the last seven days has been injurious to crops. Heavy rains have fallen, Spartanburg reporting over four and a half inches in two and a half days; also that cotton had been washed out and that farmers will have to replant. Others report wheat blown down, or land too wet to work. In the middle counties the cool wet weather has been unfavorable for cotton and corn; other crops are doing well. Bottom land inundated, but no washing or pounding has been reported. Three days of farm work has been lost by rain. Fairfield, Kershaw and Darlington report over two inches of rainfall, Newberry and Sumter over three inches, and Orangeburg and Barnwell over four

inches. The southern counties have had too much rain for cotton and corn. During the week three days have been too wet to plough.

The National weather crop bulletin for the week ending Saturday says:

"The weather has been generally favorable in the States of the Mississippi Valley, resulting in the general improvement of the crop conditions. Local storms have caused some damage in Arkansas and in Louisiana, rendering it necessary to replant cotton in some sections. The deficiency of rainfall in Mississippi is reported as having unfavorably affected crops in that section. The continued rains during the past week have retarded farm work in the Middle Atlantic States, but the condition of wheat, rye, oats and grass have been improved.

For the Yorkville Enquirer.

BETHESDA FARMERS' CLUB.

GUTHRIESVILLE, May 28.—On last Saturday afternoon, the Bethesda Farmers' Club met and reorganized, electing W. N. Elder, President; Capt. E. A. Crawford, C. L. Percival and J. R. Logan, Vice-Presidents; and Alfred Moore, Secretary.

J. F. Hinson offered the following resolutions, which, after some discussion, were unanimously adopted:

1st. Resolved, That this club approves the policy contained in the address issued by the executive committee of the Farmers' State Association.

2nd. That the farmers of this club demand the acceptance of the Clemson bequest by the State, and that the Legislature make the appropriation necessary for the establishment of an agricultural college.

3rd. This club respectfully requests all candidates for nomination to either branch of the General Assembly, to express their views through the county papers and in the canvass, upon the establishment of a separate agricultural college and the reduction of salaries in the executive and judiciary departments.

4th. That farmers should vote in the primary for no candidate who will not fully pledge himself to vote and work for the establishment of a separate agricultural college and the application of the land script fund, the Hatch fund and the privilege tax for the maintenance of said institution, and for a reduction of salaries in the executive and judiciary departments.

5th. We deprecate any party division, recognizing the fact that the Democratic party of the State is the resultant of the mutual concession among men of different sentiments, and that upon unity depends the perpetuation of good government.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES.
Williams and Allen Smith, two white men were drowned while seining in Reedy river, near Fork Shoals, this afternoon. Williams, while in deep water, was taken with a cramp, was in the act of drowning when Smith tried to rescue him. In the attempt to do so he also was drowned. J. A. Mooney, a prominent lawyer of Greenville, seeing both would drown unless help was rendered, plunged in and made a gallant attempt to save them, but without success, life being extinct from both bodies, when found a few hours later. Williams leaves a wife and four children and Smith a wife and five children.

CHICAGO, May 34.—A dispatch from Bonham, Texas, says: A destructive cyclone swept over Brownton, 25 miles east of here, yesterday evening, destroying the Methodist, Baptist and Congregational churches and eight dwellings. One building was carried across a railroad track and crushed. Amanda Willis (colored), who had taken refuge inside, was instantly killed. Eight persons, including the Sheriff and County Recorder, were fatally injured. The damage will exceed $12,000. The path of the storm was three hundred yards wide and everything within those limits, crops, fences, barns, outhouses and trees, was swept away. A terrible rain, hail and lightning storm followed.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., May 26.—Eugene Chalfant, a laborer in the glass works at New Albany, Ind., died here this morning of hydrophobia. He was bitten some weeks ago by a small Spitz dog, but as the wound healed he paid no attention to it. Yesterday he was seized with slight paroxysms of nausea which he could not explain. He sent for a doctor, who, by the time of his arrival, found Chalfant frothing at the mouth and delirious. In spite of attempts to relieve him the malady grew worse through the night until this morning. The sufferer was passing through a succession of terrible convulsions, which rapidly grew more frequent, until death. The immediate cause of death was the bursting a blood vessel.

COLUMBIA, S.C., May 27.—Great excitement is reported to exist in the upper portion of Union county, this State, in consequence of the brutal murder of Gunnings Byers, a white youth of sixteen years, by a negro named Ben Cunningham. This negro had previously had a difficulty with Byers's father, on whose farm he was a tenant, swearing vengeance against the whole Byers family. Cunningham took it on the first member he met unprotected. Meeting young Byers alone in the woods he dealt him a mortal blow on the head with an ax and then fled. A party are already in pursuit, and it is not likely that Cunningham can escape. There is much talk of lynching him, and unless he falls into the hands of the authorities before the pursuers take him he will doubtless never come to trial.

BIRMINGHAM, ALA., May 25.—A bloody and brutal tragedy occurred late last night at Helena, a small mining town, fifteen miles south of this city. A number of negro laborers were drinking together, and Jack Williams and Dick Russell became involved in a quarrel. Williams drew a long-bladed knife, and attacking Russell came near cutting his heart out. The negro's breast and abdomen were laid open by heavy blows with the dirk, and he was otherwise mutilated in a horrible manner. The second stab with the dirk laid open Russell's breast and penetrated the heart, killing him instantly. Williams was arrested by three white men. While on the way to the jail he attacked them, and succeeded in making his escape, after having severely beat one of his captors. He is still at large, but was trailed with blood-hounds to-day.

TOPEKA, KAN., May 23.—A pardon has been issued by Governor Martin to Chas. H. Rotrock of Ottawa County, who killed his wife a number of years ago while under the influence of liquor. The peculiar feature of the pardon is the fact that the Governor issued it upon the condition that Rotrock will forever abstain from the use of intoxicating liquor. Such a condition has never been imposed in a pardon issued by a Governor of this State. The Supreme Court of Iowa has held that the Governor may impose any condition he chooses in granting a pardon, and that in case the condition is ever violated the person pardoned may be rearrested on the order of the Governor and made to serve the balance of the penalty. Attorney General Bradford has advised the Governor that such a condition as imposed in Rotrock's pardon would be sustained by the courts.

COLUMBIA, S.C., May 25—An attempt at poisoning, which came near being successful, is reported from Yorkville. The household of Withers Adickes, a prominent citizen of the place, consists of six grown persons. All felt alarming symptoms immediately after breakfast; and a physician's services were required. He said their symptoms indicated arsenical poison. They all recovered after treatment. Next morning Adickes, suspecting something still wrong, went to the kitchen, and there found that a gray powder had been put into the several articles of uncooked food. Analysis by two different tests showed the presence of arsenic in these articles, including the milk. The second attempt to poison somebody was more determined than the first. Anabel Jones, a negro woman, has been arrested on suspicion and she is in Yorkville jail. The generally accepted theory is, that the attempt to poison was directed against Adickes's cook, also a colored woman.

ATLANTA, GA., May 25.—A few weeks ago a man located in Green County and called himself "Abbiddigal" or "Holy One," said he had received instruction by Divine revelation to free the negroes of Georgia from the bondage of a false religion, and deluded them into believing he was the colored Saviour. He held services in the fields and groves and adorned himself on these occasions with gaudy turbans and flowing robes. He had beads and ornaments that he sold readily as shields against the power of Satan. He was regarded by the white people as a harmless crank. The stranger secretly informed the negroes that there was a "land of promise" which he had recently discovered. There will be an effort made to send from Edgefield to the Congressional Convention twelve delegates who will support a Cleveland-Mills bill Democrat to represent the Second district in the next Congress.

A difficulty between Mr. J. Frank Kellar, white, and Thornton Hughey, colored, occurred Thursday on the outskirts of Greenwood, in which Hughey was dangerously shot by Kellar in the thigh and face.

The Rev. J. Thomas Pate, pastor of the Southern Methodist church at Florence, has recently declined a tempting offer from a large Northern publishing house to take charge of its business in the Southern States.

Barney Garrett, son of the widow of Thos. G. Garrett, died at Greenville, suddenly, a few days ago, of neuralgia, superinduced by an aching tooth. Some suppose the young man died of an overdose of an anesthetic taken to allay the pain.

A son of R. G. Sims, of Lancaster county, was recently walking through his father's fields, and while not looking he stepped on a snake. He was bitten twice before he could jump out of the way, but fortunately nothing more serious than swelling resulted.

While a party of gentlemen were seining in Reedy river, near Greenville, a few days ago, Allen Smith got into water over his head, and was drowning, when Calvin Williams swam to his rescue, and Smith clinching him around the neck, both were drowned.

The Rev. J. W. Welling, formerly of the South Carolina Conference of the Southern Methodist church, who has been spending the past several years in Brazil as a missionary, has been forced to resign his position on account of bad health, and is now en route home.

Mrs. Lewis Wingo, near Wellford, was killed by lightning Tuesday afternoon while she was sitting near the fireplace. Two children were in the room at the time, but were not hurt. The husband and the other children were in the field at work, and had taken refuge in an out-house.

The following are the nineteen varieties of cotton with which experiments are being made at the Darlington station: Williamson, McIver, Peterkin, Allen long staple, Truitt, Chambers, Rogers, Southern Hope, Crawford, Miles, McCall, Dearing, Jeff Welburn, Excelsior, Crossland, Winters, Herlong, Eureka, and Black Prolific.

State Treasurer Bamberg announces that the floating of the $400,000 of the new 4½ per cent. bonds is practically completed. The commencement exercises of the Newberry College will take place on June 17-19. The address to the graduates of the Theological Seminary will be delivered by the Rev. H. S. Wingard. The alumni address will be delivered by Burr James Ramage, of New York city. Prof. F. C. Woodward, of Wofford College, will deliver the literary address.

A terrible tragedy occurred a day or two since near Wilkinsville, in Union county. A negro man named Ben Cunningham was working on the farm of William Byers, one of the largest planters in that section, and, becoming enraged with Mr. Byers, swore he would exterminate the whole family. Next day, meeting young William Byers, the 16-year-old son of his employer, he hit him in the head with an ax, killing him.

On Oct. 31, 1880, there were 78 companies of State volunteer troops upon the rolls; a year later there were 900,000 of the United States regulation uniform, obtained at cost from the War Department, will be about $500. At the present rate of assistance rendered by the general government, all the South Carolina companies as yet unprovided for will be fully uniformed in the course of a couple of years without cost to the State, provided they adopt the United States army uniform. This, it seems probable, will be done. The militia now have a very fair equipment of arms.

A case of fatality from the use of faith cure is reported from Darlington county. Some weeks ago Annette, the daughter of W. M. Maness, a well-to-do white farmer, was stricken with dysentery, but the disease soon yielded to the treatment of a regular physician. In the meantime a corps of the
W. M. Maness, a well-to-do white farmer, was strenken with dysentery, but the disease soon yielded to the treatment of a regular physician. In the meantime a corps of the Salvation Army came along, and with it Miss Mattie Gordon, a faith cure physician. Miss Gordon appeared at the girl's bedside, and soon induced her to leave off the doctor's medicine and adopt the faith remedy. The mother protested, but the child was firm in her convictions, and refused to take the doctor's medicine. As a consequence the disease took a firmer hold, and with nothing to check it raged with more violence than ever. Day after day it sapped the substance of the victim, and with nothing but faith to sustain the system, she continued to sink. Finally, the physician was recalled, and he called in other doctors in consultation, but all their efforts were fruitless, and the victim of the faith cure doctrine breathed her last.

Correspondence of the Yorkville Enquirer. NOTES FROM UNION COUNTY.
ETTA JANE, June 4.—The abundant rain-fall of last week did great damage to the farming lands. Tuesday's rains washed the land more than any rain that has fallen this year in this section. On Capt. S. S. Walker's plantation, below the mouth of Thickety creek, the hail was heavy. It riddled the corn blades and beat down and otherwise injured his oats. There was but little wind during the storm.

Farmers are more or less disheartened about their wheat crops. The "scab" has made its appearance, which, with rust in some places, makes it entirely worthless. Oats are not so good as might be expected; too much rain for them.

An account of the wounding of Gunning Byers, by Jerry Cunningham, colored, has already reached your readers. Some of the published statements are quite erroneous—particularly that of the Atlanta Constitution. It is a lamentable fact that many newspaper reporters look upon the history of Ananias and Sapphira as a mere myth.

Of the difficulty that led to the wounding of young Byers, it is not our purpose to speak. The stone shown us as the one the negro threw and struck him with, will, we think, weigh about four pounds. The distance he threw it is claimed to be twenty-eight yards. The stone struck him above the left eye near the edge of the hair. After he was wounded the young man walked several hundred yards to his home, going a zig-zag course, unable to follow the path. Dr. M. J. Walker, who lives within a few hundred yards of Mr. Byers, was called immediately. Fortunately the messenger met the Doctor near the edge of Mr. Byers' yard, on his way to see another patient. In a few minutes he had examined the wound and removed twenty-four pieces of the fractured skull,

which were more or less imbedded in the brain. A considerable portion of the brain substance oozed out. One spicula of bone, much deeper than the others, pressed on the optic nerve. After its removal the patient regained consciousness, and has remained so ever since. The wound is suppurating freely, and at each dressing particles of injured brain are being removed. At last accounts the patient was doing well. We have studiously avoided giving the details, as the matter will undergo a legal investigation. The difficulty took place on Mr. Byers' plantation.

We regret to say that Mr. Henry Wilkinson, of Hopewell, is lying quite sick. He has been suffering for a long time with consumption. His children are mostly girls. We hope his kind neighbors will assist his wife and children in working their crop.

Miss Rebecca Davidson, whose affliction we reported some time ago, has recovered the use of her limbs. Her mind is still much impaired.

Rev. J. W. Query will preach at Salem next Sunday, 10th instant. SIGMA.

Eight Horse Thieves Lynched.
KANSAS CITY, MO., April 21.—Reports reached here Friday of the lynching of eight horse thieves in southwestern Indian territory. A deputy sheriff says that the thieves were surprised by a posse of citizens, and a running fight ensued, in which one of the posse was killed. The entire gang was later surrounded and shot or hanged. Bill Higgle, alias "Scar-Face," and Curley Frank were the only two that were known.

The president has approved the act for the purchase of the swords of the late General James Shields, and the act regulating the terms of United States courts in the northern district of Iowa.

Outlaws Summarily Disposed Of.
PURCELL, I. T., April 20.—[Special Telegram to the BEE.]—The reports of the killing of a band of horse thieves and outlaws southwest of here thirty miles, are confirmed.
It is the same outfit which lost old Bill Morgan several days ago at the hands of vigilantes. They were pursued by a posse, surprised and eight of the party strung up without a chance to make confession. A running fight was kept up in which one of the posse was killed. Those known of the gang killed are Bill Higgle, Oliver Scarface and Curly Frank. The remainder are unknown. This has been the boldest set of cut-throats and thieves this section ever had to contend with.

Charged With Malpractice.

St. Joseph, Mo., April 20.—[Special Telegram to the Bee.]—John Hordt brought suit to-day for $10,000 against Dr. C. L. E. Webber for malpractice, which the petitioner claims resulted in the death of his wife about six weeks ago. It is allaged that Webber attempted to perform an abortion. Webber's case was investigated by the grand jury, but no indictment was found against him. The verdict of the coroner's jury at the time of Mrs. Hordt's death that her death was due to criminal malpractice produced a great sensation.

Rearranging Iowa Rates.

Chicago, April 20.—The general freight agents of the Iowa railroad lines held a conference here to-day on the question of raising freight rates in that state to conform with the new law recently enacted by the Iowa legislature. A committee composed of representatives of the competing roads was appointed to arrange a schedule of distance tariffs to be submitted at an adjourned meeting to be held to-morrow.

Caused By a Misplaced Switch.

Winfield, Kan., April 20.—[Special Telegram to the Bee.]—By a misplaced switch on the Santa Fe & Walnut Valley route, a northbound freight train of grain and merchandise was ditched to-day. Fifteen cars were totally destroyed and the track torn up for several hundred feet. Fireman George Ellis was injured and Brakeman Frank Moody's leg broken and his spine crushed.

BATTLE WITH HORSE THIEVES.
WICHITA, Kan., April 20.—Ever since last fall farmers in the counties of Texas and Kansas, adjoining Indian Territory, have been annoyed by horse thieves, who have been unusually bold in their periodical raids. Visits from the marauders became so frequent that the farmers formed a Vigilance Committee to exterminate the thieves. Four weeks ago the vigilants, armed with Winchesters, six-shooters and lariats, started on the trail of the marauders, but it was not until they had been two weeks in the saddle that they found any trace of the robbers' camp.

While the vigilants were travelling through the western part of the Indian Nation ten days ago they suddenly ran across the thieves in a deep ravine. The outlaws were in their blankets, but not asleep. When the vigilants rode up the crest of the ravine the thieves, who were in command of Bill Higgins, alias "Scar Face," sprang to their horses near by, but in mounting one of their number was shot dead. The others put spurs to their animals, and were soon throwing dust and bullets in the eyes of their pursuers.

The horses ridden by the vigilants were more or less fatigued by the night's ride, and were in no condition to give the outlaws' horses any sort of a race; but the race was begun, and the trail of the thieves was easily followed. For the first ten miles there was a continual roar from the heavy rifles on both sides, although no one was injured. The fight soon resolved itself into a question of endurance.

After a furious chase lasting all day the vigilants, who had been able to keep in sight of the outlaws, succeeded in driving the gang upon a butte near a small creek, where preparations were made for a desperate resistance. As the vigilants approached flashes of fire came from the crest of every boulder on the hill and a deafening report reverberated through the narrow desiles. The first volley from the outlaws killed Peter Ackerman of Medicine Lodge, Kan. The thieves were surrounded as much as possible and the fight continued. One by one the rifles of the thieves were silenced, until but few flashes answered the volleys from the vigilants. When the sun went down a white rag was raised on the summit of the butte.

Its appearance was answered by another volley from the vigilants, who then charged up the hill with a yell. Three of the outlaws escaped in the darkness, but "Scar Face," Hank Windom, and Curly Bill were captured and killed. Curly Bill and Windom were riddled with bullets, but the true Western justice was reserved for "Scar Face," who, although nearly dead from the loss of blood, was dragged to death from the pommel of a saddle. Four other members of the gang were found dead behind their stone barriers.

curly-bill-purcell-1888-04-21.A8: THE pursuit of and battle with a band of outlaws in the far Northwest, and their capture by a troop of organized farmers, as reported by telegraph, is an incident in frontier life that has more than once been repeated. It in nowise reflected upon our civilization, until after the capture. We can have nothing but condemnation for lynch law. It is never defensible. But in a broad territory where the law cannot furnish society with authorized agents sufficient in number to guard an immense expanse of country, it becomes an absolute necessity that orderly citizens shall render voluntary aid to the officers of the law. These western outlaws were organized depredators. They roamed through the country, robbing, killing and burning. It was a necessity to treat them upon their own ground, and in the only way through which they could be approached, and that was in the open field and with the cocked rifle. They invoked the wager of battle, and it was necessary that it should be fought out. The farmers who organized, and then pursued these maruaders should not be called vigilantes, for their pursuit and capture; they did that which any Sheriff's posse would have done, had the law been equal to the needs of Western life in a territory so vast and with settlements so widely separated. As citizens the farmers without warrant had the right to pursue and arrest the highwaymen; as the foe resisted with shot, the pursuers are not to be condemned for replying in like, instead of fleeing. That they executed three of the gang after its surrender, is to be debited against them. It was a cruel, indefensible and a cowardly act. To that point they had acted up to the needs of society, beyond that they became lynchers, agents of vengeance and examples of the element of savagery remaining in man.

"Early to Bed."
Growing children should have all the sleep nature demands. To make sure of this, the bedtime should be no later than 9 o'clock for children under ten. This habit of early bedtime will take care of itself, if it be persevered in by parents at first. Some men and women would be not only stronger, but cleverer, if they had all the sleep they needed when children.

The difference between children whose parents enforce obedience in this respect and those little old people who sit up late at night is very marked. The clear eyes, rosy cheeks and round strong limbs of the former should rebuke parents who allow children to sit up late because they wish to. Nothing can be more pernicious than to allow children up late at watering places. They taste then of the highly spiced society life, none too healthy for the strongest, and in the hot house air and stimulating influences, their natures are forced to results that may break down their own health, and the health of their parents also.—Ex.

Let children sleep as late in the morning as they wish, so that it does not interfere with School hours. Many farmers, especially, arouse their children too early of a morning. The time will come soon when the children, as men, can not sleep a morning's nap. Let the dear children have as much fun and sleep as they want in early days.

The Democrats of Tennessee are in a terrible fuss about who shall be nominated for Governor. Taylor is the present Governor, and wants to be renominated, but is opposed by Col. McConnell, who wants the nomination; consequently there is a stir-up in nearly every Democratic meeting in the State. The claims of men on the party for nominations amount to very little, for generally the men who do the most work for the party never claim anything. The dead-heads in the party often get the offices and paying places, as they have done under Mr Cleveland's administration. A man who cannot live without an office is not fit for an office of any sort. Who says that is not true? Let us ignore personal claims and nominate the best men as our Democratic candidates.

It is rather amusing to old printers to see how some newspapers are conducted by editorial aspirants. They seem to think that editing a paper means only to write and spin out long pieces from their pencils or pens, and place them under the "editorial heading," and never do any editing to other parts of their paper, such as correcting communications, refusing articles that are personally offensive and calculated to engender personal strife and difficulty, making selections of the best matter from their exchanges, leaving out what is wrong and useless, and refraining from puffing everything and everybody. The writing of "editorials" is the smallest work about a paper; it is not half the work to be done by a respectable Editor. But, then, nearly everybody think they can edit a paper, run a hotel, or keep a livery stable. There are many papers but few good Editors. Editing a paper is an acquired trade or profession, as much so as setting the type and printing the paper,

Taxation for public school purposes is becoming a very serious matter in North Carolina, and many persons think that the taxes paid by the white people should be used in educating only the white children, and the taxes paid by the colored people should be used in educating the colored children. This proposition is being discussed in many portions of the State, and it is possible that a resolution will be introduced into the Democratic State Convention, on the 30th of May, advocating an amendment to our State Constitution so as to accomplish this object. Few persons are aware of the amount of money expended in this State for public schools. For several years it has been over six hundred thousand dollars a year—a sum equal to that expended for defraying all other expenses of the State government. At least three-fourths of the poll tax, and a property tax of 14½ cents on the one hundred dollars' valuation, are applied for school purposes. Every tax-payer may know from this statement how much he pays every year for the equal education of the white and colored children of the State. Of course the great bulk of the taxes collected for school purposes is paid by the white people, and yet generally throughout the State the terms of the schools for colored children are much longer than the terms of the schools for white children. The Superintendent of Public Instruction says that over 20,000 colored polls, liable to taxation, are not listed. It is no wonder that some dissatisfaction exists among the white tax payers, and that they should wish that their money be used in educating only their own children.—Pittsboro Record.

[Thousands of the white tax-payers of the State will cordially endorse what the Record says. They are tired paying taxes for mere book learning for negro youths, without the inculcation of morality and industry. Let the people send men to the next Legislature who will resist the pressure for more taxation for nothing but book schools. No reasonable person will object to paying a reasonable tax for educating the children of the State in the rudiments or lower branches of books, but a tax should not be levied for the higher branches.]

REPEAL THE WAR TAXES.—It has been exclusively shown that the Internal Revenue Taxes are War Taxes, contrary to the spirit of the compact between the States and the Federal Government, and justified only by extraordinary emergencies. They have never been levied except to carry on war for the life of the nation, and they have always been repealed as soon as the occasion for them has passed. All the early statesmen of the country united in denouncing them as unjustifiable in times of peace, and declared that custom duties were the legitimate source of our national revenue.

Notwithstanding these indisputable facts, large numbers of influential men are found, at this time, insisting upon the continuance of the existing internal revenue taxes, although it is universally recognized that they are not only not necessary for the uses of government, but that the money collected from these war taxes is a burdensome surplus, a source of corruption and a grievous injury to the business interests of the people.

Lawyers, judges and conservative men generally in Charleston give Sheriff Smith unstinted praise for shooting down the Birmingham lynchers. They only wish that more of the same kind of Smiths were Sheriffs all over the South.

In South Carolina there have been lynchings in abundance, and so far no lyncher has been punished. Some months ago Judge Pressley told the Grand Jury of York that it was almost useless to investigate the lynching of three negroes in that county as, if a bill should be found against them, it could hardly be expected that the jury would convict them. This was an extreme view, perhaps, but it is certain that no lyncher has ever been punished.

I interviewed tonight a number of prominent men here in regard to the Birmingham affair. Capt. F. W. Dawson, editor of the News and Courier, said:

"The attempted lynching at Birmingham is the natural sequence of the lynching of colored men by whites for assaults upon white women. It was inevitable that the violation of law in the one instance should lead to similar acts in the other. There was the excuse in the case of negroes that only swifter punishment than the law could give would be likely to terrify them. Experience proves that lynching has not even this redeeming feature. The deaths at Birmingham might possibly have been averted had the Sheriff been more cool, but awful as the loss of life is, under the circumstances, the event will go further to stop lynching than years of preaching by the press and in the pulpit. BEATEN BY A BRUTE.
Little Jockey Brown Assaulted by a Drunken Hotel Keeper with a Baseball Bat.
SHEEPSHEAD BAY, Oct. 27.—This village was the scene Thursday evening of one of the most brutal crimes ever committed on Long Island. Henry Granel is the proprietor of a small hotel. He is a middle aged man, weighs 190 pounds, and when intoxicated, a not unusual occurrence, he is a perfect fiend.

He was in this condition Thursday evening at 8 o'clock when Jockey Brown, a 17-year-old boy, weighing eighty pounds, entered the hotel. In a conversation that followed Granel became incensed and struck Brown. The latter retaliated, and then, before any of the bystanders could interfere, Granel grasped a baseball bat and struck the boy in the head, felling him to the floor.

The enraged hotel proprietor then turned on the spectators and they fled, leaving him master of the situation. Later they found Rem Williamson, a policeman, and it was not until they had threatened dire vengeance that he consented to act.

He arrested Granel, and thereupon the mob, characteristic of its name, talked loudly of Lynch law. Garrison Morris, another policeman, then took charge of Granel, and, drawing his revolver, held the crowd back. He took the would be murderer to Coney Island and locked him in a cell.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES.

JOHN W. WILKIN, in charge of a Pittsburgh and New York mail car, was detected opening letters in Philadelphia, on the 23d, and arrested.

JOHN S. HALLER, of Cincinnati, on the 24th, cut his wife's throat from ear to ear with a razor, with which he then cut his own throat, severing the jugular.

It is estimated that the loss to the Pennsylvania railroad by the freight collision near Tyrone, on the 23l, will reach $100,000.

By the falling of a scaffold at the new soldiers' home building, located near Minnehaha Falls, Minn., on the 21th, Henry Rietzell was so seriously injured that he died three hours afterward. Three others were badly hurt, but were expected to recover.

The National Republican committee paid $2,000, on the 25th, for the arrest and conviction of one George Gordon, for false registration in New York City.

Seven persons were poisoned, on the 25th, at a wedding party in the Bohemian Flats, Minneapolis, Minn., with "Rough on Rats" sprinkled on the dumplings, presumably by a former lover whose suit had been rejected.

In the case of the murdered paymaster and his guard near Wilkesbarre, Pa., the coroner's jury returned a verdict, on the 25th, that McClure and Flanagan came to their deaths by gunshot wounds and some blunt instrument in the hands of some person or persons unknown to the jury.

It is said that two hundred warrants are to be issued for the arrest of persons illegally registering in Jersey City, N. J.

School-books found Paymaster McClure's sachel in the woods near Taylorville, Pa., on the 25th, twelve miles from the spot where the murdered paymaster's body was found.

A club-house at Moscow, Russia, collapsed, on the 25th, and sixteen corpses have been taken from the ruins. Twenty-four persons were injured.

On the 25th Charles Warren, chief clerk and cashier of the Baltimore & Ohio freight office at Columbus, O., was arrested, charged with embezzling $5,000 of the company's money.

Mrs. P. J. Lynch, wife of a wealthy retired New York merchant, jumped from a third-story window of the Hotel Bristol, on the 26th, and was killed. She was suffering from mental trouble caused by an injury to her head, sustained during a recent voyage from Europe.

It is announced that the Babylonian expedition of the University of Pennsylvania, which left Philadelphia early last summer, was shipwrecked in the Mediterranean sea, on the night of September 29, on a rock off the Island of Samas. Passengers and crew were rescued by a Turkish brigantine.

JOHN JONES, night watchman, was burned to death in the partial destruction of Platt & Co.'s oyster and fruit-packing house at Baltimore, Md., and Frank Welty was shot and probably fatally wounded by the supposed incendiary.

DEPUTY POSTMASTER MICHAEL SHELDON of Hudson, N. Y., was arrested on the 26th for mail pilfering.

For manufacturing and passing counterfeit money Gaetano Russo and his wife Para were sentenced to twelve and four years respectively, in New York, on the 26th. Both are notorious counterteers, and have been "shoving the queer" in a number of towns throughout the United States.

At Baltimore, Md., Mrs. Henrietta Spiel, aged seventy-five, and Mrs. Martha Beckel, aged sixty-five, inmates of the German Home for the Aged, were found dead in their room on the 26th. They had been suffocated by gas.

In the trial of John C. Keegan, of Scranton, Pa., for the murder of Mrs. P. M. Barrett, in May last, the jury brought in a verdict, on the 26th, of guilty of murder in the second degree.

ANNIE CONRAD, three years old, of Ft. Wayne, Ind., fell into a kettle of boiling apple butter, on the 25th, and was not discovered for several minutes. She was taken out dead.

On the 25th Henry Garnet was narrowly saved from lynching by the indignant villagers of Sheepshead, N. Y., for striking a stripling a murderous blow with a base-ball bat. The police who arrested him were compelled to draw their revolvers to keep the crowd at bay.

A JEALOUS bar-tender, of Colfax, W. T., named David Vestor, shot and killed his wife and himself on the 26th.

A Deputy Sheriff Killed by a Negro.
KNOXVILLE, May 20.—This morning Deputy Sheriff Shipe was shot and killed by Hicks Martin, a negro, whom he was attempting to arrest on the Powell Valley Railroad works, twenty miles north of Knoxville. The negro was wanted in Alabama for a murder committed there. Deputy Sheriff Shipe learned that Martin was working on the new railroad, and went to the tent where Martin was in company with other negroes and called for him. He met the Deputy Sheriff at the door with two pistols and began firing on him. Shipe fell riddled with bullets before he had time to draw his own weapon. He died in a few minutes without speaking a word. The negro escaped, and officers and citizens are scouring the country for him. He is heavily armed, and will doubtless fight his pursuers to the last should they overtake him. Should he be taken alive he will be lynched.

One Man Shot Him but Even Then He Swam a River and Escaped. KNOXVILLE, TENN. May 24.—Hicks Car-
KNOXVILLE, TENN., May 24.—Hicks Carmichael, a negro, who, while resisting arrest last Sunday morning, killed D. A. Shipe, Deputy Sheriff of Knox county, was captured this morning near Rankin's Depot, sixty miles east of Knoxville. Officers have been scouring the country in all directions since Sunday. Last night one officer discovered him and got near enough to fire a load of buckshot into him, but the negro got away in the darkness by swimming a river. He was tracked to-day by a dozen men and surrounded. When captured he had two loaded revolvers on his person. He was brought to Knoxville on the next train, and was followed to jail by a crowd of 2,000 people. No attempt was made to lynch Carmichael, who is now in jail, strongly guarded. He is said to be a desperate character, and to have murdered a woman in Alabama some months ago.
