A DISGRACEFUL MOB.
Attempts to Get a Jailed Murderer in Knoxville.
Knoxville.

Special Dispatch to The Appeal.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn., May 24.—Hicks Carmichael, the negro who killed Deputy Sheriff Shipel last Sunday, was captured in Cook county this morning and brought to Knoxville at noon. He was seriously wounded, but not fatally before, being captured. Fully 1,000 people followed the bus in which the officers took him from the train to the jail. He was safely jailed, however, in spite of the excited but not dangerous crowd. Tonight about 8 o'clock 2,000 or more men and boys assembled at the jail. It was a howling mob with no organization. They yelled and hooted and called for the prisoner until finally the sheriff and jailor allowed them to search the jail and see that the man was not there. The officers had spirited him away. The mob was a disgrace to any city. The sheriff's father died today and he and his family were in deep trouble, but these wild animals paid no attention to that fact. The sheriff's father lived four miles in the country. The crowd was very angry when they could not find Carmichael, and at a late bed time many are still in the jail. It is feared that Carmichael will be lynched tomorrow when his trial comes up before the criminal court, now in session.
hicke-martin-rinkin-s-depot-1888-05-20.A11:
HE WILL HANG.
Sheriff Shipe's Murderer Gets His Deserts in Short Order.
Sheriff Shipe's Murderer Gets His Deserts in Short Order.
Special Dispatch to The Appeal.
KNOXVILLE, Tenn., May 26.—Hicks Carmichael, the negro who shot Deputy Sheriff Shipe last Sunday, was tried today in the criminal court, which has been in regular session during the past two weeks. An indictment was found against the murderer Thursday. He was arraigned this morning, tried and sentenced to be hung, all within two and a half hours. He is to hang on Friday, July 20. The murderer said that he was guilty and deserved to hang and would make no defense. The court assigned him able counsel. When the jury had been out ten minutes they returned with a verdict of murder in the first degree, and said: "Without mitigating circumstances." The judge asked the prisoner if he had anything to say. He replied, "No." The prisoner instructed his attorney not to take an appeal, but to ask the judge to give him as much time as he could in which to prepare for death. The prisoner is one-fourth Cherokee Indian. He takes his sentence coolly, and was the calmest man in the court-house during the trial. Thirty of the leading citizens and business men guarded him from harm with shotguns The "Knoxville Rifles" were also present under their captain. They, with citizens, are on guard at the jail tonight. There is no danger of a mob, as the citizens will not permit it. The demonstration Thursday night was by a set of loafing drunken boys. The citizens will put all such down. The judge has ordered the arrest of those who engaged in it. They will be prosecuted. Everything is as quiet and serene as on a June day.

He Expects to Be Hanged,
CHATTANOOGA, Tenn., May 25.—[Special.]—Hicks Carmichael, who murdered Deputy Sheriff Shipe of Knox county, last Sunday, is now in the Hamilton county jail, having been brought here last night to save a lynching at Knoxville. The prisoner acknowledges his guilt, and says he expects to be executed. Shipe had a warrant for his arrest on a charge of robbing Neal's store at Sunbright, Tenn., and Carmichael says he robbed the store and knew if he were arrested he would go to the penitentiary. He shot at Shipe to wound him that he could get away, but had no idea of killing him.

Thirsting for His Blood.
KNOXVILLE, Tenn., May 24.—Hicks Carmichael, a notorious murderer, has just been brought in and placed in jail, having been taken from the train by officers before getting into the city. Carmichael is the most desperate negro in East Tennessee. He has killed several men, the latest victim being Deputy Sheriff Shike. The jail is surrounded by an angry mob threatening to take the murderer out. The Chief of Police spoke to the crowd, urging that the law be allowed to take its course. The men who captured the negro also begged that the mob desist, as another negro was paid to betray the murderer, and they made positive promise that Carmichael should receive a fair trial.

The murdered Sheriff was very popular and his frends are wild with indignation. Judge Logan of Criminal Court, has promised that the man shall be tried to-morrow, but it is doubtful whether the promise will save the life of the doomed man. At 10 o'clock there were signs of an attempt to mob the jail.
hicke-martin-rinkin-s-depot-1888-05-20.A16:
HICKS CARMICHAEL.
Convicted of Murder in the First Degree. To Hang July 20.
KNOXVILLE, TENN., May 26.—Hicks Carmichael, the negro who murdered Deputy Sheriff Shipe last Sunday, was brought from Chattanooga this morning at 2 o'clock. He was met at the depot by a squad of police and twenty armed men, and taken to jail. Everything was perfectly quiet. This morning at 9 o'clock he was taken from the jail under a strong guard, taken before Judge Logan of the criminal court, now in session. The courthouse was packed with an immense crowd, but there was not the slightest disorder. Carmichael wanted to plead guilty, but was finally prevailed upon to accept the advice of a counsel. Gen. R. N. Hood was appointed counsel for him, who entered a plea of not guilty. A jury was soon empaneled, including some of the best citizens of the county. Four witnesses for the state were examined, but the defense offered none. The prisoner had no statement to make, and no arguments were made by either side. The judge's charge was brief and pointed. The jury returned with a verdict of guilty of murder in the first degree without extenuating circumstances. Gen. Hood's motion for a new trial was overruled. The prisoner had nothing to say. Gen. Hood stated that the defendant had no desire to delay execution, and only asked for time to prepare for death. He would make no appeal to the supreme court. Carmichael was then sentenced to hang Jul y20. The trial lasted three hours. The negro was then taken back to jail. There was no interference. Everything was perfectly quiet, and every one satisfied. There was no disposition whatever to lynch the negro. Reports published in the Nashville American, about attempts to lynch Carmichael, and the lawless acts of the mob, are greatly exaggerated.

On Sunday morning, May 20, 1888, as the people in the vicinity of Flat Creek church, on the new Knoxville, Cumberland Gap & Louisville railroad, fifteen miles north of Knoxville, were gathering in that little rural house to worship a scene of bloodshed occurred but a short distance away that set that entire section wild with excitement. Carmichael, a laborer on the works there, was wanted in Morgan county, this State. Deputy Sheriff D. A. Shipe had a warrant for the negro's arrest, and fearing trouble secured W. A. Coram, a constable, to go with him. Reaching Carmichael's tent, the officer asked for his man.

"Here I am," replied the robber in firm tones.

"Well, I have come to arrest you," answered Shipe.

"Read your warrant first," said the negro.

This the officer proceeded to do, but it proved to be his own death warrant. Carmichael seized two revolvers and fired at both officers. Instantaneously Shipe fell dead in the doorway, and Coram had his coat pierced by a bullet. The murderer ran out over the prostrate form of the officer and escaped to the hills near by.

The news of the killing spread rapidly. People in that locality and officers from Knoxville left in every direction, and for hours, without rest or food, were on the hunt for the fleet-footed criminal.

The remains of the deputy sheriff were laid to rest beneath the sod of his native country by kind and sympathetic friends. The excitement did not diminish and reached dangerous proportions when the capture of Carmichael was effected in a Cocke county barn. The murderer fought bravely, but was compelled to flee before odds, bleeding from a score or more of wounds. He swam the river and finally was caught beneath the hay in an exhausted condition. Manacled with ropes and other rude means of safety, Carmichael was brought to this city.

Upon his arrival threats of lynching were freely made, and an attempt to carry them out was made that night. The feeling against the prisoner grew so strong that he had to be removed to Chattanooga for safety. After remaining there twenty-four hours Carmichael was brought back to the city and surrounded by an armed guard of fifty leading citizens, and was given a trial on Saturday morning, May 6. The trial lasted but two hours, yet in that time the prisoner was tried, convicted and sentenced to hang today. He asked for no appeal and was put back in jail.

On June 20, at the same hour he had killed Shipe and just one month later, the murderer professed religion. After this time he seemed contented and willing to die. Carmichael's mother, small brother and grown sister reside near Rankins, in Cocke county. They will have charge of the remains and burv them there.

SEVEN NEGROES KILLED AT A CAMP-MEETING.
Birmingham, Ala., Sept. 9 (Special)—A special from Eufaula gives meagre particulars of the killing of seven negroes on Friday night in Henry County. A negro camp-meeting was in progress near the house of a white man named Milburn. The negroes got their drinking water from his well until it was almost dry, when he refused to let them have any more water. One of the negroes attempted to take the bucket by force, when Milburn picked up a pistol and shot him in the neck, inflicting a slight wound. That night about one hundred of the negroes surrounded Milburn's house and fired several shots through the door. The following night Milburn and a crowd of his friends went to the camp-meeting and killed seven negroes who were supposed to be the ringleaders.

BUTCHERING BLACKS.
The Latest Race Troubles in the Sunny South.
HILLARDSVILLE, Ala., September 9.—A fearful battle between whites and blacks took place here yesterday, in which seven colored men were killed. The trouble grew out of the fact that a white man refused to allow his well to be longer used by a crowd of "Protracted Meeting" negroes. One of the negroes expressed a determination to have some of the water, and the white man drew his pistol and shot him in the neck. That night a gang of negroes visited the house and dared the white man to come out, but he refused to do so, and, after shooting holes in the windows and doors, they left. The next night a gang, presumably friends of the white man, visited the negro camp and left seven dead bodies as a reminder to other members of the camp-meeting crew.

They Provoked a Disturbance and Suffered in Consequence.

Birmingham, Ala., Sept. 11.—A special from Eufaula gives an account of the killing of seven negroes by white men at a negro camp meeting in Henry County last Friday night. The meeting was held near the residence of a white man named Milburn and the negroes secured drinking water from his well. Thursday Mr. Milburn refused to allow his well to be longer used by the negroes. When one of them came into Milburn's yard for water he was informed of his determination.

The negro said he would have at least one-half of the last bucket drawn, and started into the house for it. This conduct was objected to, and the white man shot the negro in the back of the neck. That night a crowd surrounded the house and shot a great many holes in his door and went away. The following night the ringleaders of the negroes were visited by a crowd of unknown white men and seven of them were shot dead. No arrests have been made.

hillardsville-hillardsville-1888-09-07.A17:
SHOT BY A MOB.
Seven Negroes Killed At An Alabama Camp Meeting.
In Henry county, in the extreme south-eastern portion of Alabama, a camp meeting was held last week. The meeting was held at a negro church near the residence of a white man named Milburn. The negroes attending the meeting obtained drinking water at Milburn's well. On Thursday the water in the well was getting very low and Milburn took the bucket away.

One negro attempted to enter the house to get the bucket and was shot in the neck by Milburn. That night about one hundred negroes surrounded Milburn's house and called upon him to come out, which he refused to do. They then fired several shots through the door, without doing any damage. The following night a mob of masked men, supposed to have been Milburn's friends, went to the camp meeting and shot down seven of the negroes. The negroes offered no resistance, but scattered in every direction when the shooting began. No arrests have so far been made.

jack-thornton-wichita-1888-09-22.A3:
SHOT DEAD.
OFFICER HENRY EBENHACK, OF
THE POLICE FORCE,
Killed by John Thornton, of the McMahan Patrol---Full Account of the Inquest.
almost instantly killed by John Thornton, of the McMahon patrol.

The shooting happened between 6 and 7 o'clock, and was the theme of conversation during the day; every person seemed to have some opinion regarding the guilt or innocence of Thornton, and many were the warm discussions that arose over the fatal affair. There are some circumstances of the utmost importance in establishing by the trial the fate of the young man, of which different statements are made; but of the main facts there appears to be no controversy. The story then, briefly told, is that Ebenhack in company with another Officer, Hartzell, went up to a bawdy house at the corner of Main and Central where he believed Thornton was staying. Ebenhack went to the rear door, Hartzell to the front and knocked; when it was opened Thornton in his uniform appeared just as Ebenhack, coming around the rear, placed him under arrest. Thornton said he was there on business for McMahan; Ebenhack told him he must go with him and that he could make his explanation in the court or words to that effect. The three men then started quietly down street towards the station. The prisoner made some remark about the officer "having it in for him," and some angry words followed. They turned east on Second and had just passed the Christian church on Market when Thornton suarring himself and pushing up his coat sleeves proposed to "fight it out." Ebenhack struck him over the head with the butt end of a whip. Hartzell attempted to separate the two men, grabbing Thornton around the waist. He had, however, free use of his hands and drew from his pocket a revolver, which he commenced firing. The first shot, it seems, struck the officer in the heart. He reeled backward, trying to draw his revolver from his hip pocket. Thornton fired a second time, the shot just grazing Ebenhack's coat; the third time the ball struck a house on the opposite side of the street. The fatally wounded man reeled back to the middle of the street and fell. Thornton turned to Hartzell and, handing his two revolvers over to him, said he was ready to die; he was taken to the city prison and placed behind the bars. The dying man was brought up to the engine house by persons who were attracted by the pistol shots and their died without saying a word after he was shot. His remains were then taken to his former home, No. 618 South Market.

Thornton was taken before Justice Walker and had his preliminary continued until October 12. His attorneys were Dale and Wall, Judge J. R. Shields and E. M. Cochran.

Coroner Percy had in the meantime been notified of the killing and set the inquest at 1 o'clock requesting Deputy Metcalf to summon a jury. This was done and resulted in the choice of the following men: J. G. McCoy, George Litzenberg, George Pray, William S. Cotter, John Herrig and L. Simpson.

As soon as the coroner arrived the jury went to view the remains of the deceased as they lay at No. 618 South Market. When they had returned to the corner's office the court house was surrounded by men, all anxious to learn the fullest particulars of the affair. The room was in a very few minutes crowded to its utmost. Judge Shields and Mr. Dale were present to represent the defense, and shortly afterwards, when Mr. J. W. Adams came in to represent the state, the inquest commenced with the examination of the man who was perhaps most able to give definite information upon the matter, Officer S. A. Hartzell. I was cleared of spectators, leaving no one within except the officers, attorneys, witnesses and members of the press.

When Officer Hartzell was not upon the witness stand he was interrogated by Mr. Adams and said:

I have been a policeman for about seven months; was acquainted with deceased; he was on the force before I was; I am, too, acquainted with Mr. Thornton and have been for five months. About half past 6 I was coming down from breakfast on a street car, when Ebenhack motioned me to come to him. I did so and he asked me to go up to the corner of Central and Main and "pull" John Thornton, who was "laying up" with one of the women in the room (pointing to one of two who had been summoned into court as witnesses.) We went to the house and I went to the front door and Henry to the back door. I knocked on front door and found Thornton in the room when it was opened. I called Henry to come around; he came and said to Thornton, "I want you." Thornton said, "I came here on business for McMahan." When he and Ebenhack started down town to the police station he said Henry had it in for him and began talking and continued telling what he could do with Henry until we got to the corner of First and Market, just past the Christian church, when Thornton said "I can do you," and turned half around, facing the west, and began rolling up his sleeves. Henry struck at Thornton with a light whip handle and hit him on the shoulder or the face. don't know exactly which. I grabbed hold of him around the waist but somehow he got his revolver out of his pocket and commenced firing. He fired three shots; the first seemed to take effect for Henry reeled back and put his hand as if to feel for his gun. Then followed the second and third shots, Henry getting each time further from Thornton until at the last shot he staggered and fell almost in the middle of the street. After he had shot Ebenhack he handed me his gun, saying: "Here is my gun, and I have another." He then reached into his pocket and pulled out a second revolver, and I gave them to Knight.

I said then you have killed him and it will go hard with you. Hesaid, well I am ready to die.

Hartzell said, upon cross examination that Ebenhack told him he was going to arrest Thornton. He never told him that he had it in for Thorton. We had no warrant for Thornton. I do not know whether Ebenhack wrote at Thornton when he
jack-thornton-wichita-1888-09-22.A4:
ing they were going into houses of prostitution. We understood that he had reported to the commissioners that Fenner had gone into a house of prostitution. The first man I saw at the scene of the shooting was Charley Dixon.

James Tobin next testified as to hearing Thornton make a remark about getting a gun that would kill.

Officer John Knight, who had just started for the station as the three men were coming down Market street, gave his version of the shooting as he saw it from where he was, and was followed by Charles Dixon, who was at the time on the opposite side of the street, and had still another view. In the main they did not differ from the statement of Hartzell; the trio stopping, Hartzell holding Thornton, the three shots and Ebenhack reeling, staggering back from the man who was firing at him.

Dr. McClees, the city physician, examined the body almost immediately after the shots were fired. The shot he said had entered the left breast about two inches above the nipple and passed directly through the heart. The shot might kill him instantly or he might have staggered away thirty feet as seemed in this case. It was evidently an over shot; still a great depends upon the position of the man as well as the manner in which the weapon was held.

Alf. Brownell, a member of hose company No. 1, said he had lived four years in the city; acquainted with both men; Ebenhack for about a year, Thornton for about a month. When I first saw the men they were coming down toward the engine house. I saw them stop and Ebenhack commence to beat Thornton over the head The next thing was a shot. At the time the shot was fired Hartzell was holding Thornton; the latter shot by reaching around the former's body. I could not see Ebenhack strike at Thornton in the street. I was standing near the body when it was examined by the doctor.

At the conclusion of Brownell's testimony the inquest concluded for the day; adjourning to meet this morning at 9 o'clock.

The two men implicated in this sad affair were both considered brave, valiant men and two of the best on the forces to which they belonged. Ebenhack was brought up on the cattle range and was an excellent rider and an expert shot. He was at the time of his death about 28 years of age and had been on the force since November, 1887. He was but recently married, his young wife surviving him.

Thornton came here several months ago and was engaged first as a hack-driver, next as a coachman, and lastly was patrolman. He was considered a good-looking man, quiet and orderly. When he applied for the position upon the patrol he said that he had been discharged from the St. Louis police force. Chief McMahan making an investigation found that the charge against him was "conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman." Nothing further was said against him and he was engaged and was becoming very popular on his beat.

The funeral of the deceased will take place from his late residence No. 618 South Market. and will be under the auspices of the Red Men, of which he was in his life time a member. The sermon will be delivered by Dean Adams. It will no doubt be well attended for the deceased had many warm friends and was much liked and respected by his associates.
jack-thornton-wichita-1888-09-22.A6:
Never heard Ebenhack say he had it in for Thornton. He once said that he would catch the men and the girls they were laying up with. "I will fool them yet, some time," he said. He told me, furthermore, that Thornton had been reporting him and Fenner, and used words to indicate that he would "catch him" or "play even."

This witness was sent out to measure the sidewalk, and soon returning, found it 5 feet 3¼ inches wide where the difficulty took place.

At this point of the proceeding the jurors asked for the defendant but his attorneys refused to allow him to be brought before the jury. They then asked for Mr. McMahan and a subpoena was issued for him.

McMahan first gave a description of the manner of working and the government of the patrol. I keep the patrol to hunt up evidence as well as do their other duties, and there is work of this kind placed upon them. Every morning they take their turns at this work. The patrol and the police are on good terms. The men are expected to visit a joint or a house of prostitution in search of evidence. There was a "silver plant" upon which we have been working for five months. I had Thornton in my room and he said he had reason to believe he could get information regarding this by visiting two women and I directed him to go and look it up. I expect each man to know every person doing "loose" business on his beat. My patrol are sworn in by the police commissioners same as the metropolitan police. They were to turn over all arrests to the regular police and be registered under the name of the latter. No officer has a right to arrest a man in a house unless he is found doing some crime or offense. While this witness was giving evidence the funeral procession of the deceased officer passed and created considerable of an impression in the room.

Nora Medsgar, being recalled, said Mr. Thornton had been at her home two or three times; he was up Monday morning to tell them about a house they had asked him to rent for them and to tell them about the location; that is all he spoke about.

THE VERDICT.

This concluded the testimony and the case was given to the jury. After they had been out for about two hours they returned the following verdict:

STATE OF KANSAS,
COUNTY OF SEDGWICK,
ss.

An inquisition holden at Wichita City, Sedgwick county, Kan., on the 24th and 25th days of September, 1888, before me, O. F. Pearcey, coroner of Sedgwick county, on the dead body of Henry Ebenhack, there lying dead, by the jurors whose names are hereunto subscribed. The said jurors, upon their oaths, do say that from the testimony given the deceased came to his death from a gunshot wound at the hands of one John Thornton, on the 24th day of September, 1888, and we further find that said shot was fired without felonious intent, but under great provocation and danger of bodily injury.

JURY:

J. G. McCoy, L. SIMPSON,
WM. L. COTTER, GEO. J. GRAY,
G. H. LITZENBRG, JOHN HEREIG.

In testimony whereof, the said jurors have hereunto set their hands the day and year above written.

Attest: O. F. PEARCEY, Coroner.

It soon became known upon the streets and to disinterested persons was looked upon as the only verdict that under the testimony given could be rendered.

All the members of the coroner's jury were personally acquainted with Mr. Ebenhack but none of them knew Thornton. In fact three of the jurymen were personal friends of Ebenhack but all seemed under oath unable to find from the testimony that Thornton was guilty of murder.

From interviews obtained with members of the grand jury it was learned that all of them were of the opinion that the arrest of Thornton was a grave mistake. The jury believed from the testimony that the arrest was a scheme to disgrace Thornton, and that Ebenhack saw Thornton going into a disreputable place the proper conclusion for him should have been that his fellow officer was there in discharge of his duty.

The jury did not believe the officers would have arrested Thornton if there had been no enmity between them. They also claim that the reports as published in the evening papers is incomplete and is calculated to mislead the public in regard to the findings of the jury. Most of the jury said that Mr. Ebenhack was a brave officer but that he had made a mistake in this instance.

THE SERMON.

The lily is the queen of Bible flowers. The rose may have disputed her throne in modern times, and won it; but the rose originally had only five petals. It was under the long-continued and intense gaze of the world that the rose blushed into its present beauty. In the Bible train, cassia and hyssop and frankincense and myrrh and spikenard and camphire and the rose follow the lily. Fourteen times in the Bible is the lily mentioned; only twice the rose. The rose may now have wider empire, but the lily reigned at the time of Esther, in the time of Solomon, in the time of Christ.

Caesar had his throne on the hills. The lily had her throne in the valley. In the greatest sermon that was ever preached, there was only one flower, and that the lily. The Bedford dreamer, John Bunyan, entere] the House of the Interpreter, and was shown a cluster of flowers, and was told to "consider the lilies."

We may study or reject other sciences at our option. It is so with astronomy, it is so with chemistry, it is so with jurisprudence, it is so with physiology, it is so with geology; but the science of botany Christ commands us to study when he says: Consider the lilies." Measure them from root to tip of petal. Inhale their breath. Notice the gracefulness of their poise. Hear the whisper of the white lips of the Eastern and of the red lips of the American lily.

CONSIDER THEM ALL.

Belonging to this royal family of lilies is the lily of the Nile, the Japan lily, the Lady Washington of the Sierras, the Golden Band lily, the Giant lily of Nepaul, the Turk's Cap lily, the African lily from the Cape of Good Hope. All the lilies have the royal blood in their veins. But I take the lilies of my text this morning as typical of all flowers, and this Easter day, garlanded with all this opulence of floral beauty, seems to address us saying: "Consider the lilies, consider the azallias, consider the fuchsias, consider the geraniums, consider the ivies, consider the hyacinths, consider the heliotropes, consider the oleanders. With differential, and grateful, and intelligent, and worshipful souls, consider them. Not with insipid sentimentalism, or with sophomoric vaporing, but for grand, and practical, and everyday, and, if need be, homely uses, consider them.

The flowers are the angels of the grass. They all have voices. When the clouds speak, they thunder; when the whirlwinds speak, they scream; when the cataracts speak, they roar; but when the flowers speak, they always whisper. I stand here to interpret their message. What have you to say, O ye angels of the grass, to this worshipful multitude?

This morning I mean to discuss what flowers are good for. That is my subject, "What Are Flowers Good For?"

WHAT FLOWERS ARE GOOD FOR.

First—I remark, in the first place, they are good for lessons of God's providential care. That was Christ's first thought. All these flowers seem to address us to-day, saying: "God will give you apparel and food. We have no wheel with which to spin, no loom with which to weave, no sickle with which to harvest, no well-sweep with which to draw water; but God slakes our thirst with the dew, and God feeds us with the bread of the sunshine, and God has appareled us with more than Solomonic regality. We are prophetesses of adequate wardrobe. If God so clothed us, the grass of the field, will He not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?"

Men and women of worldly anxieties, take this message home with you. How long has God taken care of you? Quarter of the journey of life? half the journey of life? three-quarters the journey of life? Can you not trust Him the rest of the way? God does not promise you anything like that which the Roman Emperor had on his table at vast expense—five hundred nightingales' tongues—but He has promised to take care of you. He has promised you the necessities, not the luxuries—bread, not cake. If God so luxuriantly clothes the grass of the field, will He not provide for you, His living and immortal children? He will.

No wonder Martin Luther always had a flower on his writing-desk for inspiration. Through the cracks of the prison floor a flower grew up to cheer Picciola. Mungo Park, the great traveler and explorer, had his life saved by a flower. He sank down in the desert to die, but seeing a flower near by, it suggested God's merciful care, and he got up with new courage and traveled on to safety. I said the flowers are the angels of the grass. I add now that they are the evangels of the sky.

FOR THE BRIDAL DAY.

Second.—If you insist on asking me the question, What are flowers good for? I respond, they are good for the bridal day. The bride must have them on her brow, and she must have them in her hand. The marriage altar must be covered with them. A wedding without flowers would be as inappropriate as a wedding without music. At such a time they are for congratulation and prophecies of good. The first section of the broad-gauge railroad up Lookout mountain has been completed, and trains are running. The roadbed is said by railroad engineers to be the most marvelous piece of engineering skill ever exhibited in the South. The entire road will be completed May 15.

Horace Parker was killed by Robert Youngblood, of Childersburg, Ala., a few nights ago. The two men got into a dispute, when the latter killed the former with a billet of wood. Youngblood claims to have acted in self-defence. Youngblood was arrested.

A queer tale comes from Perry County, Tenn. A man named Williamson stole a hog from a butcher and made off with it. Before he reached home he had a fence to cross, and, it seems, threw the hog over before him. He had failed to take out the "gammon stick," and it caught him by the neck, and when found next morning he was dead and cold, with his prey on one side of the fence and his body on the other.

William and Joe Hopkins were recently convicted at Clayton, Ga., of the unprovoked murder of Willie Thomas, whom they stoned to death as he came out of church at Mount Carmel. The crime, arrest and conviction only covered a week's time.

A bale of cotton recently received at Bremen was found to contain 146 pounds of seed cotton, and it was traced back to a farmer named Snipes in Banks County, Ga. The latter, however, declines to settle the damage, and legal proceedings will involve more than the cotton is worth.

A terrible storm of wind and hail swept over Boliver County, Miss., a few evenings since, doing much damage to the planting interests. Trees were uprooted and many fences destroyed. The store-house of E. S. Maller, of Kentucky Landing, was carried off its foundation and upset.

Advices from all parts of Georgia show that the recent enormous rainfall throughout the State has resulted in great damage to railroads and farming interests.

Chas. Floys, a cooper by trade, aged twenty-eight, fell under the cars on the Louisville & Nashville road at Memphis, Tenn., a few nights ago, and both of his legs were cut off. His home is in Greenville, Ind.

Rufus Settle, a special examiner of the United States Pension Bureau, who arrived at Gainesville, Tenn., a few days ago from his field of labor in Georgia, died at his father's home, a few miles west of Gainesville, of consumption.

The private banking house of Thos. P. Miller & Co., at Mobile, Ala., after thirty-six years' existence amid all sorts of financial difficulty, has succumbed, and leaves but a wreck behind.

It has rained almost constantly in Mississippi, lately, interfering very materially with planting prospects. All the creeks are out of their banks and flooding the country.

Andrew Jones, the eighteen-year-old son of Mr. Wm. Jones, of Brownville, Ga., died a few nights ago. The young man was stung on the neck by a spider two weeks previous. The sting was very painful, and the neck and side of his face were greatly swollen. Erysipelas set in, which produced death.

Johnny Bertelkamp, twelve years old, was reported dying in the City Hospital at Louisville, Ky., of trichinosis. Johnny's parents are Germans, and the chief article of their diet is pork. The boy preferred this raw, and was allowed to eat the meat that way.

It is not generally known, but it is, nevertheless, true, that Georgia furnished one regiment of infantry to the Federal service during the civil war. It was not a full regiment, and somehow the officers and men were never paid for their services. They are now before Congress seeking a settlement.

James Derossett, who is charged with murdering Ras Smith at Dayton, Tenn., was taken to Chattanooga and locked upin jail to prevent him from being lynched. A mob intended to hang him at Dayton.

A party of Louisville (Ky.) men have been working to develop lead mines in Scott County. Silver prospecting was also indulged in, and after six months of patient work silver has been struck on the Brown farm, about ten miles from Georgetown.

John Moyer, a tramp, boarded a car filled with lumber on the Western & Atlanta road, at Dalton, Ga., a few nights ago. While the car was en route to Chattanooga the lumber fell on the man, killing him instantly. His dead body was not discovered until the train arrived at its destination.

Jeff Sims, a farmer, and his wife, living near Hernando, Miss., have been getting along badly for some time. She was found dead in her room a few days ago, with several knife wounds on her person. Sims claims that she killed herself, but he was arrested as the murderer.

The body of a white man was found in the Alabama river above Selma, a few days ago. It had probably been in the water a week. It was discovered by a boatman catching drift. No papers to identify the man were found on his person. The neck was broken, through which was a bullet hole. He was properly buried. Nothing has developed to lead to his identity.

In Chatham County, N. C., a few days since, Deputy Collector Spence Taylor captured and destroyed an illicit still. When they were near the still they saw five men, who hastily fled and escaped. A WRETCH STRUNG UP.
Disciples of Judge Lynch Deal Our Stern Justice.

HENDERSON, Ky., June 11.—At 11:55 last night a well-armed and organized mob, consisting of about sixty men, mounted, a part of whom were negroes, approached the jail quietly, captured Jailer Johnson and compelled him to deliver the keys. They then took James Foster, the negro who raped a little colored girl eight years old near this city, last Thursday, and hung him to a tree about a mile from the jail. Your correspondent followed the mob, but, being encouraged by several revolvers to keep at a respectful distance, did so, but succeeded in viewing the remains after the mob had departed. The victim was neatly hung to a limb, with his hands and feet tied and dangling about four feet from the ground.

After hanging Foster the mob took a vote whether they should return to jail and lynch the negro who was recently brought here from Hopkinsville for a similar crime. The vote was close, but it was decided to disperse without further action. The mob came to the city by the Knoblic road. They were orderly, but determined. Foster confessed the crime and richly deserved his fate.

A KENTUCKY MOB
Have a Necktie Party With a Lecherous Brute at Henderson.

EVANSVILLE, Ind., June 12.—At Henderson, Ky., twelve miles below here, at 1 o'clock Sunday night, James Foster, colored, was taken from jail by a mob and hanged.

Foster was arrested Thursday morning at the instance of John Howard, charged with outraging the latter's little eight-year-old daughter, a few miles from Henderson, in the country. Foster, on being arrested, strenuously denied his guilt, but most conclusive evidence of his guilt was found on his clothing, which was stained with blood.

The greatest indignation was created throughout the neighborhood, and threats of lynching were heard on all sides. A mob came in from the country Sunday night, but they found Jailer Johnson on the alert, and they returned to their homes, determined to come back and avenge the brutal crime. As the quiet little city was asleep at midnight two hundred Kentuckians, mounted on horseback and armed to the teeth, to repel any official resistance, rode into the city. Pulling up at the jail, they made a dash for the barred doors, and before the jailer was fully alarmed they were inside. Breaking down the cell door, they dragged the lecherous brute out into a vehicle started with him to the scene of his crime before the town was aware of the intrusion.

All along the road the prisoner begged and beseeched his captors to spare his life, and told all manner of stories to prove his innocence. But Kentuckians have learned to turn deaf ears to the pleas of those who so cruelly wreck and stain the fair name of the state, and when the party had arrived at the woods where the outrage was committed they selected a strong oak, threw the fatal rope over a limb, and strung the wretch up. Then they quietly dispersed.

The incomparable ticket placed before the country by the Democratic National Convention at St. Louis—Grover Cleveland and Allan Granberry Thurman—is received everywhere with demonstrations of hearty approval, while the "platform is one," as Mr. Watterson expressed it, "that every democrat can stand upon without feeling away from home." The document entire is given in another column and it is a full and free declaration of democratic principles. There is no uncertain sound about the plank on tariff reduction. It is to be interpreted in the light of President Cleveland's message thereon and a bolder, braver expression on the subject could not be made than that document. There was a long fight in the committee-room on the question between Senator Gorman and his following and Henry Watterson, but the latter finally triumphed and his work and presence were unanimously endorsed and warmly applauded by the convention. His committee recommended an endorsement of the Mills bill and that too was adopted without dissent. It would have been impossible to have named a stronger ticket. Cleveland's record is enough to satisfy the country that he can be trusted under any and all emergencies, while Mr. Thurman is as Senator Edmunds, a distinguished republican expresses it, "the ablest and the grandest, the bravest and the truest democrat in the Union." There is no combination that can beat that of Cleveland and Thurman, which is as sure of success as the November election day arrives. Three cheers for it and the glorious work of the great convention!

A scoundrelly preacher (and a preacher can be the biggest scoundrel in the world when he is one), named Pendleton, who desecrates the city of Worcester with his foul presence, said in an interview after visiting Washington that he had been informed that Mrs. Cleveland's married life was unhappy, and that the President was abusive in his demeanor toward her and otherwise unkind. A lady friend in Boston sent Mrs. Cleveland a copy of the interview and she replied to her as follows: "Every statement is basely false. I pity a man of his calling who has been made a tool to give circulation to such wicked, heartless lies. I can wish the women of our country no greater blessing than that their homes and lives may be as happy and their husbands as kind, attentive, considerate and affectionate as mine."

It is so rare that great men show their appreciation of those who have assisted them to greatness that it is peculiarly gratifying to record the subjoined:

FRIEND WALTON:—Remembering with a thankful heart that you have stood by me through thick and thin, through evil as well as through good report, and recognizing that mainly through your untiring and faithful efforts I have been able to get bestride the pinacle of fame, I make bold to ask another favor of you. Will you not go to Chicago next week to assist as you only can, in obtaining for me the vice presidential prize from the republican convention? I shall need you, so do not fail yours gratefully,

BILLY O'B.

If the national convention had been held for the benefit of the afternoon papers it could not have served them better. The Louisville Times, as usual, with its own T. G. Watkins on the ground, swept the platter clean, leaving the morning papers nothing to do but to rehash the glorious story. SENATOR VOORHEES, of Indiana, says in an interview that Gray's friends will not falter in their support of Thurman, and that, in his opinion, the democrats will carry Indiana. Gov. Gray himself telegraphed congratulations to the Old Roman and pledged his warmest support.

DEMOCRATIC newspapers and democratic statesmen from Maine to California and from the Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico unite with one accord in saying that it is a glorious ticket and a clean-cut platform. Read the comments on them published on our first page.

THE Jackson Club serenaded Senator Thurman en route from the convention and he greeted them with a cheering speech, which showed how much life there is in him yet. Said he: "People may say I am too old to run for vice-president, but they do not understand the effect upon an old democrat of such kindness as I received at your hands and at the hands of the rest of the democracy of the United States. Why, I feel about ten years younger at the least calculation. I should not be surprised if I should make such a fool of myself between now and the second Tuesday, or the first Tuesday, or whatever Tuesday it is in October—November, I mean, that I should be prancing round making speeches like a young man just out of his teens." He continued in this happy strain and closed with this splendid eulogy of the president: "There scarcely ever happened in the history of this world a sublimer spectacle than the renomination of Grover Cleveland by the unanimous vote of the convention. (Great applause.) And now I say you did a wise thing in that, a patriotic thing in that. The people of the United States love a brave man, and Cleveland is a brave man; they love an honest man, and God knows he is an honest man; they love a man of good sound judgment, and I do not know any man of sounder judgment than his; they love a man who stands up for the people, who stands up for principle and does not fear to take the consequences, and such a man is Grover Cleveland. Gentleman, it will be an honor to every man of that St. Louis Convention as long as he lives that he was there to cast his vote for this worthy President of the United States."

THE democratic ticket was nominated by acclaim and the proceedings of the convention were harmonious and altogether lovely. There will be no such unanimity at Chicago next week, where every little rooster will aspire to be a leader. DAVE BRAXTON KILLED.
Shot In An Attempt to Escape From the Henderson Jail.
Our readers will remember the details of the horrible assault made by Dave Braxton, col., upon one Mrs. Patzke, a white lady, several weeks since; also the result of the trial which fixed the guilt upon the fiend and his subsequent removal to Henderson to escape the violence of an outraged public. Latterly it has developed that Braxton had insulted 25 or 30 of the most refined ladies in this city and was in all respects a beast. This same Braxton has at last met his reward and that, too, before the law could lay its clutches upon him. The facts are detailed by a special from Henderson Wednesday night, as follows:

"One of the most daring efforts at jail breaking ever attempted in this section, was made this afternoon about 2 o'clock. It seems as Turnkey James Turner was entering the jail with dinner for the prisoners, he was attacked by one Braxton, who had crouched against the wall. In the scuffle Turner succeeded in drawing his pistol and fired, shooting Braxton through the left lung, the ball coming out of his back. Braxton's wound is pronounced fatal. Only three prisoners escaped, two of which have been recaptured. Albert Hatchett, colored, charged with perjury, is still at large. Braxton is charged with rape and was recently brought here from Hopkinsville to escape lynching, and is the same that the mob talked of hanging when they lynched Jas. Foster, Sunday night last. Valuable assistance was rendered the officers by prisoner Wm. Boine, and without his assistance the jail would, in all probability, have been emptied and Turner used up."

Several Manitoba People Seriously Injured by the Explosion of Cartridges.

WINNIPEG, Man., June 12.—Several people were badly burned at the Central Pacific railway depot at Gratna, owing to the explosion of a box of cartridges thrown carelessly from an express car onto the platform. N. R. Burley and family, Walhalla, Dak., on the way to Napanee, Ont., were sufferers. Mrs. Burley's dress took fire and burned up to her knees before extinguished. ONLY TWO STORES LEFT.

Fire Consumes the Business Portion of Chesley. Ont.

CHESLEY, Ont., June 12. -A fire broke out in a furniture store here, and in a short time the whole business portion of the town, with the exception of two stores, was entirely destroyed. The loss is estimated at $150,000. The insurance does not exceed $40,000. No lives were lost.

DANIELLE VA. June 25 Information

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

DANVILLE, VA., June 25.—Information reached here to-day of a nameless assault on a little girl of this county on Sunday last—Jennie Polkot, about nine years of age, living near Sandy Creek with her father and grandfather. On Sunday she went to a spring near the house to get a bucket of cool water for her grandfather, and Jed Pritchett, a negro brute, caught and assaulted her. At one time the little girl's life was despaired of, but she is reported better to-day. A party was organized here to-day to go in search of the fiend, and if he is caught it is needless to say he will meet with the fate he deserves.

Danville Register.
Sunday afternoon little Jennie Pollok, the eight year old daughter of Mr. W. C. Pollok, who lives on Sandy Creek, nine miles from Dansville, went to a spring about one hundred and fifty yards from the house to get a small bucket of cool water for her grandfather.

Jed Pritchett, an infamous negro field, who had formerly worked for Mr. Pollok, was lying in the shade near the spring.

When the villian saw the little girl tripping along the path, the spirit of the devil entered his soul. The details of what followed are too sickening to be recorded here.

Suffice it to say—in a half hour little Jennie dragged her lacerated and bleeding form to the house and told her grandfather of the horrible outrage which the negro had committed.

The father was not at home, but the grandfather seized the double-barrel shot gun and went in search of the villain. He had fled and could not be found.

The little girl suffered intensely, and at one time her life was despaired of. Yesterday morning, how ever, she was much better, and it is now hoped her recovery may be complete and speedy, though she is still prostrated and her condition is pitiful in the extreme.

Officers and friends of Mr. Pollok are scouring the country for the fiend and it goes without saying that when caught his vile carcass will never darken the door of a jail and the rope which ends his earthly career will not cost the state anything.

Wisner. Neb., June 5.—Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—The high water of last week swept away the iron bridge over the Elkhorn, opposite Wisner, and the citizens constructed a temporary flatboat for the crossing of foot passengers. At 1 o'clock to-day, while a party of eight persons were crossing from the west bank, the boat dipped, and the current being strong, swept the whole party off. Lena Matthis, aged sixteen years, Anna Matthis, aged five years, Otto Matthis, aged eleven yerrs, all children of Ferdinand Matthis, of this place, and Franz Marx, aged fifteen years, a son of William Marx, a farmer living five miles south of Wisner, were drowned. The wife and eldest daughter and eldest son of Ferdinand Matthis were saved by the prompt action of some who witnessed the accident. The Matthis family were returning from the wedding of their son, Frank, which took place last evening, six miles south. An effort was made by the citizens to recover the bodies, but the high water and swift current made it impossible to do anything and the search was abandoned.

Murder at Culbertson.

CULBERTSON, Neb., June 5.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—A little before noon today, John B. Hunter, a hardware merchant of this place, deliberately shot and killed Harry B. Hill, a farmer living two miles east of town. The shooting took place in a billiard hall and was the result of a dispute between Hunter's father, Galant V. Hunter, and Mr. Hull. Weir, Shugart & Co., of Council Bluffs, Ia., Deere, Wells & Co., of Omaha, and Berryman, Patterson & Co., of Central City, Neb., the heaviest creditors have attached all his property. A Church Dedication.

A Church Dedication.

HASTINGS, Neb., June 5.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]

An important event in the history of the First Presbyterian church of Hastings was witnessed to-day by the impressive ceremonies attending the laying of the corner stone of an elegant and commodious new house of worship, situated on the corner of Seventh street and Lincoln avenue. The auditorium is constructed in a circular form with an operatic floor, and will have a seating capacity of 1,500 people. The modern style of architecture prevails, and no feature appropriate to such a structure will be spared to beautify the wisely planned interior or adorn the stately exterior of the magnificent building. When completed and suitably furnished throughout and supplied with a fine $3,500 pipe organ, the total cost will aggregate $50,000.

The church was first organized August 10, 1873, by Rev. N. C. Robinson, synodical missionary, and the first regular minister was Rev. J. A. Grippes. The present able and much loved pastor is George T. Crissman. The membership is the largest of any church in the city.

The ceremonies to-day were presided over by Rev. Crissman, assisted by Revs. Holden, Walters and Britt, of this city, and Rev. W. W. Morton, of Blue Hill, moderator of this presbytery. The leading address was delivered by Rev. Ringland, president of the Hastings Presbyterian college. A. L. Wigton read a brief history of the church in this city, and Hon. J. B. Heartwell gave an interesting sketch of Sabbath school work. The operations of the building committee were explained by Samuel Alexander. A bible, the church manual, copies of important church documents, and numbers of all the city papers were inclosed in a tin box and firmly cemented in a receptacle provided in the stone.

A large number of people, members of the church, and Sabbath school children were present at the ceremonies. The stone was safely laid, and the exercises concluded with prayers, songs of praise and thanksgiving.

Boston, Mass., June 7 - [Special Telegram]

Systematic Embezzlement.
BOSTON, Mass., June 7.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Detectives are now investigating what is claimed to be a systematic plan of embezzling goods from one of the largest printing concerns in the city. Many of the concern's oldest employees are said to be implicated, and the value of goods stolen is estimated at $200,000. The mode of operation is said to have been for those employed in different departments to steal stock and ship it to other houses in a similar line of trade. They also carried off copies of books in process of construction and smuggled them into the hands of binders who were in the "ring," and from the bindery they were placed upon the market.

A Sensational Case.
CHICAGO, June 7.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—A sensational suit involving the names of some of Chicago's best known people has been begun. It will cause quite a flutter in social circles. The plaintiff is the divorced wife of Edward H. Waldron, the well known board of trade man. The defendant is the present Mrs. Waldron, from whom the plaintiff seeks to recover $100,000. The bill of particulars are not yet filed, but it is understood the cause of action is "trespass." This may mean alienating her husband's affections. The plaintiff lived with Waldron upwards of twenty years. In June, 1887, she procured a divorce, and in the following November Waldron married Mrs. Joseph Alexander, widow of E. A. Alexander, the railway supply merchant. Mrs. Alexander is said to be worth nearly $750,000. The plaintiff's attorneys will say nothing yet, but the defendant's attorney and the defendant himself say they cannot imagine why the action is brought unless as a scheme to extort money.

A TRAGEDY AT CULBERTSON.
CULBERTSON special to the Omaha Herald: This city was thrown into a flurry this morning by the hearing of two shots fired in the billiard saloon of Trout & Manarron on Taylor avenue. In a short time the place was crowded, although at first there had been a general evacuation of the premises. Your corrspondent saw Judge G. V. Hunter, supported by his son John B. Hunter, coming out of the establishment, the former profusely bleeding about the head. As the two were rushing along toward their hardware store, which is located about eighty yards from the scene of action on the opposite side of the street, John was heard to yell, "Keep back, don't touch us!" Upon investigation it turned out that John had shot Harry B. Hull, a prominent and respected farmer living close to this city. The Hunters and Hull have been in a difficulty some days over a line fence and some hot words ensued on several occasions. There has also been some trouble over a mule that belonged to the Hunters, which Hull had taken up for damages. This morning Hull came to town and John Hunter went to him and tried to pick a quarrel but failed. Then he hunted up his father and they determined to round Hull up before night. The repaired to the billiard hall, where Hull was engaged in a game of billiards. Judge Hunter started in to quarrel with Hull and provoke an assault. The sennior Hunter then started for the cue rack and Hull dealt him a blow with a cue, which he followed by another, when John rushed in and shot at Hull, the ball passing through Hull's hat. He then fired again, the ball striking Hull just back of the ear and coming out of his mouth. He fell to the floor and a doctor was summoned.

He was removed to the Grand Central hotel, where he died from strangulation from the flow of blood in fifteen minutes. John Hunter was promptly arrested. There is no doubt the murder was premeditated, as the Hunters had promised to wind him up. There was considerable talk on the streets of a mob.

BENNINGTON, Neb., Nov. 29.—[Special to THE BEE.]—Last Monday a general fight occurred here, and so far there are about eight men in town who have not got a black eye or are nursing a sore face. The fight started over a keeg of beer being stolen from one of the saloonkeepers. One man accused another of being the thief, and five jumped on to him. CULBERSTON, Neb., Nov. 28.—[Special to THE BEE.]—The district court is now in session at this place, and the trial of John B. Hunter, the murderer of Harry B. Hult, will commence next Monday. Walnut Hill.

St. Cecilia's church, the new Catholic chapel at Walnut Hill, is entirely finished and the dedication will take place next Sunday at 10:30. The furnace was tested Wednesday and gave satisfaction. The firm of Neal & Conrad kindly donated a ton of coal.

Bishop O'Connor will officiate at the dedication, and his private secretary, Father Colaneri, will act as temporary pastor.

St. John's choir will sing at the dedication. Three lots were purchased by the directors of the Episcopalian church yesterday. They are situated in a very choice location of Walnut Hill upon which will be erected a beautiful little church.

McCook, Neb., Dec. 14. —The Hunter murder trial which has been in progress at Culbertson this week, has been closed and John Hunter, who took the life of Harry Hull by shooting him through the heart with a revolver, goes to Lincoln for twelve months. OGDEN'S VERSON.

A dispatch from Upper Marlboro', dated March 25th, says: "Lemuel Ogden, who is confined in the county jail, charged with having committed a felonious assault upon Miss Catharine Fowler, of Hyattstown, Monday last, says he made no assault upon Miss Fowler. He admits remaining at Mrs. Fowler's house. He says he did remain Monday night at Fowler's, and did not leave there until 9 A. M. Tuesday. From there he went nearly to Wilson's Station, on the B. & P. R. R., and returned to Mrs. Fowler's and asked for a bundle left there for him. He saw Miss Fowler when he returned to the house, and she gave him the bundle. He went from there to his home, which is in Montgomery county, and made no attempt to escape. He says he was not arrested until Wednesday night. He states that he asked to be taken to Miss Fowler's, but was told he would not be allowed to see her until the trial. Court will begin here on Monday, April 2, when Ogden will be tried."

THE ASSAULT ON MISS FOWLER.
Lemuel Ogdon's Trial on a Serious Charge Begun at Upper Marlboro'.
Lemuel Ogden's Trial on a Serious Charge Begun at Upper Marlboro'.

Correspondence of THE EVENING STAR.
UPPER MARLBORO', MD., April 12.

The case of Lemuel R. W. Ogden, the young man from near Four Corners, Montgomery County, charged with a felonious assault on his sister-in-law, Miss Catherine S. Fowler, at her home near Hyattsville, on the night of March 19 last, was called for trial this morning before Judges Brooke and Crane. The court-room was crowded when the case was called. State's-Attorney Brandt was assisted in the prosecution by Gen. Edward Carrington, of Branchville, and Marion Duckett, of Bladensburg, who had been retained by friends of the prosecuting witness. The defendant was represented by State Senator Peter, of Montgomery, and George C. Merrick, of Marlboro'. It was nearly 1 o'clock when a jury was secured and sworn. State's-Attorney Brandt opened the case for the prosecution, and stated what he expected to show in support of the indictment. Miss Fowler was the first witness called. She testified that on the night charged she retired about 11 o'clock. She gave her brother-in-law, the defendant, a lamp and told him to go to the room in which he usually slept when he visited them. Later in the night witness was aroused by the falling of a chair between her bed and the door. She saw the prisoner standing near her, and she said: "Oh, Lem." He told her that he would ruin her if she made any noise. He then put his hand over her mouth and she attempted to scream, but he covered her mouth with bedclothing and assaulted her. After the recess of the court Miss Fowler was again put upon the stand and cross-examined. She said that she made no complaint to her brothers until Ogden had left the house the following morning, because he had threatened her if she gave any alarm and because her brothers were not able to handle a man like Ogden. In conducting the examination, State Senator Peter asked if that was the first time Ogden had ever come to her door, and she replied "Yes." The court then adjourned until to-morrow when the case will probably be finished.

The Jury Find Him Guilty of Feloniously Assaulting his Sister-in-Law.

Correspondence of THE EVENING STAR.
UPPER MARLBORO', MD., April 13.

In the trial of Lemuel R. W. Ogden, the young man charged with committing a felonious assault on his sister-in-law, Miss Fowler, at her home near Hyattsville on the night of March 19th last, the complainant finished her testimony yesterday afternoon. The prosecution called Miss Susan Fowler, the mother, and Edward and Benjamin, the two brothers of the complainant, who testified to the presence of the prisoner at their home on the night charged. The brothers also testified to the circumstances attending the arrest. When court opened this morning the defense called Ogden to the stand. He testified that on the night charged he was at his mother-in-law's house. After supper he said he remained talking with the family until about 10 o'clock, when the brothers retired, leaving him with the prosecuting witness. About 11 o'clock he kissed her and then went to his room. When he left Miss Fowler began to read her Bible, and in a few minutes he heard her go to her room. When he awoke during the night he went into Miss Fowler's room and walked against a chair, as she had said. When he entered the room Miss Fowler said, "For God's sake, Lem, go out; you cannot come in here to-night." He said, "Why?" and she said, "You cannot and must not to-night." She further said, "You will ruin me." He assured her he would not. He said he accomplished his purpose, but did not state that she gave her consent. He added, in response to a question from Senator Peter, that the same thing had been going on since 1885.

States Attorney Brandt did not cross-examine the prisoner because he said that the prisoner had convicted himself. The defense then called a number of witnesses who testified to the good character of the defendant. Miss Fowler was called to the stand and she denied the testimony of Ogden as to his intimacy with her previous to the night charged. The court limited the arguments to two hours and a half for each side. Marion Duckett opened for the prosecution and was followed by Gen. Carrington. Senator Peter, and George C. Merrick argued for the prisoner. States Attorney Brandt closed the arguments, and the court instructed the jury. The case was given to the jury about 6:30 o'clock, and at 8:45 o'clock the court-house bell was rung announcing the fact that the jury had agreed upon a verdict. Fifteen minutes later the jury returned with a verdict of guilty. The extreme penalty is death.

THE CITY MARKETS.—The Official Price Current of the Washington Produce Exchange says: The flour market is regular and current demand steady. Wheat in active demand and higher. Corn and oats firm. The long-continued bad condition of the county roads has affected the supply of hay and a firmer market is the result. The condition of the butter market is unsettled and top figures can only be obtained for strictly fancy quality. The market price of eggs has been gradually falling back from day to day. The supply or old fowls is light and market strong. Spring chickens find ready sale within range of quotations. A better demand is noted for sun-cured apples and peaches. At the same time there is a scarcity of stock on this market. Stock of sound apples is growing scarce and advancing in price. Oranges in good demand and market firm.

NEW YORK AVENUE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH.—The annual report of the session of the New York Avenue Presbyterian church, just published, shows that the contributions to the church boards and other benevolence during the year 1888 amounted to $13,799.39. The total annual receipts from all sources were $30,139.55. The aggregate contributions during the pastorate of Dr. Bartlett for congregational and benevolent purposes were $150,200. This is a very flattering showing for Dr. Bartlett.

UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA ALUMNI.—At a gathering last evening at the home of Prof. and Mrs. W. D. Cabell of graduates and non-graduate students of the University of Virginia who reside in this city, an Alumni Association was formed. Officers were elected as follows: President, Senator Dan el, of Virginia; vice-presidents, Hon. Hilary A. Herbert, of Alabama, and Prof. E. T. Fristoe, of the Columbian University, of this city; secretary and treasurer, Mr. S. Prentiss Knut. Addresses were delivered by Hon. D. B. Lucas, of West Virginia, and Col. Chas. S. Venable, chairman of the faculty of the University of Virginia. The executive committee consists of the officers of the association and the following-named gentlemen: Prof. Wm. D. Cabell, Henry Wise Garnett and Hon. John B. Moore.

THE RAILROAD STRIKE.—At a meeting of locomotive engineers and firemen held in this city last night Mr. John J. Hannahan, of Chicago, of the Firemen's Brotherhood, and Mr. J. C. Porter, of Aurora, Ill., of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, delivered addresses showing the condition of affairs on the "Q" road. Resolutions were adopted condemning the officers of the Burlington system for refusing to treat with their employees and pledging moral and financial aid to the strik-
of affairs on the "Q" road. Resolutions were adopted condemning the officers of the Burlington system for refusing to treat with their employees and pledging moral and financial aid to the striking engineers and firemen.

JOHN DEURINGER'S WILL—Yesterday the will of John Deuringer was filed. He leaves his entire personal estate, house No. 920 8th street southeast, and two life insurance policies amounting to $8,000, to be divided equally between his two children, August and Elsa Deuringer. John Rochon is named as executor.

THE EDUCATIONAL AND INDUSTRIAL UNION.—The Woman's Educational and Industrial Union has elected the following officers: Mrs. John A. Logan, president; Mrs. Stanford, Mrs. Hearst and Mrs. Sherman, Miss Dawes, Mrs. Horatio King, Mrs. Dr. Lamb, Mrs. James B. Wilson and Mary E. McPherson, vice-presidents; Lucy A. Leggett and Hannah B. Sperry, secretaries; Sophronia Snow, treasurer; board of directors, Mrs. Dr. Newman, Mrs. Dr. Talbot, Miss Caroline Ransom, Mrs. Lucklman, Mrs. Barney and Mrs. Henrietta Metzerott.

THE EXPENSE OF THE BISCOE TRIAL—Mr. Enoch E. Abell, of Leonardtown, Md., has submitted for the consideration of Gov. Jackson an argument in favor of reconsideration of the governor's veto of the bill passed by the legislature refunding to St. Mary's County $2,000 expenses incurred in the two trials of John Benjamin Biscoe, who is to be hanged April 27 for the murder of Capt. Dixon.

MRS. THOMAS HYDE has recently presented to St. John's church, Georgetown, a very beautiful alms basin. It is of sterling silver and etruscan gold, 15½ inches in diameter, very beautifully chased with the design or the passion flower, and on the rim the text: "The Lord remember all thine offerings." Around the outer edge is engraved the following inscription: "In memoriam, Charles Edward Rittenhouse. Died April 17, 1880." This beautiful piece of work was designed and executed by Messrs. J. & R. Lamb, of New York.

NEWS OF THE DAY.
A fire in Wheeling, W. Va., yesterday entailed a loss of about $50,000.

Rumor has it that a new line of steamers is projected between Baltimore and Norfolk.

The commander of the Roumanian flotilla has been sentenced to prison for embezzlement.

Mrs. Mary Jane Masson has sued the Philadelphia, Wilmington and Baltimore Railroad for $10,000 for the death of her husband.

The French steamer Yorouba, loaded with metals and cotton, which left Marseilles for Havre and London, has been wrecked on the Island of Guernsey. The crew were saved.

In the examination, yesterday, at Belfast, of the case of the persons charged with defrauding the New York Equitable Life Insurance Company, it was discovered that large sums of money had been secured on policies which had been issued on fraudulent certificates.

Lemuel R. W. Ogden has been found guilty at Upper Marlboro', Md., of feloniously assaulting Miss Catharine S. Fowler, his sister-in-law. Ogden, when put upon the stand, admitted having committed the offense, but denied having used force. Ogden will take an appeal.

The marriage of Miss Bessie Hillyer to Grassie Bulkley, which produced such a sensation in social circles in Washington at the time of its occurrence, and the subsequent events, culminated on Thursday night in the death of young Mrs. Bulkley from a dose of arsenic, which she took in a fit of despondency. Since Mrs. Bulkley lived apart from her husband she had resided at her father's house, and was supposed to be happy.

There is a prospect that the difference in the Protestant Episcopal Church in South Carolina, which involved the withdrawal of a large number of clerical and lay delegates from the convention last May, will be adjusted at the convention to meet at Anderson on the second proximo. The immediate occasion of the withdrawal last year was the rulings of the bishop in the organization of the convention, but the underlying question was the right of a colored clergyman to sit in that body by virtue of his ordination under the constitution of that diocese.

STILL PUZZLED.
NO IDENTIFICATION OF RALEIGE'S MUSICAL PRISONER Y&T.
The North Carolina Teachers-A Boy Gored to Death by a Cow-Confessed a Murder.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
RALEIGH, N. C., June 29.—There has been no abatement to-day of the interest in the remarkable case of the man in jail here who is suspected to be Scott Partin, but who stoutly asserts that L. is Robert Leeson Porter. All day as rapidly as the jail was emptied of one crowd of sight-seers Partin, or Porter, was eagerly gazed at by another crowd. Finally the sheriff brought him to the heavily-barred window of the jail, and there he sat some hours, while hundreds of people saw and talked to him. The majority believe that the prisoner is Partin. Some say that he has not changed greatly. When he was asked this morning to sign the name of A. W. Partin he did so, and the signature was compared with one known to be Partin's, written many years ago. There are some resemblances between the signatures. This afternoon a man named Myatt came here to endeavor to identify Porter by means of birthmarks, which it was alleged were prominent on Partin. They were not found, it is said. This fact shook the belief that the man is Partin. Every Irishman in this city has seen Porter. Only two believe that he is, as he claims, a native of Ireland.

Partin told your correspondent to-day that he was born at Port Arlington, near Dublin; that in 1873, at Fort Preble, Maine, he enlisted in Battery M. Fifth United States artillery, of which G. V. Weir was captain, Ives first heutenant, and McCullion second heutenant. Two years later he says he went with four companies to Fort Barranca, Fla. He is careless in manner, but his eye is restless. He plays the flute almost incessantly, and sells photographs of himself. His case will probably come up before the court week after next. People who do not believe him to be Partin think he is a suspicious character.

THE TEACHERS.

The North Carolina Teachers' Assembly, which for a fortnight has been in session at Morehead City, ended its fifth session last night. The closing exercises was a grand concert, which was conducted by Miss Southgate, of Durnam, and in which all the mustal talent of the assembly was represented. This morning the teachers scattered in all directions. One hundred of them left on a steamer for Norfolk, hence they will go to Baltimore, New York, and Boston. During the session of the assembly 2,500 members were present. A vote of thanks was tendered Secretary E. G. Harrell, and an oil portrait of him was ordered.

A LYNCHING PARTY OUT.

At Manly yesterday a negro assaulted a white woman. At daylight this morning a large number of white men were mounted and in search of him, intending to lynch him.

Yesterday at Keyser a negro woman named Kennedy was on trial charged with killing her child, aged four years. She at first swore that she was walking across the railway trestle over a creek, and that seeing the train approaching she was so frightened that she knocked the child off the trestle and into the stream. Later she broke down and confessed that she had broken the child's skull with a lightwood-knot and then threw the body in the creek.

Ground has been broken for the large addition to the Eastern North Carolina Asylum for colored patients at Goldsboro'.

GORED TO DEATH.

At Charlotte yesterday Lerov Taylor, aged eight years, son of W. J. Taylor, was gored to death by a cow which he was attempting to drive home.

A construction train on the Roanoke and Tar-River railway was thrown from the track by logs. Seven cars were broken to pieces and one train-hand hurt.

Governor Scales is yet considering the matter of commuting the death sentence of W. A. Potts, of Beaufort county. The superintendents of the three State insane asylums are called as a board of experts to advise the Governor as to the question of Potts's sanity.

OYSTER WAR THREATENED.

There is considerable excitement in the northeastern counties over the continued depredations of Virginia oystermen on the public oyster-beds. Governor scales has written a letter in regard to these trespasses. It is to a prominent resident of that section, and says: "I have communicated the facts to the Governor of Virginia and asked his aid and cooperation in suppressing these outrages. Why, as the trespassers have to pass through the Albemarle and Chesapeake canal, could they not be arrested and bound over to court." If necessary to do this, I will order out the State Guard in sufficient numbers, and make them subject to the local authorities, that they may aid in bringing these fellows to justice. If the trouble can be suppressed without calling the Legislature together, it would be greatly preferable. I could issue a proclamation, but it would do no good without sufficient force behind it, and I think it best to await Governor Lee's answer."

A CYCLONE.

At Laurinburg yesterday evening a cyclone did some damage. It wrecked the colored Baptist church, blew chimneys from the hotel and through the roof, threw a tree upon a cottage, crushing the latter, and injured the crops considerably. Copious rains have fallen at last and fears of a drought are ended.

GATHERED ABOUT THE TOWN.
Of three boys, named Robert Eaton, Mark Dorlon and George Strong, who left Brooklyn a few months ago for Western adventures, only one, Eaton, has returned to his father's house. He reports that Dorlon was lynched for horse-stealing in Arizona, and Strong enlisted in the army to escape starvation. After a long series of adventures Eaton worked his way back to Brooklyn.

There are 450 prisoners in Raymond Street Jail.

The Board of Estimate yesterday voted to appropriate $110,000 from the excise funds to charitable institutions, on the same basis as last year.

An unknown man hanged himself in an ice-wagon under a shed attached to De Castro & Donner's sugar refinery, at the foot of North Third-st., yesterday. He was apparently a German, about thirty-five years old, and commonly clad.

The suit of Nelson King to recover $25,000 as damages for the alienation of his wife's affections by James McLaughlin, the well-known jockey, was set down for trial yesterday in the Supreme Court, but in the absence of some of the plaintiff's witnesses the case went over. Mr. King was formerly a post office employee. He alleges that McLaughlin met his wife at the races, in June, 1885, and captured her affections. The charge is denied by Mrs. King and McLaughlin.

A committee of the alumnae of the Packer Institute recommends that steps be taken to found the Packer College. New buildings, costing $200,000, and an endowment fund of $250,000 are deemed necessary.

The Rev. H. J. Heyser has begun a suit to compel the consistory of the Zion German Church at Smith and Atlantic aves. to pay him $550 of balance of salary and give him a letter of dismissal.

About 200 members of the Kings County Democratic Club propose to attend the inauguration of Governor Hill.

The receipts of the Bridge last week amounted to $19,606 52.

El Paso (Tex), October 2d.—A short time ago a dissolute, wandering dentist, named Martin, having a wife and family at Prescott, went to Fort Hanson, the military post on the Mecalero Apache Reservation in New Mexico. There he chloroformed and outraged a servant girl working on a cattle ranch adjoining the fort. As soon as it became known he hurriedly made his escape, taking a bee line for El Paso, where he intended to cross the Rio Grande into Mexico.

A posse of cowboy soldiers took after him and would have lynched him if caught, but he managed to get into the fastness of the Sacramento mountains, where his pursuers could not follow. Then the fugitive dentist regained heart and concluded he could with safety go back to his family in Arizona, which he did, but the wronged girl's friends determined to see her avenged and sent the Sheriff of Lincoln county to Prescott to arrest him.

His trial came off last week, and resulted in his conviction, and he was sentenced to the Penitentiary for five years. Martin's wife stuck to her worthless spouse during his trouble, and after his conviction a subscription was raised to send her back to her home in Arizona.
