The First National bank of Butte was assessed at $387,520 this year, a large increase, which included the undivided profits; the bank protested, but the board of equalization refused to reduce.

In the Sacramento police court Judge Buckley held George Lang, aged sixty years, on a charge of committing rape on Cora Morris, aged thirteen, and Teresa Rankin, aged nine years. Bail was fixed at $1,000 in each case.

Dr. Harry Lane, superintendent of the Oregon insane asylum, reports 509 patients, and the number still increasing. They are largely foreigners, and he claims that other countries send their insane here to get rid of them.

The White Pine News says: The recent death of Tom Roberts at the county hospital is attributed to his bad luck in winning $15,000 in the Havana lottery. It was too much for his nerves, and he sported and drank himself to death.

Some time ago a dissolute, wandering dentist named Martin, who was married, chloroformed and outraged a servant girl on the Mascalero reservation, New Mexico, and made his escape from a band of lynchers. Lately he was arrested, convicted, and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary.

The Caldwell (Idaho) Tribune says: News come over the telephone that Rev. J. D. Flenner was "fired" bodily out of the Methodist fold by the conference now sitting here, and that Elder Eads is likely to get a healthy impression of the same boot. Flenner was fired for taking liberties with the sisters, unbecoming his cloth. He was tried about a year ago and acquitted, but the prosecution appealed to the conference with the above result. Charges were also brought against Elder Eads, who presided at the former trial, for using his official position to screen Flenner. We understand that a minister or two who served on the jury are also in hot water. The conference seems to be making a clean sweep.

WINDSOR, Mo., June 4.—Three days ago John Owsley was taken suddenly ill, and it was found that rat poison had been given him. The 12-year-old negro servant girl was suspected, but denied the charge. Yesterday Owsley and his wife and four children were taken violently ill, and it was discovered strychnine had been placed in the coffee. The servant again denied that she was guilty, but refused to drink the coffee. She was forced to drink, and died in half an hour. Count Arthur Burchardt's Sweetheart.

Letters found in the pocket of Count Arthur Burchardt who died in the Westchester County Alms House of wounds inflicted on himself while he was violently insane, show that he had been an officer in the German army, and that he had voluntarily resigned. A letter from "Martha" postmarked at Frankfort-on-the Oder, expresses a hope that she will soon be able to join him in the "land of freedom," but another letter from the same person contains these words: "I have found out too late, alas, that you have broken your vows to me. But write me one line, if it is only to say: You love me." Coroner Tice has not been able to find the satchel the Count carried when he left Mr. Shield's boarding house in Mount Vernon, where his insanity first showed itself. Among his letters was a recommendation as to character from Henry Welch, a wholesale grocer of this city. He will be buried by the county.
negro-girl-poisoner-windsor-1888-06.A6:
A YOUNG FIEND'S WORK. Three of a Family Dying and the Poisoner Dead—Spite the Cause.
Clinton, Mo., June 3.—R. N. Ousley, a well-known business man of Windsor, this county, some weeks ago hired a 14-year-old colored girl to do housework and cooking in his family. A short time ago she stole some clothes and sold them to Gypsies. She was chastised, but was not discharged.

This morning the girl's actions were suspicious and soon it was found that there was a queer taste in the breakfast coffee. The fact was mentioned and the girl denied having mixed poison or other ingredients in the coffee. She was told by her mistress to taste the fluid and after doing so ran out of the house and down the street in frantic madness. She was overtaken a mile and a half away and brought back, but died instantly.

It was then discovered that three members of the Ousley family were in a very critical condition, and up to the present they are no better. Medical aid was summoned but it is given out that they can not recover. It was found that the faithless servant had put rough on rats in the coffee.

Poisoned by Jimson Weeds.

Hannibal, Mo., June 4.—Mrs. John Harding yesterday morning went out to pick greens for her Sunday dinner, and, being near sighted, mistook jimson weeds for mustard plants, took them home and cooked them with the greens. She, her husband and her son partook freely of the dish, and were soon thrown into convulsions by the poison, and this morning Harding died. The others will probably recover.

2 WINDSOR, Mo., June 3.—What might have terminated in a fatal poisoning affair was only prevented by the suspicion of one of the victims, but too late to escape a portion of the effects of a dose of Rough on Rats. The particulars are as follows: A few days ago a negro girl employed by R. N. Owsley, a prominent citizen of this city, gave some sugar and a number of other small things to some gypsies. When the articles were missed the gypsies were arrested and the goods recovered. Mr. and Mrs. Owsley corrected the girl, which made her mad. This morning about 8 o'clock at the breakfast table Mr. Owsley became very sick. Mrs. Owsley suspicioned that something was wrong and asked the girl if she hadn't put something in the coffee to make them all sick; to which she replied in the negative, but she refused to drink any of the coffee. Mrs. Owsley accused her of being afraid. She replied that she was not, and drank of the poisoned coffee and ran. Mr. Owsley started in pursuit, but became so sick that he was compelled to give up the chase. He returned to the house.

CHATTANOOGA, TENN., Feb. 25.—This afternoon Oscar Fifer, white, and Matt Whiteside, a mulatto, renewed an old quarrel at Athens, Tenn., when the latter assaulted the former with a knife. Fifer drew a revolver and shot his antagonist through the heart, killing him instantly. Negroes have surrounded the jail where Fifer is confined, and say they will lynch him before morning.

OUTRAGES AGAINST NEGROES.
The White Population Bound to Punish the Perpetrators.
BREAUX BRIDGE, LA., Sept. 16.—An awful crime was perpetrated in this city Friday night, when a gang, supposed to be composed of five members (so far unknown), attacked a negro cabin and, shooting through the walls, mortally wounded a colored woman, who died a few hours afterward. From there they went to another cabin, where they outraged a colored woman and then whipped a colored man. The negroes have made no affidavit as yet. The white population is very much excited over this matter. Last night they held an indignation meeting, 300 whites being present. Resolutions were adopted pledging protection to the colored people, and declaring that the perpetrators of the outrage shall be punished.
sam-polk-named-as-one-of-the-gang-not-a-.A6:
Southern Outrages and Negro Sufferers.
NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 17.—A Picayune special from Breaux Bridge, La., says that on Friday night five unknown men attacked a negro cabin, and shooting through the walls killed a colored woman. At another cabin they outraged a colored woman and whipped a colored man. A mass meeting of 300 white men was held Saturday night to express indignation at the outrages. Resolutions were adopted pledging protection to the colored people and punishment to the perpetrators of the crime.
sam-polk-named-as-one-of-the-gang-not-a-.A8:
A Brutal Crime.
A St. Martiusville special of the 17th inst., to the Times-Democrat, says:

News reached here this morning of one of the most cowardly crimes that ever was committed in this parish. Friday night, at about 11 o'clock, in the vicinity of Breaux Bridge, a gang of four or five parties, some of them so far unknown, whipped a black man, criminally assaulted one black woman and killed another. The particulars gathered from the mother of the dead woman are about as follows:

"On Friday night the gang called at the door of the woman's house and knocked, saying that it was the sheriff. She opened the door and recognized one of the parties, Sam Polk. She shut the door on them. They then fired through the door several shots, one of them taking effect in the woman's abdomen, and she died next morning."

The coroner's inquest revealed the fact that she bore seven months' twins, one of them having the ball through his head. The man Polk was recognized as having engaged in the three crimes. His hat was also found at the door of the cabin. He was not found when search was made for him.

The white people are indignant and very much excited. Warrants have been issued against Polk and three other parties suspected to have participated in the crimes. The white people will see that the colored people are protected and justice done.

Baby Carriages, at Albert's. Double Murder in St. Landry.

An Opelousas special, of the 17th inst., to the N. O. Picayune, says:

"Yesterday morning, at Ville Platte prairie, a crowd of armed men rode to the house of two negroes named Jean Pierre-Salet and Sidairo, and after leading them a short distance, riddled them with buckshot, killing both men instantly. This killing is supposed to have been brought about by the incendiary language recently used by these two negroes. The affair created intense excitement in the neighborhood where it occured.

Princess Letitia Bonaparte, who has just married her uncle, the Duke of Aosta, can amuse herself by calculating the odd relationship which she has entered into. She will be at the same time the daughter and sister-in-law of her own mother; niece and sister-in-law of the King of Italy, and cousin and mother-in-law of the duke's children by his former marriage. She will also be the aunt of Princess Amelia d'Orleans, the present Duchess of Braganza. The duke is not far behind, for he will be the son-in-law of his sister and of his brother-in-law, also brother-in-law of his nephews and nephew of his brother and of his sister.
sam-polk-named-as-one-of-the-gang-not-a-.A10:
Horrible Murder.
The particulars are about as follows: The murderers went to the cabin and called the husband of the woman it is believed to whip him. He being afraid to open the door asked who was there when the reply came that it was the Sheriff. The name of the Sheriff reassured the woman who opened the door and as the moon was shining brightly she recoguized one of the four murderers and slammed the door when she was shot through the belly with a rifle.

The mother of the dead woman says that before she died she made a deposition to Coroner Guilbeau who was immediately called to the bedside of the dying
sam-polk-named-as-one-of-the-gang-not-a-.A11:
woman. The hat of one of the murderers was found near the cabin and was brought here and placed in the hands of the District Attorney. Several persons it is said have recognized the hat.

The husband and mother of the murdered woman came before Justice DeBlanc Monday and made affidavits against a young white man of Breaux Bridge named Sam Polk. The officers and the citizens of Breaux Bridge are after Polk who is in hiding in that vicinity. The following persons were arrested and brought here by Sheriff Gardemal and a posse, who are accused of having participated in the murder: Vil-Hollier, Detour Hollier, Didier Hollier and Numa Boudreau. Vilmont Hollier was about a year and a half ago convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to the penitentiary for five years, but after serving five or six months of his term was pardoned by Gov. McEnery.

The same night of this murder a negro was badly whipped and a negro woman outraged by four or five persons, supposed to be the same gang who committed the murder.
sam-polk-named-as-one-of-the-gang-not-a-.A12:
Preliminary Trial.
The preliminary trial of Vilmont Hollier Didier Hollier Detour Hollier, and Numa Boudreau was begun at 3 o'clock Wednesday evening. Detour Hollier one of the accused was placed on the stand as State witness but nothing could be got out of him, and he was therefore discharged. on Thursday, upon the resolution offered by Senator Chandler, instructing the committee on privileges and elections to inquire into the Lousiana election of April 17, 1888, made prominent the facts that political murders and outrages are being committed in Louisiana and Texas for the purpose of influencing the presidential vote. Senator Chandler, in the course of the debate, said:

"I stated when this resolution was before the Senate on a former occasion that these methods of politics which were resorted to in order to secure a return of 136,746 votes and a majority of 84,753 for Nicholls in Louisiana on the 7th of April were a continuing system; that the same species of intimidation, violence, and murder was being continued in the state of Louisiana as a preparation for the election which is to give the electoral votes of the state of Louisiana to Grover Cleveland. Recent facts justify the assertion which I then made, and, disagreeable as I know it is, painful as I know it is, harshly as I know it grates upon the sensitive and patriotic nerves of the senator from Louisiana to contemplate the fact that in his state to-day black men, Republicans, are being butchered in order that the presidential electoral vote of that state may be cast for Grover Cleveland, yet I conceive it to be my privilege and my duty to bring these facts to the attention of the American Senate, to the attention of the people of New Hampshire, if the senator will have it so, and to the attention of the American people, in order that possibly they may be aroused to the enormity of the wrongs that are being perpetrated upon the humble colored voters in this state of Louisiana upon which the senator has passed such a eulogy."

Mr. Chandler quoted from the New Orleans Picayune of Sept. 17 a despatch from Breaux Bridge, La., stating that on the previous Friday evening a gang of unknown men had murdered one black woman, outraged another, and then whipped a black man; also, a despatch to the same paper from St. Martinsville, La., dated Sept. 17, which stated that an affidavit had been made against Sam Polk, as one of the party who had committed the outrages and that he had fled, and which concluded as follows: "The whipping and bulldozing of negroes is getting to be too frequent, especially by irresponsible parties, who, when banded, are criminally inclined. These outrages will be stopped and at once." A New Orleans despatch to the Washington Post, dated Sept. 16, was also quoted. It gave the particulars of the Breaux Bridge outrages and said: "A mass meeting of three hundred white men was held Saturday night to express indignation at the outrages. Resolutions were adopted pledging protection to the colored people and punishment to the perpetrators
With reference to the latter despatch Mr. Chandler said: "I make the prediction, as I did on a previous occasion, that the indignation will end in resolutions. There will be no indictment and no punishment of the perpetrators of these outrages upon these negroes, the object of which is to affect the approaching presidential election, when the parish of St. Martin is to be converted from a Republican parish into a Democratic parish. In the parish in 1874 there were 1,631 white votes and 1,771 colored votes. The vote returned in 1888 was for Nicholls, 1,107; for Warmoth, 1,624. This is one of the few parishes in which at the last election the Republicans managed to obtain a majority. The decree, however, has gone forth from the Democrats of Louisiana that St. Martin shall not be in the presidential election a Republican parish, but shall cast a majority for Grover Cleveland. The Louisiana Standard of September 22 gives the following account of this Breaux Bridge atrocity.

Democratic Murder—An Epidemic of Assassination—Organized Gangs of Democratic Murderers Making the Killing of Negroes a Pastime—How Louisiana Negroes are Being Reduced to Mexican Peonage—Assassination Items as Told in Democratic Specials—No Politics in It, But the Murderers All Good Democrats.

St. MARTINSVILLE, LA., Sept. 17, 1888.

News reached here this morning of one of the most cowardly crimes that ever was committed in this parish. Friday night, at about 11 o'clock, in the vicinity of Breaux Bridge, a gang of four or five parties, some of them so far unknown, whipped a black man, criminally assaulted one black woman, and killed another.

The particulars gathered from the mother of the dead woman are about as follows: On Friday night the gang called at the door of the woman's house and knocked, saying it was the sheriff. She opened the door and recognized one of the parties. Sam Polk. She shut the door on them. They then fired through the door several shots, one of them taking effect in the woman's abdomen and she died next morning. The coroner's inquest revealed the fact that she bore seven months' twins, one of them having the ball through the head. The man Polk was recognized as having engaged in the three crimes. His hat was also found at the door of the cabin. He was not found when search was made for him."

Extarcts from the Picayune, Times-Democrat, and other Louisiana newspapers were submitted in proof of the charges, that these murders and other crimes were committed in August and September. Later in the debate, Mr. Chandler said in reply to Senator Reagan of Texas:

"The senator from Texas complains there was no averment in the case of the

killing of colored people in Louisiana, which I submitted to the Senate, that they were murdered on account of their politics. If the senator had listened to my remarks he would have understood distinctly that I took the ground that these murders were part of a deliberate system; that whether admitted to be political or not they were in fact such; that these disarmings and assassinations of the Louisiana colored people were for the purpose of creating a state of terror as a preparation for the election in November. The same state of things exists in the state of Texas, and I now submit to the senator from Texas the account which I send to the desk of a recent murder, since the late debate, in the state of Texas, which clearly appears to have been the killing of a Republican because he was a Republican.

CHRIST—A SOLEMN WARNING.
Chattanooga, Tenn., June 13 (Special).—A colored crook, who pretended to be Christ, has thoroughly excited the community at Soddy, a mining town a few miles from here. He says that he fasted forty days. When he appeared at the end of the ordeal, poor white and negro women embraced and kissed him. Outsiders were indignant, and ill-spelled anonymous communications have been sent out among the followers of the alleged Savior, whose real name is Brown, warning them to depart or they will "catch —." The Sheriff and his deputies are already on the ground and it is hoped that serious trouble may be avoided.

The following from the news columns of the Chattanooga Times tell of some very cranky doings of two mischievous cranks one white and one colored-over at Soddv, Tenn:—

Ten days ago A. J. Brown, colored, emerged from the woods above Soddy after having, as he claimed, fasted forty days and nights. G. W. Patterson, a white man, who was in with Brown, had a large crowd gathered to await the appearance of Brown, and when he saw him emerging from the woods half naked announced that he was the real Christ, and many of the ignorant people assembled bowed before him and kissed his hands and begged to be allowed to touch the hem of his garments. The excitement ran so high at the meetings which followed that Sheriff Conner was appealed to for the purpose of mob violence were frequent. The sheriff went to Soddy and after consulting with some of the colored heads, succeeded in putting an end to the meetings and for a week past the excitement.

HAD ABOUT DIED OUT.

Word reached the city yesterday that there was great excitement again. Brown had a large number of hand bills struck, announcing that he was not onle the true Christ, but that he would be crucified to-day to atone for the sins of the whole world. These bills were posted up all over the town and naturally caused much curiosity. What will be the result of the announcement remains to be seen. In the bills Brown does not state whether he will be crucified by his friends or his enemies, but he claims that he will meet his death on the cross.

A WILD STORY.
How a Colored Preacher Is Said To Be About To Precipitate a Bloody Riot.

New York Graphic.

Soddy, Tenn., is a little mountain village, with a church, a school-house and a couple of hundred people, white and black. There is a large colored population within a radius of twenty miles from the place.

For some time past meetings have been held in the neighborhood, by one G. W. Patterson, who claims to be a regular ordained minister. These meetings were of such a nature as to attract quite a number of the more ignorant and excitable among the people, both whites and negroes. One excess led to another until, finally, the moving spirit of the new sect, Patterson, began to warn the people that the second coming of the Saviour was at hand, and that the millennium would soon be ushered in.

Associated with Patterson is a negro named A. J. Brown, who was to be the incarnation of Christ. This doctrine was promulgated and accepted by the society. It was also declared necessary for Brown to go into the wilderness and fast forty days. The negro obeyed this heavenly injunction, but it is claimed that Patterson made daily visits to him. The society, however, was given to understand that no man could look upon his face during his retirement and live. In the meantime Patterson industriously preached the advent of the negro upon whom this transforming miracle was to be wrought, and zealously warned his hearers to make ready. As the day of his appearing approached the enthusiasm and excitement of the society knew no bounda. Last Sunday was the day upon which the forty days' fast was to end. During the preceding week meetings had been held nightly, and spiritual fervor had been wrought to the highest pitch. There was no doubt in the minds of the faithful that the day was to be one of signal victory and divine manifestations. It was said that the Saviour was to come in the likeness of the flesh, but his body was to be a spiritual body with the exception of a girdle about the loins. Another feature of the day was to be the offering up of a human sacrifice. The victim, Lulu McLure, a young girl, had been designated and acquiesced. In short, this was to be the great day for which all other days were made.

Sunday morning broke cold and cheerless. A drizzling rain had set in early in the day, and it looked as if the advent of this Ethiopian Savior was to be a failure. The faithful regarded it as most auspicious, inasmuch as the contrast would be all the more striking and the victory more complete. Thousands of people gathered from all parts of the country. The congregation assembled in the open air, and while waiting Patterson preached upon the glory they were about to behold. Suddenly some one shouted:

"The Savior is coming."

Instantly the faithful rushed up the hill. The women gathered around him, and white and black-alike lavished caresses upon him. Excitement was at fever heat, but the conduct of these women so incensed the publicans and sinners who were in the congregation that they sprang forward, and but for the presence and interference of the deputy sheriffs, who fortunately were present, having been notified of the meeting, Brown and his fanatical followers would have been torn limb from limb. A riot and murder were prevented, but the meeting, of which so much had been expected, broke up in the wildest confusion, while Brown and his coadjutor slipped away from the crowd and strongly barricaded themselves in Patterson's house.

Had the matter ended there perhaps nothing would have been done by the now thoroughly disgusted populace. But after the first spasm of fear had passed, Brown, who now claimed to be no longer Brown, but the Savior, and his followers became more bold, and were preparing to launch forth afresh. But the populace had come to the conclusion not to tolerate these fanatical doings any longer. Letters of warning were posted up, declaring that if, in ten days' time, "Old Man Thurman and family, Buck Thurman and family, Tom Black and family, Arthurs and family, together with Patterson and Brown, have not left the country, their souls will be sent to h—l." The letters bore skulls and cross-bones, while others have a roughly sketched coffin, at the bottom of which is written, "A coffin for you all." Patterson dispatched a letter to Sheriff Connor at Chattanooga imploring protection. The sheriff found that unless the objectionable characters heeded the words of warning bloodshed will follow.

None of the people, so far as known, have left, and it is feared that some of them will even be foolhardy enough to remain. If they do lynching will take place. Any one who is acquainted with the determined character of these orthodox mountaineers knows that they will be as good as their word. The ten days' limit expires today, and Sheriff Connor is holding himself in readiness for any emergency that may arise. If the course of affairs is not checked everything will be ripe for the biggest excitement and sensation this part of the country has ever experienced. Things became so feverish that it was deemed best to immediately dispatch an extra force here, and to-night fifty armed men are on duty, and hundreds of people are astir. A wild rumor prevails that since Sunday two children have been offered in sacrifice. Things are ripe for the bloodiest massacre the South ever knew.
tom-black-soddy-1888-06-24.A7:
WORSHIPED AS A GOD.
A Sacreligious Tennessee Negro Who Says That He Is a New Christ.

Chattanooga Special to Pittsburg Dispatch.

Soddy, a mining village below here, has a sensation that has for the time being paralyzed business, attracted thousands of people and necessitated the presence of an armed force to prevent violence and bloodshed that are imminent. For several months G. W. Patterson, who claims to be a regularly ordained minister, has been holding meetings there. From the first he had a following which grew in fanaticism and numbers. He became bolder and bolder in his preaching, until finally he announced the coming of Christ a second time. A negro named A. J. Brown, a helper of Patterson's, was announced as the one who was to be the incarnation of Christ. Strange to say, there were many believers, and when Brown announced that in order to complete his work he must go into the mountains and fast forty days, enthusiasm knew no bounds. Brown disappeared and, so far as outsiders know, was not in communication with any of his dupes.

Last Sunday was the day fixed for the expiration of the long fast and a vast multitude assembled. A human sacrifice in the person of Allie McLung had been prepared. The day was rainy and gloomy, but the faithful regarded this as a good omen: In the afternoon Brown suddenly appeared and a wonderful scene ensued. Men and women embraced and bowed down to him. His feet were kissed, and sick and lame asked for healing. The proceedings became so sacrilegious that outsiders interfered and a bloody fight followed. Brown and Patterson only escaped death by rushing to the latter's house, where they barricaded themselves. Disorder continued far into the night. Brown's followers claimed only his great goodness prevented him from slaying all his assailants. On Monday letters bearing skull, crossbones and coffin were sent to Patterson, Brown and their leading followers, ordering them to leave the county at once on pain of death. Patterson at once sent to Sheriff Connors for help. The sheriff went on Tuesday and learned that the citizens had determined to drive the fanatics out, and Thursday, the 21st, is fixed as the limit for their stay. The wildest stories are affloat. It is said that Brown has raised one dead person, and it is charged that two human sacrifices have been offered. Excitement reached such a pitch to-day that the sheriff sent fifty armed men there. The prospects are for the biggest and bloodiest tragedy this section has known for years.

upchurch-1888-11-02.A1:
REPUBLICAN OUTRAGES.
A Deputy Marshal Narrowly Escapes Lynching—The State Safe.
Lynching—the State Sale.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch]
SALEIGH, November 3.—At Gibson's St

RALEIGH, November 3.—At Gibson's Station, Richmond county, yesterday a United States deputy marshal from Raleigh, named Upchurch, attempted to arrest W. F. Gibson, the registrar of election. Upchurch was sent there by A. N. Shaffer, of Raleigh, who is a United States commissioner. Upchurch could not show the authority for the warrant, and so instead of arresting Gibson he was himself taken in custody. The people are furiously angry at this radical outrage. Upchurch wants to get out of that section as quick as possible.

To-night Deputy Upchurch arrived here. He said that he was in danger of lynching all day yesterday. He was only saved from five hundred infurished people by the speeches and appeals to the crowd made by Gibson, the man whom he was sent to arrest, and also Gibson's brother and others. There were three hundred South Carolinians who had come over to help hang Upchurch. The latter was last night driven in an ambulance to Laurinburg, and thence came here. People in all that section—men, women, and children—are wrought up to the highest pitch of indignation. Upchurch says Gibson is to appear before the United States Commissioner at Laurinburg. It was evidently the purpose of Shaffer, who is chief supervisor, to have Gibson brought to Raleigh to be tried before him. To-day Democratic Chairman Spier Whitaker met Shaffer and told him that he would join with him in sending a telegram to Upchurch to notify Gibson to appear before the nearest commissioner. Shaffer would get agree to do this, saying he first wanted to know what had become of Upchurch. Gibson could not have been brought here.

This afternoon J. C. Crawford, who was the head of Radical-Chairman Eaves's detective force in North Carolina, and had been stopping at the Yarboro' House here three weeks, fled from the city in company with one Bedell, his assistant. They were followed by Democratic detectives as they went to Greensboro'. They bought tickets for Richmond. To night a telegram was received saying that one of the Republican detectives had been arrested at Henderson and was held there in custody. He gave his residence as New York, but no such man can be found in the directory of that city. Another man named William Powelson has been at Rocky Mount, and yet another named W. H. Genet at Weldon. It is believed that both these men skipped to-day. All these men were steadily watched and were badly frightened. Only the personal efforts of Chairman Whitaker saved them from attack while in the State.

Judge Fowle arrived here this afternoon from the East.

Oliver H. Dockery and Judge Russell spoke here to-night.

Another Republican outrage is reported in Richmond county. Two men went to the house of a registrar of election at night while he was absent and asked his wife to let them have the registration-books. She refused to give them up. The men were very abusive and threatened her. Her husband soon returned and followed the men. One of the latter showed fight and tried to draw his pistol, but the registrar was too quick for him and shot him. The plucky registrar then pursued the other fellow and made him get on his knees and beg pardon for the insulting language addressed to the registrar's wife.

There will now certainly be a heavy vote in this State. Two weeks ago this was not believed possible, but there has been a great change, thanks to the outrageous conduct of the Republicans. It is estimated now by some of the best informed Democrats that Fowle's majority (and Cleveland's also) will not be less than 20,000. This gives the Republicans 130,000, the Democrats 150,000 to 160,000, and the Third party 5,000. This gives the Republicans the largest vote they have ever polled.
upchurch-1888-11-02.A2:
A HIGH-HANDED MEASURE.
United States Commissioner Shaffer has a Democratic Registrar Arrested.
Raleigh News-Observer, 3d.

A gentleman who came to this city last night on the train from Hamlet, brought intelligence of a very outragous and unwarranted proceeding yesterday at Gibson's Station

United States Commissioner Shaffer yesterday sent Deputy Upchurch to Gibson's with a warrant for the arrest of W. F. Gibson, registrar at that place. On his arrival there he attempted to serve the warrant but Mr. Gibson and his friends demanded him to show the authority upon which the warrant was based which he failed to do. Upon failing to produce sufficient authority Upchurch prepared to return to this city without arresting Mr. Gibson but the latter insisted that he should either show sufficient cause for attempting to arrest him and unless he did he should not return. The result is Upchurch is still at Gibson's beaten at his own game and does not know what to do.

The attempt to arrest Mr. Gibson was utterly unwarranted as is proven by the very fact that Upchurch himself offers to leave Mr. Gibson unmolested and returned home. It is an infamous and high-handed Radical outrage and shows to what villainy they propose to resort in the election. They will find that such violent interference with honest men will recoil on their own heads in a rebuke which will not soon be forgotten.

There was the most intense indignation at Gibson's yesterday when the train passed through. Mr. Gibson, it is learned, was reported to Commissioner Shaffer by Deputy Sheriff Cameron, of Kichmond county, in which county Gibson's station is situated.
upchurch-1888-11-02.A3:
IT WAS RIGHT FUNNY. United States Deputy Marshal Upchurch, of Raleigh, passed through this place yesterday with a warrant for the arrest of Mr. William F. Gibson, the Registrar for Williamson's township, for the neglect of duty. He will be taken to Raleigh for examination — [Rockingham Spirit of the South, Radical organ, Nov. 3rd THE SEQUEL.
Mr. Upchurch went to Gibson's Station and spent a day or two there. The Chronicle's Extra, published last Saturday, gave the people the information that Mr. Gibson declined to be arrested. The Gibsons kept Mr. Upchurch a day or two and told him that he should not leave until he could show probable cause for attempting the arrest.

Mr. Upchurch went to arrest Mr. Gibson. The Spirit of the South says "he will be taken to Raleigh for examination." Mr. Upchurch says he was never scared so near to death in his life and that he was glad to escape with his life.

It was a funny case of "the biter getting bit."

"Some guns there are that so contrive it. To miss their game what e'er they aim at. And whether charged for duck or plover Fly back and kick their owner over."

A GENTLEMAN tells the Chronicle that Dockery got on the train at Cameron yesterday morning and looked very "glum," having nothing to say to anybody. We also hear that he says that the attempt to arrest Gibson by his Radical friends was a great mistake, and lost his party hundreds of votes.

Now, this time Col. Dockery is right. The result on Tuesday proved beyond question that you cannot bull-doze North Carolina Democrats by threats or Pinkerton detectives.
